sections.text: (7) Geometric Tolerances
In design, the axis of the inner bore of the cylinder body (tube) is generally determined as the datum element.
1) Circularity of Inner Bore

The circularity of the inner bore of the cylinder body (tube) is divided into four grades, and its tolerance value is expressed as a percentage less than the inner diameter tolerance value. The corresponding relationships are as follows: Grade A—50%; Grade B—60%; Grade C—70%; Grade D—80% (generally not recommended for selection). Alternatively, the circularity tolerance of the inner bore of the cylinder body (tube) may be required to be no less than Grade 8 (or Grade 7) specified in GB/T 1184-1996, and the circularity tolerance value can be found in Table 2-31.
2) Straightness of Inner Bore Axis

The straightness of the inner bore axis of the cylinder tube is divided into four grades: Grade A—0.06/1000; Grade B—0.20/1000; Grade C—0.50/1000; Grade D—1.00/1000 (generally not recommended for selection). The corresponding values can be found in Table 2-31.
Note: 0.06/1000 means that the straightness tolerance for a length of 1000 mm is 0.06 mm, and so on.
3) Straightness of Surface Element Line of Inner Bore

Alternatively, the straightness tolerance for any 100 mm length of the surface element line of the inner bore of the cylinder may be required to be no less than Grade 7 (or Grade 6) specified in GB/T 1184-1996, and the straightness tolerance value can be found in Table 2-31.
4) Parallelism of Inner Bore Surface Relative to Element Line

The cylindricity error of the inner bore consists of the circularity of the inner bore, the straightness of the inner bore axis, and the parallelism of the inner bore surface relative to the element line. The parallelism tolerance of the inner bore surface element line should be no less than Grade 8 (or Grade 7) specified in GB/T 1184-1996, and the corresponding value can be found in Table 2-31.
5) Cylindricity of Inner Bore

Depending on the functional requirements, the cylindricity tolerance value of the inner bore of the cylinder may be specified separately, especially when the cylindricity tolerance value is required to be less than the combined result of its components. The cylindricity tolerance of the inner bore of the cylinder should be no less than Grade 8 (or Grade 7) specified in GB/T 1184-1996, and the corresponding value can be found in Table 2-31.

6) Perpendicularity of Cylinder Body (Tube) End Face The two end faces of the cylinder body (tube) should be perpendicular to the axis (centerline) of the inner bore. The perpendicularity tolerance of the flange end face of the cylinder body to the axis of the inner bore should be no less than Grade 7 (or Grade 6) specified in GB/T 1184-1996; the axial circular runout tolerance of the flange end face of the cylinder body should be no less than Grade 8 (or Grade 7) specified in GB/T 1184-1996. The corresponding values can be found in Table 2-31.

7) Perpendicularity and Position of Trunnion When there is a fixed trunnion on the cylinder body (tube) (at the front end, middle, or rear end), the perpendicularity tolerance of the centerline of the trunnion to the centerline of the cylinder body should be no less than Grade 9 (or Grade 8) specified in GB/T 1184-1996; the distance between the centerline of the trunnion and the centerline of the cylinder body should not be greater than 0.03 mm.
8) When the cylinder body (tube) is connected to the cylinder bottom (head) or end cap using threads, a fine-pitch ordinary thread M with Grade 6 precision should be selected.

9) If the electro-hydraulic servo valve mounting base is set on the cylinder body, the mounting surface of the electro-hydraulic servo valve should comply with the technical requirements of the electro-hydraulic servo valve, and under the specified torque of the mounting screws for the electro-hydraulic servo valve, the deformation of the cylinder body should not exceed the allowable value.

10) If the oil passage block (such as the hydraulic protection module) is installed on the cylinder body, the mounting surface of the oil passage block should comply with the relevant standard specifications, and under the specified torque of the mounting screws, the deformation of the cylinder body should not exceed the allowable value.

Note: 1. For hydraulic cylinders used in hydraulic presses, some standards stipulate that the locking nut of the hydraulic cylinder and the fixed joint surface of the (upper) crossbeam, as well as the flange shoulder of the hydraulic cylinder and the (upper) crossbeam, should fit tightly.
2. The tolerance grades in parentheses are mainly for servo hydraulic cylinders, and specific references can be found in reference [118].
3. For more stringent geometric tolerances of the cylinder body, see Section 4.4.3 Six-High Cold Rolling Mill for Strip Steel.
2.4.5  Mechanical Properties
The mechanical properties of a cylinder tube completely manufactured by machining should not be lower than the mechanical property requirements specified in the standard for the material used.

The mechanical properties of cold-drawn cylinder tubes are influenced by the material and processing technology, and the mechanical properties of the material are determined by mutual agreement between the supplier and the demander.
The mechanical properties, process properties, etc. of steel pipes with steel grades 45, 25Mn, Q355B(C,D), 27SiMn, etc. shall be in accordance with the provisions of GB/T 32957-2015.
2.4.6  Surface Quality
(1) Inner Bore Surface
1) The surface roughness value of the inner bore surface is generally not greater than Ra0.4μm, and can also be selected from Table 2-32 according to design requirements.

sections.caption: Table 2-31 Geometric Tolerance Values (Excerpted from GB/T 1182—2018, GB/T 1184—1996)

sections.text: Note: The parallelism of the inner bore surface to the generatrix is line-to-line parallelism, with the datum line being another generatrix relative to the tested one.

2) The inner bore surface should be smooth, without any visually detectable defects such as shrinkage cavities, inclusions (slag), white spots, waviness, scratches, nicks, dents, pits, cracks, scabs, laminations, or corrosion.

sections.caption: Table 2-32 Surface Roughness Values for Inner Bore Surfaces (Unit: μm)

sections.text: (2) External Surface

The external surface should not have any visually detectable defects such as shrinkage cavities, inclusions (slag), folds, waviness, cracks, scratches, nicks, or cold-drawing marks caused by built-up edge on the external die.
Sharp edges on the cylinder barrel, except for the edges of sealing grooves and valve ports, which are not shown in the working drawing, should be removed.

The external surface of the cylinder barrel should be treated with anti-rust treatment, or a coating layer, passivation layer, or paint layer may be used for corrosion protection. Before painting, the external surface should be free of oxide scale and rust pits. When painting, apply anti-rust paint first, then the topcoat. The paint layer should not have any defects such as nodules.

For hydraulic cylinders with requirements for moisture resistance, heat resistance, salt spray resistance, and mildew resistance, the relevant standards (including test methods) and required levels should be clearly specified in the technical requirements of the cylinder barrel, along with specific methods or measures, such as the type of paint (including the designated manufacturer) and operating procedures.
2.4.7 Density
For cylinder barrels made of forgings, 100% ultrasonic testing should be conducted; after non-destructive testing, the cylinder barrel should meet Class I requirements specified in NB/T 47013.3.

156.page_header: Chapter 2  Design of Hydraulic Cylinders and Basic Components  145

sections.text: Welded seams between the bottom (head) and cylinder body shall be inspected 100% using the method specified in GB/T 5777, and the quality shall meet the Class I requirements specified in NB/T 47013.3.

For airtightness test, eddy current testing shall be performed according to the Class A acceptance level specified in GB/T 7735-2004, or magnetic particle testing shall be performed according to the Class L4 acceptance level specified in GB/T 12606.
Under the action of pressure test pressure, no leakage shall occur on the outer surface of the cylinder (tube) or at the welded seams.
For the definition of the term "leakage," please refer to standards such as GB/T 241-2007 "Metal Pipe Hydraulic Test Method," or refer to Section 1.3.2.
2.4.8  Other Requirements

1) Currently, thick steel plates can be rolled into a tubular shape, welded, inspected, and annealed to serve as a cylinder blank, or cold-drawn high-frequency welded pipes can be used for hydraulic cylinder tubes.

2) The chamfer for installing seals shall be determined according to the requirements of the selected seals, but the junction with the inner bore must be rounded. When installing seals, grooves, keyways, flow channels, and other junctions that require processing shall be rounded or chamfered, and burrs shall be removed.

3) Generally, the finishing process of the cylinder (tube) should be compatible with the sealing material of the seals (rings); after honing the inner bore of the cylinder (tube), it is advisable to polish it; rolling the bore, including the combined boring-scraping-rolling (scraping rolling) process using two or three cutting tools, the inner bore of the cylinder tube can also be polished.

Scraping rolling, depending on the tool combination type, can be three-combination or two-combination, and depending on the number of scraping edges, can be three-edge or two-edge. Further reference can be made to the article "Scraping Rolling Technology for Inner Hole Processing of Hydraulic Cylinders" by Jiang Hua (Journal of Manufacturing Technology, Issue 5, 2019).

4) The inner bore of the cylinder (tube) can also undergo surface treatment, including hard chromium plating, but it must be polished or ground after plating. Further reference can be made to relevant content in Chapter 6.

Note: 1. In YB/T 017-2017, it is stipulated that the inner wall of the hydraulic cylinder and the outer surface of the piston rod should be hard chromium plated, with a plating thickness of 0.03～0.05 mm.

2. In JB/T 13566-2018, it is stipulated that the inner wall of the hydraulic cylinder should be hard chromium plated, with a smooth surface, and the hardness should not be lower than 60 HRC, and the plating thickness should not be less than 0.08 mm.

5) Conduct sampling inspection and record the magnetism of the cylinder (tube), and demagnetize it to below 12 Gs (Gauss, 1 Gs=10⁻⁴T) when necessary. Other components that constitute the wet volume of the hydraulic cylinder cavity should also be treated the same.
6) When necessary, the strength and stiffness of the cylinder (tube) should be checked and calculated.

Taking the hydraulic cylinder for hydraulic presses as an example, the cylinder body of a hydraulic cylinder for hydraulic presses is generally a cylindrical part with one end open and one end closed. The structure of the cylinder body generally includes three parts: the bottom, flange, and intermediate thick-walled cylinder (cylinder tube).
The hydraulic cylinder of a hydraulic press bears a large load and operates frequently, and is prone to premature damage due to improper design, manufacturing, or use.

① Stress analysis of the cylinder body. When the hydraulic cylinder is working, high-pressure working medium enters the cylinder body and acts on the piston or piston rod, while the reaction force acts on the bottom of the cylinder and is transmitted to the flange through the cylinder tube (wall). The supporting reaction force on the supporting surface of the crossbeam is used to balance it.
The stress condition of the cylinder body can be analyzed from three aspects: the bottom, flange, and intermediate thick-walled cylinder (cylinder tube).

Both theoretical analysis and stress testing have shown that only in the middle section of the cylinder tube, which is 0.75D₁ away from the upper surface of the flange (supporting surface with transitional arc end) and the inner surface of the bottom (with transitional arc), i.e., the so-called intermediate cylinder, can it be calculated for strength as a thick-walled cylinder. The other two sections (parts) cannot be calculated using the general thick-walled cylinder formula due to the influence of the bending moments of the bottom and flange.

The stress analysis of the bottom also has the same problem. If calculated according to the elastic mechanics formula for a circular thin plate with fixed periphery under uniformly distributed load, without considering the actual role and influence of the cylinder wall and the stress concentration in the transitional arc area, the calculated stress may be much lower than the actual stress. Reference [36] proposes a ring-shell coupling solution, which analyzes the bottom, cylinder wall, and flange as a connected whole, and also considers the change in the cross-section of the transitional area. Therefore, the calculated result of the bottom thickness may be closer to the actual value.
If the finite element method is used to analyze and calculate the bottom, the result will be more accurate.

② Strength and deformation calculation of the cylinder tube. For the hydraulic cylinder with front-end round flange or front-end boss installation type, the middle section of the cylinder tube made of low-carbon steel, non-hardened medium-carbon steel, and annealed ductile iron, etc., can be calculated for strength using the von Mises strength criterion according to the theory of elastic mechanics, i.e., the fourth strength theory strength condition. The maximum equivalent stress on the inner wall of the cylinder and the strength condition are:
σₘₐₓ = (√3 R₁²)/(R₁² - R²) p ≤ [σ]  (2-40)
When the inner diameter D of the cylinder and the allowable stress [σ] of the material are known, the outer diameter D₁ of the cylinder tube is derived as:

Where: D—inner diameter of the cylinder, D = 2R; D₁—outer diameter of the cylinder tube, D₁ = 2R₁; [σ]—allowable stress of the material, [σ] = σₛ/nₛ, where nₛ is the safety factor, which can be taken as 2～2.5;
p—pressure test pressure of the hydraulic cylinder.
For the hydraulic cylinder with rear-end round flange installation type, the maximum equivalent stress on the inner wall of the cylinder and the strength condition are:
σₘₐₓ = (√3R₁² + R⁴)/(R₁² - R²) p ≤ [σ]  (2-42)

Under the action of the working medium pressure p in the cylinder, the radial displacement value u₁ of the outer surface of the middle section of the cylinder barrel, that is, the radial (single-sided) expansion amount is:
u₁ = -3μR₂²R₁²p / E(R₁² - R₂²)

Where: μ—Poisson's ratio of the cylinder barrel material; E—elastic modulus of the cylinder barrel material; other symbols are the same as above. JB/T 12098–2014 and JB/T 12099–2014 stipulate that the booster cylinder should undergo ultrasonic testing, and maintain pressure for 3 minutes under the test pressure of 1.1 times the maximum working pressure. There should be no leakage, and the deformation amount of the cylinder barrel should be less than the specified value of H8 at the measured value of the middle section of the outer diameter. GB 25974.2–2010 stipulates that columns (including extended sections) and supporting hydraulic jacks should not fail when subjected to a static load of 1.5 times the rated force and a mechanical impact dynamic load reaching 1.5 times the rated working pressure, and the residual expansion deformation of the cylinder barrel should be less than 0.02% of the cylinder diameter.

7) From equation (1-2) δ₀ ≥ D/2 × (√([σ]/[σ] - 3/pₘₐₓ) - 1) it can be concluded that when pₘₐₓ = [σ]/3, δ₀ = ∞. If the allowable stress [σ] of the material is less than 3p, the strength condition cannot be guaranteed. Therefore, when the nominal pressure is too high, simply increasing the wall thickness of the cylinder body may not necessarily ensure sufficient strength of the hydraulic cylinder, and other measures must be taken, such as using a combined cylinder barrel or a wire-wound prestressed structure.
8) In the design of single-layer (non-prestressed structure) cylinder body hydraulic cylinders, the most reasonable relationship between various (basic) parameters is shown in the following formulas.

items: Nominal force: F = (1/4)πD²p
Outer diameter of the cylinder barrel: D₁ = √2 D
Nominal pressure: p = (1/(2√3))[σ]
Another expression for the nominal force is: F = (1/4)πD²p = (1/4)πD² × (1/(2√3))[σ] = (√3/8)πD²[σ]

sections.text: Considering factors such as the safety of the hydraulic cylinder, the highest rated pressure of the actually designed hydraulic cylinder should not be higher than (1/(2√3))[σ], generally it is advisable to take (0.7–0.8)p.

Note: "Nominal force" is a term stipulated in forging machinery (hydraulic press), which is borrowed here; for hydraulic cylinders, "theoretical output force of the cylinder" is more similar in meaning.
2.5 Design of Hydraulic Cylinder Piston

In GB/T 17446–2012, the term piston is defined, that is, a cylinder part that moves in the cylinder bore under the action of fluid pressure and transmits mechanical force and motion. Usually, the piston is matched with the cylinder bore through sealing components, and divides the cylinder bore into two chambers. Author's note: The definition of piston given in JB/T 4174–2014 is: composed of a piston head and a piston rod, which transmits hydraulic energy during movement, and the piston head is matched with the cylinder bore through sealing to divide the cylinder bore into two chambers. Comparing the above two standards, the problem is not only that the industry standard issued and implemented later is inconsistent with the national standard issued and implemented earlier, but also that the "piston" defined in JB/T 4174–2014 itself is not quite reasonable.
2.5.1 Structural Type

The hydraulic cylinder piston should have sufficient strength and guiding length (or sealing length). For pistons that need to be welded to the piston rod, the material should have good weldability. According to the structural type of the sealing groove on the piston, it is decided whether the piston adopts an integral or combined structure. The sealing system of the piston (combination of sealing, guiding and other components) or gap sealing should be reasonable, reliable, and have a long service life; the connection between the piston and the piston rod must have a reliable connection structure (including locking measures), sufficient connection strength, and be convenient for assembly and disassembly. The piston has two structures: integral and combined. Pistons using V-rings and other seals are of combined structure. The combined type is also called assembled type in GB 2880–1981 "Dimension Series and Tolerances for Narrow-Section Dynamic Sealing Grooves of Hydraulic Cylinder Pistons and Piston Rods". Various structural types of pistons can be found in Section 4.9 of the Hydraulic Cylinder Design and Selection Reference Drawings. Pistons of the same model produced by the same manufacturer must have interchangeability. During the design process, the piston should be given remanufacturability, that is, the piston should have inherent remanufacturability.
2.5.2 Materials
Except for the piston and piston rod being of the same integral structure material, other commonly used materials for manufacturing pistons are as follows:

items: Carbon structural steel grades: Q235, Q275.
High-quality carbon structural steel grades: 20, 30, 35, 45.
Alloy structural steel grade: 40Cr.
Low-alloy high-strength structural steel grade: Q355B(C,D).
Gray cast iron grades: HT200, HT225, HT250, HT275, HT300, HT350.
Nodular cast iron grades: QT400-15, QT400-18, QT450-10.
Compacted graphite iron grade: RuT300.

158.page_header: Chapter 2  Design of Hydraulic Cylinders and Basic Components  147

sections.text: ● Others include deformed aluminum and aluminum alloys, bimetallic materials, composite materials, plastics, etc.

The commonly used materials for hydraulic cylinder pistons given in reference [115] are: wear-resistant cast iron, gray cast iron (HT300, HT350), steel (some with wear-resistant rings made of nylon 66, nylon 1010, or cloth-phenolic plastic on the outer diameter), and aluminum alloys. After checking, there is no standard named "wear-resistant cast iron" in the current national standards, or it should refer to JB/T 11843—2014 "Wear-resistant spheroidal graphite cast iron parts".

Piston materials generally use 35 or 45 high-quality carbon structural steel, and some also use cast iron and aluminum alloys. More specifically, they can be divided as follows: Pistons without support rings (guide rings) can use gray cast iron HT200-350 or ductile iron, aluminum alloys, plastics, etc. Pistons with support rings (guide rings) can use 20, 35, 45, or 40Cr steel, etc. According to actual conditions or if there are no special requirements, medium carbon steel generally does not require heat treatment, but excluding heat treatment aimed at stress relief.

When conducting hydraulic cylinder pressure test, the piston should not produce permanent deformation, including crushing. No failure modes specified in JB/T 5924—1991 "Test methods for rated fatigue pressure and rated static pressure of hydraulic component pressure cavities" (already abolished) should appear in the tested pressure cavity under rated static pressure.

The bonding strength between bearing alloy material and steel backing in bimetal should meet design requirements. The yield strength of piston material for large hydraulic cylinders should not be lower than 280 MPa. For piston materials with H8/f8 or H9/f9 fit between cylinder bore and piston outer diameter, or even smaller clearance fits (or piston materials in direct contact with steel cylinder), steel should not be used.

Note: The term "crushing" not only has the meaning defined in GB/T 17446, but also in the above applications refers to the failure (mode) caused by extrusion stress between contact surfaces of parts, but different from the failure mode of high-pair mechanisms due to extrusion stress. The meaning of "crushing" in the following text of this manual is the same.
2.5.3  Heat Treatment

quenched and tempered steel pistons should be quenched and tempered; quenched and tempered steel pistons with an integrated structure with piston rod should be quenched and tempered together with the piston rod. Pistons welded to piston rods should use heat treatment or other methods to reduce stress to eliminate internal stress. CB/T 3812—2013 "Hydraulic Cylinders for Ship Hatch Covers" stipulates in 4.2 that piston material should use 45 steel with tempering treatment.
2.5.4  Geometric Dimensions and Geometric Tolerances
In design, the piston inner hole axis (or piston rod axis) is generally determined as the datum feature.

(1) Basic Dimensions. The basic dimensions of the piston include piston (nominal) outer diameter, piston mating outer diameter, piston thickness, sealing, guiding, and connection dimensions. (2) Piston (Nominal) Outer Diameter. 1) The piston (nominal) outer diameter should preferentially select the recommended dimensions in Table 2-33.

sections.caption: Table 2-33  Recommended Dimensions for Piston (Nominal) Outer Diameter (Unit: mm)

sections.text: Note: Values in parentheses are non-preferred.

2) The dimensional tolerance of the outer diameter of pistons that slide directly on the inner surface of the cylinder body (tube) should adopt f8 or f9 (or f6 or f7) specified in GB/T 1801—2009, with the fit selected as H9/f8 (H8/f8), H9/f9 (or H7/f6 or H8/f7). For piston outer diameter with clearance seal, the dimensional tolerance can adopt h6, h7, or h8 specified in GB/T 1801—2009, but the designed clearance seal clearance should be ensured through selective assembly.

3) Standard-specified piston mating outer diameter. In GB/T 6577—1986 "Types, dimensions, and tolerances of sealing grooves with support rings for hydraulic cylinder pistons", the dimensions of piston (nominal) outer diameter D and piston mating outer diameter D₁ are shown in Table 2-34.

sections.caption: Table 2-34  Dimensions of Piston Mating Outer Diameter (Excerpted from GB/T 6577—1986) (Unit: mm)

sections.text: Note: 1. Values in parentheses are non-preferred. 2. The dimension D in the table is equal to the dimension of the sealing groove outer diameter (cylinder bore) in the standard; the dimension D₁ is equal to the dimension of the piston mating diameter in the standard.
4) Piston outer diameter

The dimensions, dimensional tolerances, geometric tolerances, surface roughness, etc. of the piston outer diameter shall be selected according to relevant standards and the selected sealing type and requirements of sealing components.
(3) Piston thickness

The piston thickness is determined by the guide length and sealing structure (sealing system), generally 0.6-1.0 times the (nominal) outer diameter of the piston. The thickness of the piston for clearance seal should meet the design requirements.
(4) Circularity tolerance

For pistons with H7/f6 or H8/f7 fit, the circularity tolerance of the outer surface shall be Grade 6 as specified in GB/T 1184-1996; for pistons with H8/f8 or H9/f9 fit, the circularity tolerance of the outer surface shall be Grade 7 as specified in GB/T 1184-1996.
(5) Cylindricity tolerance

For pistons with H7/f6 or H8/f7 fit, the cylindricity tolerance of the outer surface shall be Grade 6 or 7 as specified in GB/T 1184-1996; for pistons with H8/f8 or H9/f9 fit, the cylindricity tolerance of the outer surface shall be Grade 8 as specified in GB/T 1184-1996.
(6) Concentricity tolerance

The concentricity tolerance of the piston outer surface to the inner bore axis (or piston rod axis) shall not be lower than Grade 8 as specified in GB/T 1184-1996; for pistons with H7/f6 or H8/f7 fit, the concentricity tolerance of the outer surface to the inner bore axis (or piston rod axis) shall be Grade 6 as specified in GB/T 1184-1996; for pistons with H8/f8 or H9/f9 fit, the concentricity tolerance of the outer surface to the inner bore axis (or piston rod axis) shall be Grade 7 as specified in GB/T 1184-1996.
(7) Perpendicularity tolerance

The perpendicularity tolerance of the piston end face to the axis shall not be lower than Grade 7 (or Grade 6) as specified in GB/T 1184-1996; the radial circular runout tolerance of the piston end face to the axis shall not be lower than Grade 8 (or Grade 7) as specified in GB/T 1184-1996.
Note: The tolerance grades in parentheses are mainly for servo hydraulic cylinders, and can be referred to Reference [118].
2.5.5 Surface quality
(1) Outer surface

1) For pistons with H8/f8 or H9/f9 fit, the surface roughness value of the outer surface is generally not greater than Ra0.8μm, and can also be selected from Table 2-35 according to design requirements.

2) The outer surface should not have visually detectable defects such as shrinkage cavities, inclusions (slag), white spots, ripples, scratches, bumps, pits, cracks, scabs, peeling and rust, etc. The sharp edges on the piston, except for the edges of the sealing groove or valve port, which are not shown on the working drawing, should be removed.

sections.caption: Table 2-35 Surface roughness values of piston outer surface (Unit: μm)

sections.text: (2) End face

The surface roughness value of the piston end face is generally not greater than Ra3.2μm, and can also be selected from Table 2-35 according to design requirements. However, the end face used as the inspection datum, its surface roughness value should generally not be greater than Ra0.8μm.
2.6 Design of hydraulic cylinder piston rod

GB/T 17446-2012 defines the term piston rod, i.e. the cylinder part that is coaxial with and integrated with the piston, transmitting mechanical force and motion from the piston. In a plunger cylinder, since there is no piston, the hydraulic oil pressure directly acts on the piston rod, so defining the piston rod as the cylinder part that transmits mechanical force and motion is more accurate.
2.6.1 General principles

The hydraulic cylinder piston rod should have sufficient strength, stiffness and impact toughness. For combined (hollow or welded piston and piston rod) piston rods that need to be welded, the material should have good weldability, and the strength of the weld seam should not be lower than the strength index of the base material, and the weld quality should reach Grade II as specified in GB/T 3323.

The connection between the piston rod and piston must have a reliable connection structure (including locking measures), sufficient connection strength, and be convenient for disassembly (such as when the piston and piston rod are detachable).
The piston rod and the buffer plunger in the fixed buffer device are preferably made into one piece.
The structural design of the piston rod must be beneficial to improve its bending strength and stability under pressure.

For piston rods with external threads or internal threads at the end, suitable standard wrench flats should be provided. When the piston rod is too small to set the specified flats, they can be omitted.

When welding combined closed hollow piston rods, ventilation holes must be reserved at the outer connection end of the piston rod. For open hollow piston rods, the increase of the hydraulic cylinder internal cavity wet volume should be avoided.
Various structural types of piston rods can be found in Section 4.9 Hydraulic Cylinder Design and Selection Reference Drawings.
Piston rods of the same model of hydraulic cylinders produced by the same manufacturer must have interchangeability.
During the design process, the piston rod should be given remanufacturing properties, i.e. the piston rod should have inherent remanufacturing properties.
2.6.2 Structural types

Piston rods that are coaxial with and integrated with the piston, or piston rods without pistons, can be solid or hollow. However, hollow piston rods should not be made open towards the cylinder bottom side, as that would form too large a rodless cavity wet volume.

160.page_header: Chapter 2  Design of Hydraulic Cylinders and Basic Components  149

sections.text: An excessively large internal cavity volume is generally harmful. Regardless of whether it may affect the inherent frequency of the hydraulic system, hydraulic (spring) stiffness, (step and/or frequency) response characteristics, etc., when the pressurization ends, the elastic potential energy stored in the liquid inside the cylinder may be too large, and when the pressure is released, it may also cause severe vibration of the hydraulic machinery and pipelines.

There may also be a boss at the end of the piston rod in the plunger cylinder, which is used to limit the stroke of the cylinder by abutting against the inner end face of the guide sleeve with this boss shoulder and prevent the piston rod from coming out (shooting out). This boss can also be called the piston rod head, and such a piston rod can also be called a piston rod with a piston rod head.

Some piston rods are designed with a buffer plunger at the end, which is used to slow down the return speed of the piston (rod) at the bottom of the cylinder to prevent the piston from severely impacting the bottom of the cylinder. The end of the piston rod with external threads for connecting to a flange has a thread on the piston rod that is often designed to only transmit the cylinder return force and cylinder return motion. Therefore, the thread on the piston rod may not comply with the provisions of GB 2350-1980 "Thread Types and Dimension Series for Hydraulic and Pneumatic Systems and Components", and its thread length may be shorter.
2.6.3 Materials

The mechanical properties of the material used to manufacture the piston rod, ReL (lower yield strength), should generally not be lower than 280 MPa. For piston rods with chromium coating, the tensile strength of its body should be greater than or equal to 375 MPa. The commonly used materials for manufacturing piston rods are as follows.

items: High-quality carbon structural steel grades: 35, 45, 50.
Alloy structural steel grades: 27SiMn, 30CrMo, 30CrMnSiA, 35CrMo, 38CrMoAl, 40Cr, 42CrMo.
Low-alloy high-strength structural steel grades: Q355B(C, D), Q355E.
Stainless steel grades: 20Cr13, 06Cr9Ni10 (304), 06Cr17Ni12-Mo2 (316), 12Cr18Ni9, 14Cr17Ni2.
Cast carbon steel grades: ZG270-500, ZG310-570.
Others, such as deformed aluminum and aluminum alloys (aluminum alloy forgings), machined bronze, malleable cast iron, chilled cast iron, etc.

sections.text: Piston rods are generally made of high-quality carbon structural steel 45 or 50, using forging or casting methods; for large-sized piston rods, there are also those made by forging or casting in sections and then welding them with electroslag welding; small piston rods are also made of chilled cast iron.

Now there are piston rods made of alloy structural steel, such as 42CrMo steel, used in hydraulic cylinders for hydraulic presses. For piston rods working under corrosive conditions, stainless steel is mostly used, and stainless steel can also be deposited on the surface of the piston rod.

Special attention should be paid to the detailed requirements of the hydraulic press (machine) for the hydraulic cylinders it uses, such as those stipulated in JB/T12510: "The plunger of the working cylinder is generally made of an integral forging of carbon structural steel specified in JB/T6397, and can also be manufactured by the method of welding split forgings, and should be subjected to corresponding heat treatment. The chemical composition and mechanical properties of the material should comply with the provisions of the selected material standard. The surface of the plunger should be hardened, and the hardness of the working surface should not be lower than 48 HRC, and the thickness of the hardened layer should be greater than 3 mm." It is not recommended to use materials with higher carbon content, such as 65 steel, as piston rod materials.
2.6.4 Heat Treatment

Piston rods should generally be quenched and tempered after rough machining. For piston rods that only bear unidirectional loads, those with low nominal pressure, small cylinder inner diameter, or short stroke, and those with low action frequency, tempering treatment may not be performed. The sliding surface of the piston rod diameter is best to be surface quenched (the piston rod of the static pressure bearing structure should be surface quenched), and after surface quenching, it must be tempered. The process code for surface induction hardening and tempering is 521-04.

Under certain conditions, normalizing or normalizing + tempering can be used instead of tempering. For welded combined (hollow or welded piston and piston rod) piston rods, heat treatment or other methods to reduce stress should be used to eliminate internal stress.

For piston rods made of 45 steel, their tempering hardness should generally be 250-280 HBW. After surface quenching + tempering of the sliding surface, the hardness should be 45-52 HRC, and it should be relatively uniform. The recommended value of hardness deviation is shown in Table 2-36.
It is advisable to use alloy structural steel. After heat treatment, the surface hardness should not be lower than 52 HRC, and stability treatment should be performed.

sections.caption: Table 2-36  Recommended values of hardness deviation for piston rods
headers: Recommended value of hardness deviation HBW

sections.text: Note: GB/T34882-2017 stipulates the Rockwell (HRC) hardness deviation range, Vickers (HV or HK) hardness or Knoop hardness deviation range, and Shore (HS) hardness deviation range for steel parts after induction hardening and tempering.

Using nitrided steel, such as nitriding treatment of 35CrMo, 38CrMoAl, etc., the surface hardness can reach above 60 HRC; after ion soft nitriding treatment of 45 steel piston rod, the surface hardness can reach 64 HRC; after surface surfacing with stainless steel and heat treatment, the hardness can reach above 50 HRC. Reference [115] gives the heat treatment of the piston rod: "After rough machining, temper to 229-285 HBW. If necessary, then perform high-frequency quenching, and the hardness can reach 45-55 HRC."
2.6.5 Geometric Dimensions and Geometric Tolerances
In design, the axis of the piston rod is generally determined as the datum element.
(1) Basic dimensions

The basic dimensions of the piston rod include the diameter of the piston rod, the length of the piston rod (sliding surface length or guide surface length), the thread type and dimensions of the piston rod (end connection type and dimensions), the connection type and dimensions with the piston, and the type and dimensions of the buffer plunger.
(2) Diameter of the piston rod
1) The diameter d of the piston rod should comply with the provisions of GB/T23348-2018, as shown in Table 2-37.

sections.caption: Table 2-37 Piston Rod Diameter (Unit: mm)

sections.text: Note: Values in parentheses are non-preferred options.
For large hydraulic cylinders, the piston rod diameter should comply with the regulations in Table 2-38.
(2) Tolerance for Piston Rod Diameter
The dimensional tolerance for the outer diameter of the piston rod guiding surface should not be lower than f8 (or f6 or f7) specified in GB/T 1801-2009.

For hydraulic cylinders with piston rod static pressure bearing structures or with special requirements, the fit between the piston rod and guiding bushing can also use H7/h6, H8/h7, but the designed clearance (equivalent to bearing clearance) should be ensured through selective assembly method.
Generally, steel should not be used as the material for the guiding bushing (with static pressure bearing structure).
Note: 1. "Bearing clearance" is defined in GB/T 28279.1-2012. 2. In GB/T 32217-2015, it is specified that the diameter of the test piston rod is φ36 mm, with a tolerance of f8.
The limit deviations for shafts f6, f7, f8 and holes h7 are shown in Table 2-39.
(3) Tolerance for Piston Rod Length
The tolerance for piston rod length should comply with the "c" tolerance class specified in GB/T 1804-2000.

In JB/T 10205-×××× "Hydraulic Cylinder Part 3: Piston Rod Technical Conditions" (draft for approval), tolerances for piston rod length with additional machining of both end faces are also specified, but whether this is feasible is questionable.
(4) Thread Type and Size for Piston Rod

The threads on the piston rod refer to the external connecting threads on the piston rod of the hydraulic cylinder. There are three types of threads specified for piston rods, as shown in Figures 2-2 to 2-4.
Note: The chamfer angle for seal installation and the external corner radius (if required) on the shoulder of the external thread of the piston rod are not shown.

Note: 1. For internal threads, L refers to the minimum dimension; for external threads, L refers to the maximum dimension.
2. When a locknut is required, use the long thread length.
The connecting threads on the piston rod should be selected as fine-pitch ordinary threads M with 6th grade precision.

(5) Geometric tolerances
1) The roundness tolerance of the piston rod guide surface (before electroplating) should not be lower than the 8th grade (or 7th grade) specified in GB/T1184-1996; the roundness tolerance of the guide surface after electroplating and finishing (polishing or grinding) should not be lower than the 9th grade (or 8th grade) specified in GB/T1184-1996.
2) The straightness tolerance of the generatrix of the piston rod guide surface should not be lower than the 8th grade (or 7th grade) specified in GB/T1184-1996.
3) The cylindricity tolerance of the piston rod guide surface should be selected as the 8th grade (or 7th grade) specified in GB/T1184-1996.
4) The perpendicularity tolerance of the end face for piston installation relative to the piston rod axis should be selected as the 7th grade (or 6th grade) specified in GB/T1184-1996.
5) The radial runout tolerance of the piston rod guide surface relative to the cylindrical axis of the piston installation should not be lower than the 7th grade (or 6th grade) specified in GB/T1184-1996, or the coaxiality tolerance should not be lower than the 7th grade (or 6th grade) specified in GB/T1184-1996.

6) The radial runout tolerance of the buffer plunger relative to the cylindrical axis (or guide surface) of the piston installation should not be lower than the 7th grade (or 6th grade) specified in GB/T1184-1996.
7) When there is a pin hole at the end of the piston rod, the dimensional tolerance of the hole diameter should be selected as H11 (or H10) specified in GB/T1801-2009; the perpendicularity tolerance of the pin hole axis relative to the piston rod axis should not be lower than the 9th grade (or 8th grade) specified in GB/T1184-1996; the distance between the center line of the trunnion and the center line of the cylinder block should not be greater than 0.03 mm.
8) The coaxiality tolerance between the piston rod guide surface and the (guide sleeve) mating surface should not be lower than the 8th grade (or 7th grade) specified in GB/T1184-1996.

Note: 1. The tolerance grades in parentheses are mainly for servo hydraulic cylinders, and specific details can be referred to in reference [118].
2. For hydraulic cylinders used in hydraulic presses, it is usually required that the end face of the piston rod should be tightly fitted with the slider.
2.6.6  Surface Quality
1) The sliding fit between the piston rod and the guide sleeve (of the hydrostatic bearing structure) should have a surface roughness Ra of 0.2-0.4 μm.

The moving surfaces should be plated with hard chromium, and the thickness of the chromium coating (referring to one side after polishing or grinding) should generally be within the range of 0.03 to 0.05 mm; the hardness of the chromium coating should be 800 to 1000 HV; finishing after plating; the coating must be smooth and fine (uniform and dense), and must not have any defects such as peeling, delamination, or blistering; under the maximum design load and/or alternating load, the chromium coating must not have cracks. When the cylinder returns to the end of its stroke, the exposed part of the piston rod should also be plated with hard chromium.

In addition to hard chromium plating, the outer surface of the piston rod can also be coated with a chemical nickel-phosphorus alloy coating.

For piston rods with special requirements, the surface can be coated with a thermally sprayed alloy or ceramic layer.

GB/T 32217-2015 stipulates that the test piston rod should be induction hardened and then plated with a hard chromium layer of 0.015 to 0.03 mm thick.

For hydraulic cylinders with requirements for moisture, heat, salt spray, and mold resistance, the relevant standards to be followed and the required performance should be clearly stated in the technical requirements for the piston rod, and the testing (measurement) method should be provided.

For the outer surface of piston rods without hard chromium plating or before hard chromium plating, the surface should be smooth and consistent, and should not have any visible defects such as shrinkage cavities, inclusions (slag), white spots, ripples, spiral lines, scratches, nicks, burrs, pits, cracks, scars, nodules, warping, oxide scale, and rust.

Visual inspection should be conducted under sufficient light or good artificial lighting, and if necessary, it can be visually inspected with a 3 to 5 times magnifying glass.

Sharp edges on the piston rod, except for the sealing groove ridge on the piston and piston rod integrated structure, which are not shown on the working drawing, should all be removed.

2) The surface roughness value of the sliding surface of the piston rod and the guide sleeve (static pressure bearing structure) should generally not be greater than Ra0.4 μm, and can also be selected from Table 2-41 according to design requirements.

sections.caption: Table 2-41  Surface Roughness Values (Unit: μm)

sections.text:
3) For the surface roughness value already specified on the drawing [i.e., the final surface roughness value of the part], the surface roughness value before plating should not be greater than half of the surface roughness value marked on the drawing.

4) GB/T 32217-2015 stipulates that the surface roughness Ra and Rt of the test piston rod should be measured along the axial direction of the piston rod according to GB/T 10610-2009, with a sampling length of 0.8 mm each time and an evaluation length of 4 mm.

The surface roughness values of the test piston rod specified in GB/T 32217-2015 are: grinding and polishing to Ra0.08 μm to Ra0.15 μm, but the Rt value is not given.
2.6.7  Other Requirements

items: The chamfer for installing the sealing element should be determined according to the requirements of the selected sealing element, but it must be rounded at the junction with the outer diameter.
The finished piston rod should retain complete center holes.

For the piston rod connection type with the risk of accidental sliding block falling in the hydraulic cylinder-driven sliding block, a risk assessment should be conducted during design, and the expected service life should be provided; when the expected service life is reached, the user is required to consciously and timely replace the piston rod.

For plunger cylinders and others where the piston rod may be ejected (disengaged) during testing, debugging, use, and maintenance, a travel limit position limiting device should be provided. After the limiting device is invalid, released, or removed, pressure should not be applied to each working chamber of the hydraulic cylinder to prevent various dangers caused by hydraulic cylinder failure.

sections.text: 2.7  Design of Hydraulic Cylinder End Cover

Here, the end cover specifically refers to the rod end end cover (cylinder head) of the hydraulic cylinder, i.e., the front cover of the pressure-bearing shell of the hydraulic cylinder (single rod cylinder) in GB/T 19934.1-2005, but since it is impossible to distinguish between the front and rear end covers of a double rod cylinder, it is more accurate to name it "end cover".
2.7.1  Structural Type

The end cover can be made into an integral structure with the guide sleeve, or it can be made into a separate structure (such as a gland-guide sleeve, end cover-static pressure bearing sleeve), and it can also be divided into a sealed end cover and a non-sealed end cover according to whether there is a seal between the end cover and the cylinder body (barrel), piston rod, and guide sleeve.

The connection between the end cover and the cylinder body (barrel) must have a reliable connection structure (including locking measures) and sufficient connection strength, and at the same time, it should be easy to disassemble and assemble.

The connection between the end cover and the cylinder body (barrel) usually includes flange connection, internal (external) thread connection, internal (external) key connection, tie rod connection, etc. Since the end cover is generally required to be easy to disassemble and assemble, the end cover and the cylinder body (barrel) usually do not use welding connection.

For hydraulic cylinders with high pressure and large inner diameter (such as large hydraulic cylinders specified in the standard), the end cover and the cylinder body should be connected by flanges, and the end face (axial) extrusion sealing type should not be used between the end cover and the cylinder body, including various gaskets given in GB150.3-2011 "Pressure Vessels Part 3: Design". For details, please refer to the relevant content in Reference [108].

The hydraulic cylinder ports on the end cover are divided into axial ports and radial ports according to different opening positions.

The structural types of various end covers are shown in Section 4.9 of the hydraulic cylinder design and selection reference drawings.

End covers with the same structural type produced by the same manufacturer must have interchangeability.

During the design process, the end cover should be given the ability to be remanufactured, i.e., the end cover should have inherent remanufacturability.

sections.text: 2.7.2 Materials
Common materials for integral cylinder heads are described as follows:

items: Carbon structural steel grades: Q235, Q275.
High-quality carbon structural steel grades: 20, 30, 35, 45.
Alloy structural steel grades: 27SiMn, 30CrMo, 30CrMnSiA, 40Cr, 42CrMo.
Low-alloy high-strength structural steel grades: Q355B (C, D).
Stainless steel grades: 12Cr18Ni9, 14Cr17Ni2.
Cast carbon steel grades: ZG270-500, ZG310-570.
Gray cast iron grades: HT300, HT350.
Compacted graphite iron grade: RuT500.
Others, such as bimetallic, die-cast aluminum, cast copper, etc.

sections.text: For cylinder head guide sleeves or cylinder heads, cast iron may be considered when the nominal pressure p ≤ 10 MPa. Other materials may use high-quality carbon structural steel 20, 35, 45. When welding is required to connect with the cylinder barrel, generally use 20, 35 steel, and stress relief treatment should be performed after welding; for non-welded connections, cylinder heads may use 45 steel and undergo quenching and tempering treatment as appropriate.
The bearing ring is the part that directly contacts the piston rod in steel cylinder heads or guide sleeves.

When conducting hydraulic cylinder pressure tests, the cylinder head should not produce permanent deformation, including crushing. Under rated static pressure, none of the failure modes specified in JB/T5924-1991 "Test Methods for Rated Fatigue Pressure and Rated Static Pressure of Pressure Cavities of Hydraulic Components" (already repealed) should occur in the tested pressure cavity.

Cylinder heads [bearing sleeves (outer sleeves)] of press-fitted static pressure bearing sleeves made from cold-drawn steel bars of high-quality carbon structural steel or alloy structural steel specified in GB/T3078-2008 should have a (cold-drawn) tensile strength not lower than 610 MPa.
The yield strength of materials for cylinder heads of large hydraulic cylinders should not be lower than 280 MPa.
For cylinder head materials with clearance fits between the inner hole and piston rod diameter of H8/f7, H8/h7, H8/f8, H8/f9, H9/f9, and smaller clearances, steel cannot be used.
2.7.3 Heat Treatment

Cylinder heads should generally undergo quenching and tempering treatment after rough machining, especially for forged or cast steel that has not been normalized or annealed. However, tempering must be performed after quenching.

For cylinder heads of hydraulic cylinders with small bore diameters, low nominal pressures, good operating conditions, and low operating frequencies, or for cylinder heads made from non-quenched and quenched and tempered steel, heat treatment may not be performed. However, the blank should undergo aging treatment before mechanical processing.
2.7.4 Geometric Dimensions and Geometric Tolerances

In design, the axis of the cylinder head inner hole is generally determined as the datum feature. However, for integral cylinder heads, the axis of the outer cylindrical surface of the guide sleeve may also be used as the datum feature.
GB/T32217-2015 specifies that the axis of the outer cylindrical surface of the bearing ring groove body (guide sleeve) is used as the datum.
(1) Basic Dimensions
Basic dimensions of integral structure flange-connected sealed cylinder heads include the cylinder head inner diameter, outer diameter, (guide) length, seal, guide, and flange dimensions.
(2) Cylinder Head Inner Diameter
1) The (nominal) inner diameter of the cylinder head should preferentially select the recommended values in Table 2-42.

sections.caption: Table 2-42  Cylinder Head (Nominal) Inner Diameter Recommended Values (Unit: mm)

sections.text: Note: Numbers in parentheses are non-preferential values.
2) The dimensional tolerance of the cylinder head's inner diameter relative to the guide sleeve should not be lower than H9 specified in GB/T1801-2009, and H8 is generally selected.

3) For integral cylinder heads that require installation of sealing elements (including bearing rings), the cylinder head inner diameter should be determined according to the requirements of the sealing element and/or bearing ring groove.
GB/T32217-2015 specifies that the inner diameter of the bearing ring groove body (guide sleeve) is φ36.7P7, and the diameter of the piston rod to be assembled with it is φ36f8.
(3) Cylinder Head Outer Diameter
1) The outer diameter of the cylinder head [the part that fits with the cylinder body (barrel)] should preferentially select the recommended values in Table 2-43.

sections.caption: Table 2-43  Cylinder Head Outer Diameter Recommended Values (Unit: mm)

sections.text: Note: Numbers in parentheses are non-preferential values.

2) The outer diameter dimensional tolerances of the mating parts between the cylinder head and cylinder block (barrel) - Generally, f7 specified in GB/T 1801—2009 is selected, but for some hydraulic cylinders with special purposes or special requirements, the mating between the cylinder head and cylinder block (barrel) can be selected from H7/k6, H7/g6 or H8/k7 to H8/g7.
The test device given in GB/T 32217—2015 has a fit of φ60H7/g6.
(4) Flange dimensions: The outer diameter dimensions of the cylinder head flange for hydraulic cylinders (PN ≤ 25MPa) can refer to Table 2-44.

sections.text: The circumferential distribution positions of the hydraulic cylinder's oil inlet and outlet holes, fixed bolts, exhaust valve, gland, and bracket can be found in Appendix A (Normative Appendix) of JB/T 6134—2006 Hydraulic Cylinder Drawing Design.
The outer diameter dimensions of the cylinder head flange for hydraulic cylinders (PN ≤ 16MPa) can refer to Table 2-45.

sections.caption: Table 2-45  Outer diameter dimensions of cylinder head flange for hydraulic cylinders (PN ≤ 16MPa) (Unit: mm)

sections.text: The circumferential distribution positions of the hydraulic cylinder's oil inlet and outlet holes, fixed bolts, exhaust valve, gland, and bracket can be found in Appendix A (Normative Appendix) of JB/T 2162—2007 Hydraulic Cylinder Drawing Design.
(5) Geometric tolerances

items: The roundness tolerance of the inner hole of the cylinder head should not be lower than level 7 (or level 6) specified in GB/T 1184—1996.
The cylindricity tolerance of the inner hole of the cylinder head should not be lower than level 8 (or level 7) specified in GB/T 1184—1996.
The cylindricity of the mating part between the cylinder head and cylinder block (barrel) should not be lower than level 8 (or level 7) specified in GB/T 1184—1996.

The coaxiality tolerance between the outer surface of the cylinder head [and the mating part with the cylinder block (barrel)] and the inner hole axis of the cylinder head (corresponding to the guide sleeve part) should not be lower than level 7 (or level 6) specified in GB/T 1184—1996.

The perpendicularity tolerance between the end face of the cylinder head abutting against the gland or cylinder block (flange) and the inner hole axis of the cylinder head, and the end face installed inside the rod cavity of the hydraulic cylinder, should not be lower than level 7 (or level 6) specified in GB/T 1184—1996.

sections.text: The tolerance grades in parentheses are mainly for servo hydraulic cylinders, and specific references can be made to reference [118].
2.7.5  Surface quality
(1) Inner hole surface

1) The surface roughness value of the inner hole surface of the hydraulic cylinder's cylinder head should not be greater than Ra1.6μm, generally Ra0.8μm is selected, or it can be selected from Table 2-46 according to design requirements.

sections.caption: Table 2-46  Surface roughness values of cylinder head inner hole (Unit: μm)

sections.text: 2) The inner hole surface of the hydraulic cylinder's cylinder head should be smooth, and should not have visible defects such as shrinkage cavities, inclusions (slag), white spots, ripples, scratches, bumps, pits, cracks, scabs, peeling, and rust.
(2) End face

The surface roughness value of the end face of the cylinder head installed in the rod cavity should not be greater than Ra1.6μm, but for the end face used as the inspection datum, its surface roughness value should generally not be greater than Ra0.8μm.
(3) Outer surface

The outer surface of the cylinder head should not have visible defects such as shrinkage cavities, inclusions (slag), folds, ripples, cracks, scratches, bumps, and pull marks caused by built-up edge on the outer die during cold drawing.
Sharp edges on the cylinder head, except for the edges of the sealing groove, should be removed if not shown on the working drawing.

The outer surface of the cylinder head should be treated with anti-rust treatment, or it can be protected with a coating layer, passivation layer, paint layer, etc. The outer surface should be free of oxide scale and rust pits before painting. When painting, anti-rust paint should be applied first, followed by topcoat, and the paint layer should not have defects such as blisters.

For hydraulic cylinders with requirements for moisture, heat, salt spray, and mildew resistance, the corresponding standards (including test methods) and requirements that should be followed should be clearly stated in the technical requirements of the cylinder head, and specific methods or measures should be provided, such as the paint coating should specify the paint type (including the designated manufacturer) and operating procedures.
2.8  Design of hydraulic cylinder bottom

Here, the bottom specifically refers to the end cover (cylinder tail) at the rodless end of the cylinder, i.e., the rear end cover of the pressure shell of the hydraulic cylinder (single rod cylinder) in GB/T 19934.1—2005.

166.page_header: Chapter 2  Design of Hydraulic Cylinders and Basic Components  155

sections.text: 2.8.1 General Principles

The cylinder bottom of a hydraulic cylinder should have sufficient strength, rigidity, and impact toughness. For cylinder bottoms that require subsequent welding to the cylinder body (tube), the material should have good weldability, and the weld seam strength should not be lower than the strength index of the base material. The weld quality should meet the Class II requirements specified in GB/T 3323.

The weld seam connecting the cylinder bottom to the cylinder body (tube) should undergo 100% inspection using the method specified in GB/T 5777, and the quality should meet the Class I requirements specified in NB/T 47013.3.
The connection between the cylinder bottom and the cylinder body (tube) must have a reliable connection structure (including locking measures) and sufficient connection strength.
Cylinder bottoms (bodies) of the same model produced by the same manufacturer must be interchangeable.
2.8.2 Structural Forms

Based on the installation type of the hydraulic cylinder, the cylinder bottom and the rear end fixed single (double) clevis, circular (square, rectangular) flange, etc., are integrated into one structure.
The cushioning device of the hydraulic cylinder is generally installed on the cylinder bottom, except for the cushioning plunger.

The hydraulic cylinder ports on the cylinder bottom are classified into axial ports and radial ports based on their positions. Except for the cylinder bottom integrated with the cylinder body (tube), the connection forms between the cylinder bottom and the cylinder body (tube) usually include flange connection, internal (external) thread connection, tie rod connection, welding, etc. Among these, the welding connection between the cylinder bottom and the cylinder body (tube) is the most common connection (fixing) form, i.e., the welding type cylinder bottom using the lock bottom butt welding seam fixing method.

The cylinder body (tube) using the welded cylinder bottom is generally called a sealed cylinder body (tube) or a cylindrical cylinder body (tube). The inner end face forms of the welded cylinder bottom or forged cylindrical cylinder body (tube) are mostly flat cover types, and there are also concave cylinder bottoms of other types such as elliptical, disc, spherical crown, and hemispherical forms. The cylinder bottom with axial inlet/outlet holes (ports) or liquid charging valve installation holes in the cylinder bottom (center) is called a perforated cylinder bottom.
2.8.3 Materials
The mechanical properties ReL (lower yield strength) of the materials used to manufacture the cylinder bottom should not be lower than 280 MPa. The commonly used materials are as follows:

items: High-quality carbon structural steel grades: 30, 35, 45, 25Mn, 35Mn.
Alloy structural steel grades: 27SiMn, 30CrMo, 40Cr, 42CrMo.
Low-alloy high-strength structural steel grades: Q355B(C, D).
Stainless steel grades: 12Cr18Ni9.
Cast carbon steel grades: ZG270-500, ZG310-570.
Nodular cast iron grades: QT400-15, QT400-18, QT450-10, QT500-7, QT500-10, QT550-5, QT600-3.
Compacted graphite cast iron grades: RuT500.

sections.text: The material of the welded cylinder bottom should generally be the same type of steel as the cylinder body (tube).

When conducting the hydraulic cylinder pressure test, it should be ensured that the cylinder bottom does not produce permanent deformation, including crushing. Under the rated static pressure, none of the failure modes of the tested pressure cavity specified in JB/T 5924-1991 "Test Methods for Rated Fatigue Pressure and Rated Static Pressure of Pressure Cavities of Hydraulic Components" (already obsolete) should occur.
2.8.4 Heat Treatment
Cast and forged parts used to manufacture the cylinder bottom should undergo heat treatment or other methods to reduce stress to eliminate internal stress.

The cylinder bottom should generally undergo quenching and tempering treatment after rough machining, especially for forged steel and cast steel that have not been normalized or annealed, which should undergo heat treatment after rough machining. However, after quenching, high-temperature tempering must be performed, and attention should be paid to the warning in the technical requirements for the hydraulic cylinder body (tube) in this chapter.

For hydraulic cylinder cylinder bottoms with small internal diameters, low nominal pressures, and good working conditions, or cylinder bottoms manufactured using non-quenched and quenched and tempered steel, heat treatment may also be omitted.
2.8.5 Geometric Dimensions and Geometric Tolerances
During design, the axis of the buffer hole or the axis of the cooperating stop diameter of the cylinder body (tube) is generally determined as the datum element.
(1) Basic Dimensions

The basic dimensions of the welded cylinder bottom include the cylinder bottom stop diameter, stop height, outer diameter, cylinder bottom thickness, and connection dimensions; for cylinder bottoms with buffer devices designed, such as buffer cavity holes, separate provisions apply.
(2) Stop Diameter

items: The stop diameter is selected based on the inner diameter of the cylinder (body) tube to be installed.

The dimensional tolerance of the stop diameter should generally be selected according to js7 specified in GB/T 1801-2009; for cylinder bottoms with buffer cavity holes designed, the fit between the cylinder bottom and the cylinder body (tube) can be selected as H7/k6 or H8/k7.

sections.text: (3) Stop Height
The stop height of the welded cylinder bottom should be sufficient to keep the piston seal at least 20 mm away from the butt weld.
(4) Cylinder Bottom Thickness

The cylinder bottom thickness can generally be selected as 1.2 to 1.3 times the cylinder tube wall thickness; for servo hydraulic cylinder cylinder bottoms, it is recommended to select 1.3 to 1.5 times the cylinder tube wall thickness.

sections.text: 2.8.6 Surface Quality
The outer surface of the cylinder bottom should not have visually detectable defects such as shrinkage cavities, inclusions (slag), folds, waves, cracks, scratches, dents, and rust.
Sharp edges on the cylinder bottom, except for the ridge of the sealing groove, should be removed if not shown in the working drawing.

The outer surface of the cylinder bottom should undergo anti-rust treatment, or be protected by a coating or passivation layer, or paint layer. There should be no oxide scale or rust pits on the outer surface before painting. When painting, anti-rust paint should be applied first, then topcoat, and the paint layer should not have defects such as blisters.
2.8.7 Soundness
Forged cylinder bottoms should undergo 100% flaw detection inspection. After non-destructive flaw detection, the cylinder bottom should reach grade I specified in NB/T 47013.3.

Soundness inspection should be performed by eddy current testing according to acceptance grade A specified in GB/T 7735-2004, or by magnetic particle testing according to acceptance grade L4 specified in GB/T 12606.
Under the action of pressure test pressure, there should be no leakage on the outer surface or weld seam of the cylinder bottom.
2.8.8 Strength Calculation of Cylinder Bottom
Strength and stiffness verification calculations should be performed when necessary.

Forged cylindrical cylinder bodies mostly use flat cover-shaped cylinder bottoms rather than concave ones. The center of such cylinder bottoms generally has through holes such as oil inlet/outlet holes or filler valve mounting holes, as well as non-through holes such as buffer cavity holes. Therefore, in force analysis and strength calculation, they are generally regarded as circular thin plates or discs fixed or clamped around the perimeter. Up to now, there is still no relatively simple and authoritative formula for calculating cylinder bottom thickness. The reason is that in addition to the difficulty in determining the working conditions of the hydraulic cylinder bottom, the main problem lies in the mechanical model used to derive the strength calculation formula.
The commonly used formula is the strength calculation formula recommended by Soviet Mikhailov (В.А.Михеев), i.e.

In addition, there is the strength calculation formula recommended by Soviet Rozanov (Б.В.Розанов):
σd = PR²/φδ² ≤ [σ]    (2-51)
Where: φ—coefficient, taken as 0.7~0.8.

2.9  Design of Guide Sleeve for Hydraulic Cylinder
The guide sleeve is a sleeve-type cylinder part that guides and supports the piston rod.
2.9.1  Structural Types

The guide sleeve can be made as an integral structure with the cylinder cover, or as a separate structure, i.e., the so-called cylinder cover type and bushing type. Generally, the inner and outer cylindrical surfaces of the guide sleeve are designed and machined with sealing groove slots, used for piston static sealing, piston rod dynamic sealing, and piston rod dust sealing.
For steel guide sleeves, the inner hole must also be machined with a support ring installation groove slot, used for guiding and supporting the piston rod.

The guide sleeve must be positioned (with locking measures) and should be easy to disassemble and assemble. Various structural types of guide sleeves can be found in Section 4.9 of the hydraulic cylinder design and selection reference drawings.
Guide sleeves of the same model from the same manufacturer must have interchangeability.

Note: 1. The guide sleeve with sealing element groove slots is a component of the pressure-bearing shell of the hydraulic cylinder in GB/T 19934.1-2005. 2. In GB/T 32217-2015, the guide sleeve with support ring installation groove slots is called "support ring groove body".
2.9.2  Materials
The commonly used materials for manufacturing guide sleeves are mainly the following types:

Malleable cast iron grades: KTZ650-02, KTZ700-02.
Ductile iron grades: QT400-15, QT400-18, QT450-10, QT500-7.
Compacted graphite iron grades: RuT300, RuT350, RuT400, RuT450.
Carbon steel, cast carbon steel.
Others, such as bimetal, (pressure) cast aluminum alloy, cast copper alloy, plastic (non-metallic materials).

In JB/T 11843-2014 "Wear-resistant Ductile Iron Parts", five grades are specified: QTML-1, QTML-2, QTMD-1, QTMD-2, and QTMCD. Among them, L — continuous cooling quenching heat treatment; D — isothermal quenching heat treatment; CD — isothermal quenching heat treatment (resulting in a microstructure of carbides and austenite).

The guide sleeve of the hydraulic cylinder plays a supporting and guiding role when the piston rod reciprocates. The bushing-type guide sleeve can generally be made by casting and machining tin bronze alloys such as ZCuSn6Pb3Zn6, ZCuSn10P1, etc. Some are also made by centrifugal casting of cast nylon 6 with molybdenum disulfide, but due to their poor ability to resist eccentric loads, large thermal expansion, deformation after moisture absorption during processing and assembly, etc., problems such as piston rod swing or eccentricity, jamming of the piston rod, and fracture of the body may occur. Therefore, gray cast iron and ductile iron are currently the most commonly used.

When conducting a pressure test on the hydraulic cylinder, it should be ensured that the guide sleeve does not produce permanent deformation, including crushing. Under the rated static pressure, no failure mode specified in JB/T 5924-1991 "Test Method for Rated Fatigue Pressure and Rated Static Pressure of Pressure-Bearing Cavities of Hydraulic Components" (already repealed) should occur.
For the guide sleeve, the fit between the inner hole and the piston rod diameter is H8/f7.

2.10 Design of Hydraulic Cylinder Seals
2.10.1 Introduction to Hydraulic Cylinder Seals
1. Leakage and Sealing

A hydraulic cylinder is a special closed pressure vessel. It drives the piston (piston rod) to move relative to the cylinder body (tube) by changing the volume of the hydraulic working medium enclosed in the rodless cavity and/or rod cavity (taking a piston-type single piston rod double-acting hydraulic cylinder as an example), converting hydraulic energy into mechanical energy. The hydraulic working medium is under pressure, and sometimes the pressure can be very high, meaning there are ultra-high pressure hydraulic cylinders with a nominal pressure exceeding 32 MPa.

Generally speaking, the higher the pressure of the hydraulic working medium, the more severe the leakage, and the more difficult the sealing. However, the pressure of the hydraulic working medium in low pressure (0～2.5 MPa) and medium pressure (2.5～8.0 MPa) should not be ignored. In practice, there have indeed been cases where hydraulic cylinders do not leak at high pressure (16.0～31.5 MPa) and ultra-high pressure (≥32 MPa), but leak at medium and low pressure.

The leakage of hydraulic cylinders refers to the phenomenon of the hydraulic working medium flowing out from the high-pressure side to the low-pressure side across the boundary of the cavity. Leakage is generally divided into internal leakage and external leakage. For example, the hydraulic working medium in the rodless cavity of the hydraulic cylinder leaks to the rod cavity, or the hydraulic working medium in the rod cavity leaks to the rodless cavity, which is called internal leakage (inter-cavity); the leakage of the hydraulic working medium to the surrounding environment of the hydraulic cylinder is called external leakage, such as oil leakage at the weld of the bottom of the welded hydraulic cylinder, and oil on the extended piston rod, etc. GB/T 17446—2012 defines leakage as the relative small amount of fluid flow that does not do useful work and causes energy loss.

leakage, and defines external leakage as the leakage from the inside of a component or pipe to the surrounding environment. The main causes of hydraulic cylinder leakage are: (1) gaps between mating parts; (2) pressure differences (pressure) on both sides of the mating surfaces. Internal leakage affects the efficiency, speed, and cylinder travel and/or return output force of the hydraulic cylinder, and also causes further heating of the hydraulic working medium, which may lead to accidents; external leakage wastes the hydraulic working medium, pollutes the environment, and is prone to causing accidents. Therefore, for hydraulic cylinders, whether internal or external leakage exceeds the standard, it may be a very serious problem. Internal leakage (volume) and external leakage (volume) are mandatory inspection items for hydraulic cylinder factory testing. Please refer to JB/T 10205—2010 and GB/T 15622—2005 and other standards for details. The leakage of hydraulic cylinders is mainly leakage (through, bypassing).

Devices that can prevent or reduce leakage are generally called seals or sealing devices. A sealing device is a device composed of one or more sealing elements and supporting parts (such as retaining rings, springs, metal shells). The elements in the sealing device used to prevent leakage and/or prevent contaminants from entering are called sealing elements. Some also refer to sealing rings, retaining rings, guide rings (support rings), and dust rings as sealing elements (see MT/T1164—2011). The function of sealing is to seal the gaps between mating surfaces, cut off leakage channels or increase the resistance of leakage channels, so as to reduce or prevent leakage. The main indicators for measuring the quality of sealing performance are leakage rate (leakage volume/time or leakage volume/cumulative stroke, etc.), service life, and service conditions (pressure, speed, temperature, etc.). Now, due to the great progress in China's hydraulic cylinder sealing design standards and levels, processing technology and equipment, sealing element structural types and parameters, sealing (rubber and plastic, etc.) materials and additives, and testing, etc., the sealing performance of hydraulic cylinders has also been greatly improved. In short, the technical performance of hydraulic cylinders such as pressure, speed, temperature, product grade, service life (durability), and reliability largely depends on the sealing device (system) of the hydraulic cylinder and its design.

In addition to the above-mentioned meaning that sealing is a measure (behavior or practice, i.e., treatment method) to prevent or reduce leakage, "sealing" also has another meaning opposite to the phenomenon or state of leakage.

Author's note: 1. A super high-pressure hydraulic cylinder is a hydraulic cylinder with a working medium pressure not lower than 32 MPa. Please refer to GB/T 8541—2012 for details. Hydraulic cylinders with a nominal pressure ≥32 MPa can also be called super high-pressure hydraulic cylinders. 2. "Sealing" is the antonym of "leakage", but "sealing" is not defined in GB/T 17446—2012. 3. In GB/T 50670—2011 "Terminology Standard for Mechanical Equipment Installation Engineering", the term "sealing" is defined, which is the general term for measures to prevent medium leakage.
2. Classification of Sealing

Sealing is divided into dynamic sealing and static sealing. In dynamic sealing, there is relative motion between the sealing mating (matching) parts; in static sealing, there is no (obvious) relative motion between the sealing mating (matching) parts. Due to these two different sealing working states, there are many differences in the requirements for sealing elements. In addition to bearing the pressure of the hydraulic working medium, dynamic sealing elements must also withstand friction and wear (or abrasion) caused by the relative motion of the mating parts; they must ensure a certain sealing performance and meet the requirements of various motion performances, including the support and guiding requirements of motion parts. According to whether the relative motion between the sealing mating parts is sliding or rotating, dynamic sealing is further divided into reciprocating (motion) sealing and rotary motion sealing. The sealing between the cylinder body (tube) and piston, and between the piston rod and guide sleeve in hydraulic cylinders are all reciprocating motion sealing. According to the contact relationship between the sealing element and the sealing surface of the mating parts, reciprocating motion sealing can be further divided into bore sealing (or outer diameter sealing, piston sealing) and shaft sealing (or inner diameter sealing, piston rod sealing). Static sealing can also be divided into plane static sealing (axial static sealing), cylindrical static sealing (radial static sealing), and angular static sealing (see Figure 2-6). According to whether the hydraulic working medium pressure acts on the inner or outer diameter of the sealing ring, axial static sealing is further divided into internal pressure and external pressure. The one where the hydraulic working medium may leak from inside to outside is called internal pressure axial static sealing (external flow type), and the one where the hydraulic working medium may leak from outside to inside is called external pressure axial static sealing (internal flow type), as shown in Figure 2-6a,b. Cylindrical static sealing (radial static sealing)
