According to the shape and sealing type of the sealing element, seals can be classified into molded packing (molded products or molded sealing elements) seals and rubber seals, belt seals, packing seals. Molded packing seals (elements) generally refer to annular sealing rings molded from materials such as rubber and plastic, such as O-ring rubber seals, Y-ring rubber seals, etc. They have a simple and compact structure, a wide variety of specifications, a wide range of working parameters, and convenient installation and use.

Dynamic seals can also be classified into contact and non-contact seals according to the contact type of the mating surfaces of the mating parts. Contact seals rely on the sealing element being tightly attached to the sealing surface of the mating part under the action of forced pressure, with the sealing surface and the sealing element being in a state of frictional contact separated by only a very thin layer of hydraulic medium. This sealing method has good sealing performance, but is limited by friction and wear conditions, so the relative moving speed of the sealing surface cannot be too high, and most reciprocating dynamic seals in hydraulic components belong to this type. Contact seals can be further divided into compression seals and pressure-energized seals. Compression seals rely on squeezing the sealing packing installed in the sealing groove to make it expand radially and press tightly on the shaft or hole to achieve sealing; pressure-energized seals are a type of seal with self-sealing ability, and O-ring rubber seals, Y-ring seals, etc. in molded seals all belong to this type of seal. The working principle of these seals is to install the seal ring into the sealing groove and assemble it with the mating part, so that the seal element applies a pre-pressure to the mating part through elastic deformation. When the seal element is subjected to the pressure of the sealing working medium in one direction, the seal element is further deformed, and the contact pressure (stress) of the sealing surface (line) increases to adapt to the increase in the pressure of the sealing working medium, ensuring sealing. Pressure-energized seals can be divided into two categories: extrusion type and lip type. The representative of the extrusion type is the O-ring rubber seal, and the representative of the lip type is the Y-ring seal. Non-contact seals are a type of clearance seal, such as piston clearance seal. Since there is no contact and friction between the sealing mating surfaces, this type of seal has small friction and wear, low starting pressure, and long service life, but its sealing performance is poor.

According to the role of the sealing element in the sealing device, there are main seals and auxiliary seals. The role of auxiliary seals is to protect the main sealing element from damage, extend the service life of the main sealing element, and improve its sealing performance, such as dust seals, retaining rings, buffer rings, and anti-pollution protection rings.
In addition, sealing elements can also be classified according to the sealing working medium, sealing material, the different pressure of the sealed working medium, etc.

① A rubber seal with an O-shaped cross-section. O-ring rubber seals are generally made of synthetic rubber through molding and are a type of rubber sealing component with a cross-sectional shape of O in natural state (or called a rubber seal ring with a circular cross-section). O-ring rubber seals (hereinafter referred to as O-rings) have good sealing performance and can be used in static or dynamic conditions. They can be used alone, capable of sealing bidirectional fluid; their structure is simple, compact in size, easy to install and disassemble, and have low technical requirements for installation; when there is wear on the working surface, high pressure and/or large gaps require the use of (installing) retaining rings to prevent extrusion damage; O-rings can form seals on their inner diameter, end face, or other arbitrary surfaces during operation. Therefore, their applicable working parameter range is wide, and the working pressure can reach 261 in static conditions.

sections.text: 6.3 MPa or higher (referenced literature mentions it can reach 200 MPa), and can reach 35 MPa under reciprocating motion conditions; with different sealing material selections, the working temperature range is -60~200°C; the linear velocity can reach 3 m/s (generally limited to below 0.5 m/s); the shaft diameter can reach 3000 mm.

When O-rings are used as reciprocating motion seals, they have the disadvantages of large starting friction resistance and being prone to twisting and rolling, especially when used in cases of uneven gaps, large eccentricity, and high reciprocating motion speeds, they are more likely to twist and break. As the coupling's diameter (inner diameter) increases, the tendency to twist also increases. Therefore, O-rings used for dynamic sealing are only reasonable when used in light load conditions or internal (piston seal) reciprocating dynamic sealing. Specifically, it is more suitable for applications with small diameter pistons, short strokes, and medium-low pressure conditions.
O-rings can also be used for low-speed rotating motion and short running cycle trunnion seals.

② Non-standard cross-section rubber O-rings. Other special cross-sectional shapes different from O-ring cross-sections, which are extrusion-type sealing rings, or can be called non-standard cross-section O-rings. The commonly used ones are X-rings, also known as star rings.

The development and use of non-standard cross-section O-rings are mainly to overcome the disadvantages of O-rings, such as rolling, twisting, and large starting friction force. Taking the 4-lip X-ring as an example, compared with O-rings, since two of the sealing lips that contact the moving surface in the X-ring can form a lubrication cavity, it has smaller friction resistance and starting resistance. Since the parting surface of the molding die is opened at the concave part of the cross-section (similar principle to the 45° parting surface O-ring), the sealing effect is good. Its non-circular cross-section can avoid rolling during reciprocating motion, and there are now series of products that can generally be used in standard O-ring sealing grooves. Based on the above characteristics of X, X-rings are mainly used for dynamic sealing, but can also be used for static sealing, such as their application in low-leakage coaxial sealing components. In addition to X-rings and dumbbell-shaped rings, which will be introduced in detail later, other non-standard cross-section O-rings are rarely actually used on hydraulic cylinders, so only some simple introductions are provided below.

a. Square (rectangular) ring: It is easy to form, difficult to install, has poor sealing performance, and large friction resistance, and is often used as a static sealing component. But there is one special case, which is the use of hydraulic cylinder seals in automotive disc-type hydraulic brakes.

b. D-ring: It is stable in position during work, suitable for bidirectional sealing alternating pressure conditions, and mainly used for reciprocating motion seals. High pressure may cause seal failure due to extrusion damage.
c. Triangular ring: It is stable in position during work, but has relatively large friction resistance, short service life, and is generally only suitable for special-purpose seals.

d. T-ring: It is stable in position during work, resistant to vibration, has small friction resistance, and can achieve sealing with a 5% groove compression rate, generally used in medium-low pressure and vibration conditions. High pressure may cause extrusion damage.

e. Heart-shaped ring: Its cross-section is similar to that of an O-ring, but its friction coefficient is smaller than that of an O-ring, and it is generally suitable for sealing low-pressure rotating shafts.

f. X-ring: It resembles two O-rings, has four protruding sealing parts in the cross-section, is stable in position in the groove, has small friction resistance, can achieve sealing with a 1% groove compression rate, and allows a higher working linear speed. It can be used for sealing shafts with rotating and reciprocating motion that require low friction resistance. X-rings can also be used for static sealing, but are mainly used for dynamic sealing.

g. Corner-O-ring: It resembles three O-rings, has three protruding parts, the two protruding parts on the outside are higher, making it stable in position in the groove and having a large compression rate. Referenced literature mentions that its working pressure can reach 210 MPa.
Author's note: The above "can reach 210 MPa" expression is mentioned in both reference [46] and its previous edition, but the author has not conducted practical machine testing.

h. Dumbbell-shaped ring: It can replace O-rings with retaining rings for static sealing, is very resistant to extrusion and twisting, has a long service life, and the maximum working pressure can reach 50 MPa. It is suitable for working conditions with pressure pulsation and contamination intrusion, and is used on hydraulic cylinders of construction machinery, etc., and its application is becoming more and more widespread.

i. Polygonal ring: Its friction resistance is smaller than that of an O-ring, and its leakage is also less than that of an O-ring. The working pressure can reach 14 MPa, and it is used for plunger seals of hydraulic cylinders.

2) Non-rubber O-ring seals. Common non-rubber material O-rings are PTFE O-rings (including PTFE-coated O-rings) and stainless steel hollow tube O-rings. Due to the characteristics of PTFE that are not possessed by other materials, such as a wide working temperature range, strong resistance to working media, and low friction coefficient, it is also made into O-rings for use in some special occasions. The elasticity of PTFE is inferior to that of rubber. When using standard O-ring sealing grooves, it is necessary to redesign and test. Generally, the compression rate should not exceed 7%, and it is mainly used for static sealing.

3) Coaxial sealing components. It is a combined sealing assembly, whose characteristics are to obtain a compact, low-friction, lightweight, and long-life sealing assembly by combining sealing components of different materials and different functions. General coaxial sealing components are composed of plastic sliding rings and rubber elastic bodies, so this combined sealing component is also defined as a sliding ring combined seal. Since the sliding ring is made of materials with low friction coefficient or self-lubricating plastic, it has the above advantages. Its disadvantages are that the leakage is generally larger than that of lip seals, installation is more difficult, and special tools and specified process methods are often required for installation.

① National standard parts I. GB/T 15242.1—2017 specifies three types of coaxial sealing components: square for holes, combined for holes, and stepped for shafts, which are suitable for dynamic sealing of reciprocating motion of hydraulic cylinder pistons and piston rods using water-based or oil-based transmission media.

The replaced standard GB/T 15242.1—1994 stipulates: It is suitable for reciprocating motion hydraulic cylinder pistons and piston rods (plungers) with hydraulic oil as the working medium, working pressure ≤40 MPa, speed ≤5 m/s, and temperature range -40~200°C.
a. Square coaxial seal for holes. It is a piston seal with rectangular cross-section of the sealing ring, and the elastomer is an O-ring or rectangular ring.
b. Combined coaxial seal for holes. It is a piston combination seal composed of a sealing ring, a mountain-shaped elastomer, and two retaining rings.
c. Stepped coaxial seal for shafts. It is a piston rod combination seal with stepped cross-section of the sealing ring and O-ring as the elastomer.

② National standard parts Ⅱ. GB/T 36520.1-2018 specifies four types of (coaxial) seals: single-body bellows (G), T-shaped groove combined bellows (GZ), straight groove combined bellows (GZ), and single-body mountain-shaped ring (SH). Among them, the bidirectional combined bellows (GZ) installed in T-shaped grooves and the bidirectional combined bellows (GZ) installed in straight grooves are composed of polyurethane wear-resistant rings, other rubber elastic rings, and plastic support rings.
Note: If used as a coaxial seal, the statement in GB/T 36520.1-2018 that the bidirectional combined bellows is composed of polyurethane wear-resistant rings and rubber elastic rings is incorrect.
③ Industry standard parts. The standard JB/T 8241-1996 also defines two types of coaxial seals.

a. Mountain-shaped multi-piece combined ring. It is a coaxial seal composed of multiple plastic rings and rubber parts with mountain-shaped cross-sections, with the middle plastic ring serving as the friction sealing surface. It only has a definition but no product standard.

b. Toothed multi-piece combined ring. It is a coaxial seal composed of multiple plastic rings and rubber parts with sawtooth-shaped cross-sections, with the middle plastic ring serving as the friction sealing surface. It only has a definition but no product standard.

4) Bidirectional sealing rubber seals. GB/T 10708.2-2000 specifies bidirectional sealing rubber seals for reciprocating motion (bellows rubber seals and mountain-shaped rubber seals) and their plastic support rings.

GB/T 36520.1-2018 also specifies single-body bidirectional seals (single-body bellows seals and single-body mountain-shaped seals) and sealing structural types. However, it lacks the types and dimensions of plastic supports.

It is worth noting that the friction sealing surfaces of bellows rubber seals and mountain-shaped rubber seals are both rubber, not (plastic) sealing rings. Their sealing principle is similar to that of special-shaped cross-section O-rings.
(2) Lip-shaped rubber seals

Lip-shaped rubber seals have at least one flexible sealing (dust-proof) protrusion, and the pressure of the fluid on one side of the lip keeps it in close contact with the mating surface on the other side to form a seal. More directly described as: in their cross-sectional profiles, they all contain one or more angular so-called lips (or edges) with waists.

Lip-shaped rubber seals named according to their (transverse) cross-sectional shapes include: Y-shaped rubber seals, Yx-shaped rubber seals, V-shaped rubber seals, U-shaped rubber seals, L-shaped rubber seals, J-shaped rubber seals, etc., among which Yx is not defined in the standard GB/T 5719.
GB/T 36520.1-2018 and GB/T 36520.2-2018, issued on 2018-07-13 and implemented on 2019-02-01, respectively specify single-body Y×D seals and single-body Y×d seals.
Furthermore, some rubber dust seals can also be classified as lip-shaped rubber seals.

sections.text: 1) Y-shaped rubber seals. Y-shaped rubber seals (hereinafter referred to as Y-shaped seals) include equal-height lip Y-shaped seals and unequal-height lip (high-low lip) Y-shaped seals; according to their cross-sectional width (different proportions of cross-sectional height and width), there are also wide-section Y-shaped seals and narrow-section Y-shaped seals. Generally, the equal-height lip wide-section Y-shaped seal is simply called a Y-shaped seal; the equal-height lip narrow-section Y-shaped seal is called an EY-shaped seal.

The Y-shaped seal is a one-way seal. The equal-height lip Y-shaped seal is universal for shafts and holes, and there are also two types of shaft and hole types like the unequal-height lip Y-shaped seal. Although the cross-sectional shapes of the equal-height lip Y-shaped seals for shafts and holes are not much different, they are indeed divided into shaft and hole types, such as the piston Y-shaped seal. The equal-height lip Y-shaped seal for holes is marked as Y80×65×9.5; the piston rod Y-shaped seal, the equal-height lip Y-shaped seal for shafts, is marked as Y70×85×9.5, which can be found in GB/T 10708.1.

The service life and sealing performance of the Y-shaped seal are both higher than those of the O-ring. Since the lip of the Y-shaped seal is wider than that of the single V-shaped seal, its sealing performance is better. The static and dynamic friction forces of the Y-shaped seal change little, and in hydraulic cylinders

sections.text: The most commonly used reciprocating motion sealing device in sealing systems. However, since it is a one-way seal, if it is used in situations where pistons require two-way sealing, a pair of Y-rings must be used, which increases the axial size and also makes installation difficult, and sometimes it is necessary to make the groove in a split (open) form.

The characteristics of the Y-ring are that a single seal ring can only achieve one-way sealing, and it can be used under more demanding working conditions. When the reciprocating motion speed is 0.5 m/s and the gap f is 0.2 mm, the working pressure range is 0-15 MPa; when the gap is 0.1 mm, the working pressure range is 0-20 MPa; when the reciprocating motion speed is 0.15 m/s and the gap is 0.2 mm, the working pressure range is 0-20 MPa; when the gap is 0.1 mm, the working pressure range is 0-25 MPa. Generally, the sealing materials used to manufacture Y-rings are nitrile rubber, polyurethane rubber, and fluorine rubber. Y-rings made of these three sealing materials can be used without problems in the temperature range of -20-80°C.

Regarding whether the Y-ring needs to be equipped with a support ring and a retaining ring, GB/T10708.1-2000 does not mention it, but some reference materials introduce that when the pressure fluctuates greatly, an equal-height lip Y-ring needs to use a support ring, while an unequal-height lip Y-ring does not need to use a support ring. When the Y-ring made of nitrile rubber is used, when the working pressure is 14-31.5 MPa, a Y-ring made of polyurethane rubber is used; when the working pressure is >31.5-70 MPa, a retaining ring must be used. The author has no experience in using a support ring for Y-rings, but has practical experience in using a retaining ring, that is, it is decided whether to install a retaining ring according to the conditions for using a retaining ring for Yx-rings, that is, when the working pressure is >16 MPa, it is advisable to install a retaining ring; when the working pressure is >25 MPa, a retaining ring must be installed, and the actual effect is very good.

2) Yx sealing ring. The Yx sealing ring (hereinafter referred to as Yx ring) is also a lip-shaped rubber sealing ring, which is divided into shaft type and hole type, and has the following standards: JB/ZQ4265-2006 "Shaft Yx Sealing Ring" and JB/ZQ4264-2006 "Hole Yx Sealing Ring". These two standards respectively stipulate the type, size and limit deviation of the Yx ring sealing groove. The Yx ring is used under the conditions of temperature -20-80°C and working pressure ≤31.5 MPa.

The cross-sectional height of the Yx ring is 1 times or more larger than its thickness. When used, it is not easy to flip over in the groove, and even when the working pressure and motion speed change greatly, it does not need to be equipped with a support ring. Generally, no retaining ring is provided when using the Yx ring. When the working pressure is >16 MPa, or when the motion pair has a large eccentricity and a large gap, a retaining ring can be placed on the support surface of the sealing ring. It should be noted that some reference materials say that the groove specified in the standard GB/T2879-2005 is the groove specified for the use of Yx rings, which is incorrect.

3) Monolithic Y×D sealing ring and monolithic Y×d sealing ring. The monolithic Y×D sealing ring and monolithic Y×d sealing ring respectively specified in GB/T36520.1-2018 and GB/T36520.2-2018 are lip-shaped polyurethane rubber sealing rings. It is suitable for reciprocating speed of 0.5 m/s, maximum working pressure of 35 MPa, use temperature of -40-80°C, and engineering cylinders with mineral oil as the working medium.

4) V-shaped rubber sealing ring. The V-shaped rubber sealing ring (hereinafter referred to as V-ring) is a typical form of lip-shaped rubber sealing ring, and it is also the earliest and most widely used lip-shaped rubber sealing ring. According to the terms defined in GB/T17446-2012, it is now classified as a packing seal. Its characteristics are good pressure resistance and wear resistance, and it can be overlapped and used according to the pressure, but the disadvantage is that it is large in size, has high friction resistance, and must use a split (open) type sealing groove, and the length of the sealing groove is generally adjustable. On hydraulic cylinders, it is mainly used for reciprocating motion sealing of pistons and piston rods, which can seal holes (piston sealing) and shafts (piston rod sealing), but it is rarely used for rotary sealing and static sealing. V-rings are rarely used alone, and they are usually stacked with pressure rings and elastic sealing rings or support rings, called V-shaped combination sealing rings. In specific use, usually 1-6 V-rings are stacked together with pressure rings and support rings (or elastic sealing rings) to form a V-shaped combination sealing ring, forming one or more seals, with a very good sealing effect. The working pressure of such a V-shaped combination sealing ring can reach 60 MPa or higher. The working pressure of the V-ring is: rubber V-ring is generally 31.5 MPa, and the cloth-rubber V-ring can reach 60 MPa or higher; the working temperature range is -30-100°C, or higher.

5) U-shaped rubber sealing ring. The U-shaped rubber sealing ring (hereinafter referred to as U-ring) is one of the most widely used sealing rings in hydraulic cylinder sealing. It is also a lip-shaped rubber sealing ring. Whether it is used for piston or piston rod sealing, it can achieve good sealing effect.

Before July 13, 2018, there was no U-ring in the current domestic sealing standard, but there was a U-ring definition in GB/T5719-2006, while foreign sealing manufacturers' product samples rarely saw Y-rings. Like Y-rings, U-rings also have equal-height lips and unequal-height lips. Generally, equal-height lip U-rings are universal for shafts and holes, that is, they can be used for piston sealing or piston rod sealing; unequal-height lip U-rings are divided into piston sealing and piston rod sealing. In order to improve the lubrication conditions, reduce the friction force, and increase the service life, there is also a so-called double-lip U-ring (the author believes it should be called double-sealed U-ring). In order to improve the extrusion resistance of the U-ring, there are also U-rings with plastic retaining rings embedded in the bottom of the U-ring, as well as U-rings with both double lips and plastic retaining rings embedded. The U-ring is a rubber sealing ring with a U-shaped cross section. An O-ring or other shaped elastomer (rubber) is embedded in the U-shape to form another form of U-ring. This U-ring has better performance in sealing low-temperature and low-pressure working media, is impact-resistant, high-pressure resistant, and has stable sealing performance. This manual classifies it as a non-typical U-ring, or a (pre-)loaded U-ring.
In the standards GB/T36520.1-2018 and GB/T36520.2-2018 issued on July 13, 2018, monolithic U-shaped sealing rings are provided.

Sealing ring and its sealing structure type, which is a U-shaped ring with equal height lip. According to the above two standards, the lip-shaped sealing ring with equal height lip is called single U-shaped sealing ring; the lip-shaped sealing ring with unequal height lip is called single Y×D sealing ring or single Y×d sealing ring. Although such classification is debatable, at least now there are U-shaped ring products in China.

In addition, GB/T 36520.2-2018 standard also stipulates a combined lace ring (NZ), whose structure type is similar to the above-mentioned "(pre-)loaded U-shaped ring", but its usage conditions are: reciprocating speed of 0.5 m/s, maximum working pressure of 60 MPa, working temperature of -40 to 80°C, medium is water plus emulsion (oil), and application field is hydraulic support.

6) Dust seal ring. GB/T 10708.3-2000 stipulates rubber dust seal rings, which are divided into Type A, B, and C, and they all have at least one lip for dust prevention (Type C has double lips, which play a role in dust prevention and auxiliary sealing), rather than sealing the working medium of the hydraulic cylinder.

Sealing ring (part) material is abbreviated as sealing material.

HG/T 2579-2008 stipulates the classification of O-ring rubber sealing materials for ordinary hydraulic systems resistant to petroleum-based hydraulic oil and lubricating oil (grease). The O-ring rubber sealing materials stipulated in this standard are divided into Class I and Class II according to their working temperature. Each class is divided into four hardness levels. Class I has a working temperature range of -40 to 100°C, and Class II has a working temperature range of -25 to 125°C.

sections.text: 4. Operating Conditions for Hydraulic Cylinders

The operating conditions for hydraulic cylinders generally refer to the situation of driving external loads, as well as the working medium and environment. The operating conditions for hydraulic cylinders can generally be divided into light load, medium load, and heavy load.

The hydraulic cylinder and its seals are designed according to the specified operating conditions and should meet the specified conditions. The specified operating conditions for hydraulic cylinders refer to the conditions that the hydraulic cylinder must satisfy during operation and testing. Therefore, the operating conditions for hydraulic cylinders are only a part of the specified operating conditions.

For the design of hydraulic cylinder seals using hydraulic oil, it is necessary to first clarify the pressure, temperature, speed, stroke, and their ranges that the sealing system should be suitable for.

2.10.2  General Technical Requirements for Hydraulic Cylinder Sealing
1. Overview

One meaning of hydraulic cylinder sealing refers to the hydraulic cylinder sealing device, which is one of the important components of a hydraulic cylinder, used to seal all reciprocating motion areas (dynamic sealing) and connection areas (static sealing). Generally, it includes piston seal, piston rod seal, seal between cylinder body (tube) components, seal between piston and piston rod components, seal at port connections, etc. The hydraulic cylinder sealing device also typically includes dust (seal) protection for piston rods, and guidance and support for pistons and piston rods.
Another meaning of hydraulic cylinder sealing is relative to hydraulic cylinder leakage, expressing a meaning opposite to the phenomenon or state of leakage.

Hydraulic cylinder leakage refers to the phenomenon of hydraulic working medium flowing from the high-pressure side to the low-pressure side through the cavity boundary. Leakage is divided into internal leakage and external leakage.

In current hydraulic cylinder standards, the technical requirements for hydraulic cylinder sealing are an important component, and the design and manufacture of hydraulic cylinders must meet these technical requirements.

sections.text: Some technical requirements. The technical requirements for hydraulic cylinder seals listed in Table 2-67 vary in their expressions, but mainly concern the requirements for static and dynamic sealing performance of hydraulic cylinders.

Under specified conditions, the pressure resistance of hydraulic cylinder seals includes high-pressure resistance, low-pressure resistance, durability, and other performance related to hydraulic cylinder seals, such as starting pressure, minimum speed, and maximum speed. Generally, these must be ensured in hydraulic cylinder design and manufacturing, and for servo hydraulic cylinders, these indicators are also very important.

For the various hydraulic cylinder standards listed in Table 2-67, there are unreasonable or incorrect technical requirements, such as external leakage indicators, minimum speed requirements, and test pressure (nominal pressure or rated pressure) determination, etc. Please note these when determining the technical requirements (conditions) for hydraulic cylinder seals, and you may further refer to reference [102], etc.

2.10.3  General Technical Requirements for Hydraulic Cylinder Sealing Product Quality
1. Appearance Quality

Under natural conditions, when observed with a 2x magnifying glass under appropriate lighting, the surface of the sealing product should not have defects, cracks, damage, bubbles, impurities, or other surface defects exceeding the allowable limits.
The working surface of the rubber seal should be flat and smooth, without pores, impurities, cracks, bubbles, scratches, or axial flow marks.

The working surface of the fabric-reinforced rubber seal should not have broken wires, exposed fabric, delamination, bubbles, impurities, or unevenness. For fabric-reinforced rubber seals with a parting line on the working surface, the height, width, and depth of trimming should not exceed 0.2 mm. Slight unevenness of the fabric layer at the corners is allowed.
The appearance quality of O-ring rubber seals for hydraulic and pneumatic use should comply with the relevant provisions of GB/T 3452.2—2007.
The appearance quality requirements for reciprocating rubber seals, pressure rings, support rings, and retaining rings should comply with the relevant provisions of GB/T 15325—1994.
The appearance quality of polyurethane seals can refer to the relevant provisions of MT/T 985—2006.
2. Dimensions and Tolerances

The measurement of test sample dimensions for rubber seals should be carried out according to the relevant provisions of GB/T 2941—2006 "General Procedures for Preparation and Conditioning of Test Specimens for Rubber Physical Testing Methods".

According to the definition of "rubber sealing products" in GB/T 5719—2005, the definition of "rubber and plastic sealing products" for hydraulic cylinders is proposed, which refers to rubber and plastic components used to prevent fluid working medium from leaking out of the hydraulic cylinder sealing device and to prevent dust, sand, and other pollutants as well as air (for high vacuum) from entering the interior of the hydraulic cylinder and its sealing device.
The dimensions and tolerances of rubber and plastic sealing products for hydraulic cylinders should follow the following standards:

items: GB/T 3452.1—2005 "O-Ring Rubber Seals for Hydraulic and Pneumatic Use Part 1: Dimension Series and Tolerances". The corresponding groove standard is GB/T 3452.3—2005 "Groove Dimensions for O-Ring Rubber Seals for Hydraulic and Pneumatic Use".

GB/T 10708.1—2000 "Structure Dimension Series for Reciprocating Rubber Seals Part 1: Unidirectional Rubber Seals". The corresponding groove standard is GB/T 2879—2005 "Dynamic Sealing Groove Dimensions and Tolerances for Hydraulic Cylinder Pistons and Piston Rods".
GB 2880—1981 "Hydraulic Cylinder Pistons and Piston Rods"

sections.text: Dimensional Series and Tolerances for Sealing Grooves》 is temporarily unavailable for matching sealing rings.

3) GB/T 10708.2-2000《Rubber Sealing Rings for Reciprocating Motion - Part 2: Double-acting Sealing Rings》. Its corresponding groove standard is GB/T 6577-1986《Types, Dimensions and Tolerances of Sealing Grooves for Hydraulic Cylinder Pistons with Supporting Rings》.

4) GB/T 10708.3-2000《Rubber Sealing Rings for Reciprocating Motion - Part 3: Dust Sealing Rings》. Its corresponding groove standard is GB/T 6578-2008《Types, Dimensions and Tolerances of Dust Sealing Grooves for Hydraulic Cylinder Piston Rods》.

5) GB/T 15242.1-2017《Dimensional Series and Tolerances for Dynamic Sealing Devices for Hydraulic Cylinder Pistons and Piston Rods - Part 1: Dimensional Series and Tolerances for Coaxial Seals》. Its corresponding groove standard is GB/T 15242.3-1994《Dimensional Series and Tolerances for Grooves for Installing Coaxial Seals for Dynamic Sealing Devices for Hydraulic Cylinder Pistons and Piston Rods》.

6) GB/T 15242.2-2017《Dimensional Series and Tolerances for Dynamic Sealing Devices for Hydraulic Cylinder Pistons and Piston Rods - Part 2: Supporting Ring Dimensional Series and Tolerances》. Its corresponding groove standard is GB/T 15242.4-1994《Dimensional Series and Tolerances for Grooves for Installing Supporting Rings for Dynamic Sealing Devices for Hydraulic Cylinder Pistons and Piston Rods》.
7) Other sealing rings and their groove standards are JB/ZQ 4264-2006《Y-ring for Holes》, JB/ZQ 4265-2006《Y-ring for Shafts》, JB/T 982-1977《Combined Sealing Gaskets》 (already obsolete), etc.

GB/T 3672.1-2002《Tolerances for Rubber Products - Part 1: Dimensional Tolerances》 applies to products manufactured from vulcanized rubber and thermoplastic rubber, but does not apply to precision annular sealing rings. While MT/T 985-2006 stipulates that the dimensional tolerance limits of sealing rings should meet the requirements of M1 grade in Table 1 of GB/T 3672.1-2002.
3. Hardness

Whether using a Shore hardness tester or a portable international rubber hardness tester to measure rubber hardness, a certain indentation depth is formed on the rubber surface by a comprehensive effect, which is used to represent the hardness measurement result. International rubber hardness is a measure of rubber hardness, and its value is derived from the indentation depth of a indenter on a sample under specified conditions.

Although correction values for converting Shore hardness to international rubber hardness have been established for certain rubbers and compounds, it is now not recommended to directly convert Shore hardness (Shore A, Shore D, Shore AO, Shore AM) values to international rubber hardness (IRHD) values.

The hardness of vulcanized rubber and thermoplastic rubber can be determined by the methods specified in GB/T 531.1-2008《Test Methods for Indentation Hardness of Vulcanized Rubber or Thermoplastic Rubber - Part 1: Shore Hardness Tester Method (Shore Hardness)》 or GB/T 531.2-2009《Test Methods for Indentation Hardness of Vulcanized Rubber or Thermoplastic Rubber - Part 2: Portable International Rubber Hardness Tester Method》 and GB/T 6031-1998《Determination of Hardness of Vulcanized Rubber or Thermoplastic Rubber (10-100 IRHD)》.
The micro-hardness tester specified for O-ring hardness determination in GB/T 5720-2008 should comply with the relevant provisions in GB/T 6031.

The micro-hardness test method specified in GB/T 6031 is essentially a scaled-down version of the conventional test method, suitable for rubber hardness in the range of 35-85 IRHD, and can also be used for rubber with hardness in the range of 30-95 IRHD and sample thickness less than 4 mm.
MT/T 985 cites the GB/T 531 standard in its normative references. The hardness of polyurethane sealing rings specified in MT/T 985 is:

items: At 23°C, the hardness value of single-piece sealing rings should be 90 +5/-4 Shore A.
At 23°C, the hardness value of the outer ring of composite sealing rings should be greater than 90 Shore A.
At 23°C, the hardness value of the inner ring of composite sealing rings should be greater than 70 Shore A.

sections.text: 4. Tensile Strength
Tensile strength is the maximum tensile stress during the stretching of a sample until fracture. Dumbbell-shaped samples should be used to determine tensile strength.

The tensile strength of vulcanized rubber and thermoplastic rubber can be determined by the method specified in GB/T 528-2009《Determination of Tensile Stress-Strain Properties of Vulcanized Rubber or Thermoplastic Rubber》. The principle is: on a tensile testing machine with moving clamps or pulleys moving at constant speed, dumbbell-shaped samples are stretched, and the maximum force value during the continuous stretching of the sample is recorded as required.

GB/T 5720-2008《Test Methods for O-Rubber Sealing Rings》 cites GB/T 528-1998 (replaced by GB/T 528-2009) and HG/T 2369-1992《Technical Conditions for Rubber and Plastic Tensile Testing Machines》 (already obsolete) in its normative references.
MT/T 985 cites the GB/T 528 standard in its normative references. The tensile strength of polyurethane sealing rings specified in MT/T 985 is:

items: At 23°C, the tensile strength of single-piece sealing rings and the outer ring of composite sealing ring products should be greater than 35 MPa.
At 23°C, the tensile strength of the inner ring of composite sealing rings should be greater than 16 MPa.

sections.text: 5. Elongation at Break

Elongation at break is the percentage elongation at break of a sample. Ring-shaped samples can obtain approximately the same elongation at break values as dumbbell-shaped samples under the following conditions:

items: The elongation of ring-shaped samples is calculated as a percentage of the initial inner circumference.
If the "calendering effect" is obvious, the dumbbell-shaped sample is cut perpendicular to the calendering direction along the length.

sections.text: The elongation at break of vulcanized rubber and thermoplastic rubber can be determined by the method specified in

194.page_header: Chapter 2  Design of Hydraulic Cylinders and Basic Components  183

sections.text: Methods specified in GB/T 528—2009 "Determination of Tensile Stress-Strain Properties of Vulcanized Rubber and Thermoplastic Rubber" are used for measurement. The principle is: The dumbbell-shaped or ring-shaped standard specimen is stretched on a tensile testing machine with a moving clamp or pulley moving at constant speed, and the elongation value of the specimen at break is recorded as required.
In the normative references of GB/T 5720—2008 "Test Methods for O-ring Rubber Seals", GB/T 528—1998 (replaced by GB/T 528—2009) is cited.
In the normative references of MT/T 985, GB/T 528—1998 (replaced by GB/T 528—2009) is cited. The elongation at break for polyurethane seals specified in MT/T 985 is:

items: At 23°C, the elongation at break for single-piece seals should be greater than 400%.
At 23°C, the elongation at break for the outer ring of composite seals should be greater than 350%.
At 23°C, the elongation at break for the inner ring of composite seals should be greater than 260%.

sections.text: 6. Compression Set

When rubber is under compression, physical and chemical changes will inevitably occur. After the compressive force is removed, these changes prevent the rubber from returning to its original state, resulting in permanent deformation. The magnitude of compression set depends on the temperature and time under compression, as well as the temperature and time during height recovery. At high temperatures, chemical changes are the main reason for compression set in rubber. Compression set is measured after removing the compressive force applied to the specimen and allowing it to recover to a standard height. When testing at low temperatures, changes caused by hardening and crystallization in the glassy state are the main factors; these effects disappear when the temperature rises. Therefore, the test height must be measured at the test temperature.
The test principles given in GB/T 7759 are divided into room temperature/high temperature test principles and low temperature test principles:
(1) Room Temperature and High Temperature Test Principles

At standard laboratory temperature, the specimen of known height is compressed to the specified height according to the compression requirements, maintained under standard laboratory temperature or high temperature for a certain time, then the compression is removed at a certain temperature, and the specimen is allowed to recover freely for a specified time before measuring its height.
(2) Low Temperature Test Principles

At standard laboratory temperature, the specimen of known height is compressed to the specified height according to the compression requirements, maintained for a certain time at the specified low temperature test temperature, then the compression is removed at the same low temperature, and the specimen is allowed to recover freely before measuring its height; measurements can be taken at regular intervals (obtaining a logarithmic curve of specimen height versus time to evaluate the compression set characteristics of the specimen), or measurement can be taken after a specified time.
Normal temperature compression set. Testing is conducted at normal temperature, with test temperature of (23±2)°C or (27±2)°C.
In the normative references of GB/T 5720—2008 "Test Methods for O-ring Rubber Seals", GB/T 7759—1996 is cited.
In the normative references of MT/T 985, GB/T 7759—1996 is cited. The normal temperature compression set for polyurethane seals specified in MT/T 985 is:

items: The compression set for single-piece seals should be less than 25%.
The compression set for the outer ring of composite seals should be less than 30%.

sections.text: High temperature compression set. Testing is conducted at high temperature, with test temperature options of (40±1)°C, (55±1)°C, (70±1)°C, (85±1)°C, (100±1)°C, (125±2)°C, (150±2)°C, (175±2)°C, (200±2)°C, (225±2)°C, or (250±2)°C.
In the normative references of GB/T 5720—2008 "Test Methods for O-ring Rubber Seals", GB/T 7759—1996 is cited.
In the normative references of MT/T 985, GB/T 7759—1996 is cited. The high temperature compression set for polyurethane seals specified in MT/T 985 is:

items: The compression set for single-piece seals should be less than 45%.
The compression set for the outer ring of composite seals should be less than 50%.
The compression set for the inner ring of composite seals should be less than 30%.

sections.text: 7. Fluid Resistance Properties
The action of liquids on vulcanized rubber or thermoplastic rubber typically results in the following:

items: Liquid is absorbed by the rubber.
Soluble components are extracted from the rubber.
Chemical reactions occur with the rubber.

sections.text: Generally, the amount of absorption (1) is greater than the amount extracted (2), causing the rubber volume to increase. This phenomenon is called "swelling". Absorption of liquid causes significant changes in the physical and chemical properties of rubber such as tensile strength, elongation at break, and hardness. Additionally, plasticizers and antioxidant-type soluble substances in rubber are easily extracted by volatile liquids, and the physical and chemical properties of the dried rubber also change significantly. Therefore, it is important to test the properties of rubber after soaking or further drying.

GB/T 1690—2010 "Test Methods for Fluid Resistance of Vulcanized Rubber and Thermoplastic Rubber" specifies testing the changes in properties of rubber before and after soaking in test fluids to evaluate the effects of liquids on rubber.

In the normative references of GB/T 5720—2008 "Test Methods for O-ring Rubber Seals", GB/T 1690—1992 (replaced by GB/T 1690—2010) is cited, and GB/T 5720 provides calculation methods for percentage mass change and percentage volume change.
In the normative references of MT/T 985, GB/T 1690—1992 is cited. The fluid resistance properties for polyurethane seals specified in MT/T 985 are:

items: The mass change rate should be less than 15%.
The volume change rate should be less than 25%.

sections.text: Polyurethane sealing rings specified in the 1690-1992 standard and MT/T 985 shall meet the following hydrolysis resistance requirements: For polyurethane single-piece sealing rings and the outer rings of composite sealing rings, the hydrolysis resistance performance (over 8 weeks) shall meet the following requirements: 1) Hardness change decrease shall be less than 9%. 2) Tensile strength change decrease shall be less than 18%. 3) Elongation at break change decrease shall be less than 9%. 4) Volume change shall be less than 6%. 5) Mass change shall be less than 6%.
8. Heat Aging Performance

The heat aging and heat resistance test of vulcanized rubber or thermoplastic rubber under atmospheric pressure is a test in which samples are aged in high-temperature air under atmospheric pressure, and their performance is measured and compared with that of unaged samples. The physical properties often measured include tensile strength, elongation at a specified stress, elongation at break, and hardness.
GB/T 5720-2008 "Test Methods for O-Ring Rubber Seals" normatively references GB/T 3512-2001 "Heat Aging and Heat Resistance Test for Vulcanized Rubber or Thermoplastic Rubber".
MT/T 985 normatively references GB/T 3512-2001 standard.

MT/T 985 stipulates that after aging, the performance of polyurethane single-piece sealing rings and the outer rings of composite sealing rings shall meet: 1) Hardness change decrease shall be less than 8%. 2) Tensile strength change decrease shall be less than 10%. 3) Elongation at break change decrease shall be less than 12%. MT/T 985 stipulates that after aging, the performance of the inner rings of polyurethane composite sealing rings shall meet: 1) Hardness change decrease shall be less than 8%. 2) Tensile strength change decrease shall be less than 10%. 3) Elongation at break change decrease shall be less than 30%.
9. Low-Temperature Performance

GB/T 7758-2002 "Determination of Low-Temperature Performance of Vulcanized Rubber - Temperature Retraction Method (TR Test)" stipulates the method for determining the temperature retraction performance of stretched vulcanized rubber. The principle is: stretch the sample at room temperature, then cool it to a sufficiently low temperature at which no retraction occurs when the stretching force is removed. Remove the stretching force and raise the temperature at a uniform rate. Measure the temperature at which the specified retraction occurs.
GB/T 5720-2008 "Test Methods for O-Ring Rubber Seals" normatively references GB/T 7758-2002 standard.

MT/T 985 normatively references GB/T 7759-1996 "Determination of Compression Set of Vulcanized Rubber and Thermoplastic Rubber at Room Temperature, High Temperature, and Low Temperature". Please refer to Section 6 of this paper for the principle.

MT/T 985 stipulates that after low-temperature treatment, the performance of the inner and outer rings of polyurethane single-piece sealing rings and composite sealing rings shall meet: 1) Hardness change decrease shall be less than 8%. 2) Tensile strength change decrease shall be less than 10%. 3) Elongation at break change decrease shall be less than 12%. However, the measurement of the above three performance parameters lacks standard basis.
10. Reliability

The reliability of sealing rings refers to the ability to ensure their sealing performance under specified conditions for a specified time. Reliability is determined by various factors such as design, manufacturing, use, and maintenance, and is therefore a comprehensive performance index. The term reliability is sometimes used in a general sense to indicate availability (effectiveness) and durability. The reliability of sealing rings specified in JB/T 10205-2010 mainly includes pressure resistance performance (including low-pressure resistance performance) and durability performance. Please refer to JB/T 10205-2010 "Hydraulic Cylinders" for details.

MT/T 985 stipulates that polyurethane sealing rings shall meet the requirement of 21,000 test cycles for reliable sealing. However, durability tests conducted without "specified conditions" generally do not have repeatability and comparability.
Therefore, it is still appropriate to follow the relevant provisions in JB/T 10205-2010 regarding the reliability of sealing rings.
11. Operating Temperature Range

According to the provisions of JB/T 10205-2010 "Hydraulic Cylinders" standard, generally, the operating temperature of hydraulic cylinders should be within the range of -20 to 50°C, and the working medium temperature should be within the range of -20 to 80°C. At the same time, it is also stipulated that when the product has high-temperature requirements, under rated pressure, 90°C working oil should be input into the tested hydraulic cylinder, and reciprocating operation for 1 hour should meet the high-temperature requirements of the hydraulic cylinder agreed upon by both parties.

HG/T 2810-2008 "Materials for Reciprocating Rubber Seals" standard stipulates that reciprocating rubber seal materials are divided into two categories: A and B. Category A is nitrile rubber material, divided into three hardness grades and five types of rubber, with an operating temperature range of -30 to 100°C; Category B is castable polyurethane rubber material, divided into four hardness grades and four types of rubber, with an operating temperature range of -40 to 80°C.
MT/T 985 stipulates that polyurethane sealing rings should be able to adapt to temperatures in the range of -20 to 60°C.
12. Sealing Pressure Range

Sealing pressure refers to the pressure of the sealing medium that the sealing ring bears during operation. Generally speaking, the sealing pressure of a sealing ring is closely related to factors such as the sealing material and structure type of the sealing ring, the sealing medium and temperature, groove type and dimensions and tolerances, unilateral radial clearance, surface quality and relative movement speed of the mating parts. Therefore, the sealing pressure or sealing pressure range must be specified under certain conditions.
GB/T 3452.1-2005 "O-Ring Rubber Seals for Hydraulic and Pneumatic Use - Part 1: Size Series and Tolerances" and GB/T

196.page_header: Chapter 2 Design of Hydraulic Cylinders and Their Components 185

sections.text: 3452.3-2005 "Hydraulic and Pneumatic O-Ring Groove Dimensions for General Applications" standard does not specify sealing pressure and range, but GB/T 2878.1-2011 "Hydraulic Connections with Metrical Threads and O-Ring Seals - Part 1: Ports" standard specifies that the maximum working pressure for ports is 63 MPa. The allowable working pressure should be determined based on factors such as port size, material, structure, working conditions, and application.

In GB/T 10708.1-2000 "Reciprocating Rubber Seals for Hydraulic and Pneumatic Applications - Part 1: Single Acting Seals" standard, Appendix A provides the working pressure range for Y-type rubber seals as 0-25 MPa, the working pressure range for U-cup rubber seals as 0-50 MPa, and the working pressure range for V-type combination seals as 0-60 MPa.

In GB/T 10708.2-2000 "Reciprocating Rubber Seals for Hydraulic and Pneumatic Applications - Part 2: Double Acting Seals" standard, Appendix A provides the working pressure range for D-type rubber seals as 0.10-70 MPa, and the working pressure range for M-type rubber seals as 0-35 MPa.

Although C-type dust seals specified in GB/T 10708.3-2000 "Reciprocating Rubber Seals for Hydraulic and Pneumatic Applications - Part 3: Rubber Dust Seals" standard have auxiliary sealing functions, the sealing pressure is not provided.

GB/T 15242.1-1994 "Coaxial Seals for Reciprocating Hydraulic and Pneumatic Pistons and Piston Rods - Part 1: Dimensions and Tolerances Series" (has been superseded) standard specifies that this standard is applicable to reciprocating hydraulic cylinder pistons and piston rods (plungers) with hydraulic oil as the working medium, pressure ≤40 MPa, speed ≤5 m/s, and temperature range of -40 to 200°C.

JB/ZQ 4264-2006 "YX Type Seals for Holes" and JB/ZQ 4265-2006 "YX Type Seals for Shafts" standards specify that these standards are applicable to YX type seals for holes (shafts) that provide sealing function under the conditions of temperature -40 (-20) to 80°C and working pressure p ≤31.5 MPa in various mechanical equipment with air or mineral oil as the medium.

JB/T 982-1977 "Combined Gasket" standard specifies that this standard only specifies combined gaskets for welded, ferrule, flared tube joints and plugs, with nominal pressure of 40 MPa and working temperature of -25 to 80°C.

GB/T 13871.1-2007 "Radial Shaft Seals with Elastomeric Sealing Element - Part 1: Basic Dimensions and Tolerances" standard specifies that this standard is applicable to radial shaft seals with shaft diameters of 6 to 400 mm and matching housings of 16 to 440 mm, but is not applicable to radial shaft seals used under high pressure (>0.05 MPa).

MT/T 985 specifies the sealing pressure range for polyurethane seals: the sealing pressure range for bidirectional polyurethane seals is 2-60 MPa, and the sealing pressure range for unidirectional polyurethane seals is 2-40 MPa.
1.3 Other Performance Requirements

GB/T 5720-2008 "O-Ring Rubber Seals - Test Methods" standard specifies test methods for dimension measurement, hardness, tensile properties, heat air aging, constant deflection compression set, corrosion test, fluid resistance, density, shrinkage, low temperature test, and compression stress relaxation for solid vulcanized O-ring rubber seals, but does not provide performance indicators for seals.

MT/T 985-2006 "Technical Conditions for Polyurethane Seals for Coal Mine Props and Jacks" standard specifies terms and definitions, seal groove dimensions, requirements, test methods, inspection rules, marking, packaging, transportation, and storage for polyurethane seals used in coal mine props and jacks, which are applicable to polyurethane seals for coal mine props and jacks with high water content hydraulic oil (including emulsion) as the working medium, but does not specifically provide seal performance test methods, only references the following documents in normative references:
GB/T 528-1998 "Determination of Tensile Stress-Strain Properties of Vulcanized Rubber or Thermoplastic Rubber"
GB/T 531-1999 "Test Method for Indentation Hardness of Rubber Using a Pocket Hardness Tester"
GB/T 1690-1992 "Test Methods for Fluid Resistance of Vulcanized Rubber"
GB/T 3512-2001 "Accelerated Aging and Heat Resistance Test for Vulcanized or Thermoplastic Rubber"
GB/T 3672.1-2002 "Tolerances for Rubber Products - Part 1: Dimensional Tolerances"

GB/T 7759-1996 "Determination of Compression Set of Vulcanized Rubber and Thermoplastic Rubber at Room Temperature, High Temperature and Low Temperature". GB/T 7759-1996 has been superseded by GB/T 7759.1-2015 "Determination of Compression Set of Vulcanized or Thermoplastic Rubber - Part 1: At Room Temperature and High Temperature". GB/T 7759 also has Part 2, i.e. GB/T 7759.2-2014 "Determination of Compression Set of Vulcanized or Thermoplastic Rubber - Part 2: At Low Temperature".
The test specimens specified in the above standards are generally "test specimens" prepared according to the relevant standards, rather than actual seal products.

In addition to the above standards, there are also some current standards for seal (ring) performance test methods, such as wear resistance, adhesion to metal and swelling index, which can be used to further determine seal performance.
Note: Some of the standards referenced in the normative references of MT/T 985-2006 have been updated.

Performance testing methods given in the paper "Research on Polyurethane Elastomer Sealing Materials for Coal Mining Machinery" by Han Shengguang, Wu Bin, and Qiu Zhaopei are as follows: Hardness is tested according to GB/T 531.1—2008; Tensile strength, elongation at break, and tear strength are tested according to GB/T 528—2009; Rebound resilience is tested according to GB/T 1681—2009; Tear strength is tested according to GB/T 529—2008 using crescent-shaped specimens. Heat resistance testing is conducted on a tensile testing machine after baking for 0.5 h at the set temperature; Water emulsion medium resistance testing involves sealing the sample in a container and baking in an oven for 21 days.
2.10.4 Test Methods for Performance of Hydraulic Reciprocating Seal Elements

The test conditions and methods for performance of hydraulic reciprocating seal elements specified in GB/T 32217—2015 are applicable for evaluating the performance of hydraulic reciprocating seal elements using hydraulic oil as the transmission medium.

To obtain comparative data on reciprocating seal performance and provide a basis for seal design and selection, the following factors affecting seal performance must be strictly controlled in testing hydraulic reciprocating seal elements:

items: (1) Installation
1) Seal system design including support rings, seal elements, and dust wipers
2) Installation tolerances including seal groove, piston rod, support ring, and extrusion gap
3) Piston rod material and hardness
4) Piston rod surface roughness - values outside Ra0.08-0.15μm or greater than Rt1.5μm will seriously affect seal performance. The optimal surface roughness varies with different seal materials
5) Groove surface roughness - should be less than Ra0.8μm to avoid static leakage and seal wear during pressure cycling
6) Support ring material including effects on piston rod texture and boundary layer
(2) Operation
1) Fluid medium including viscosity, lubricity, compatibility with seal material and additives, and contamination level
2) Pressure including pressure cycling
3) Speed especially speed cycling
4) Speed/pressure cycling such as start-stop conditions
5) Stroke length especially short strokes (2 times or less than the seal contact width) that prevent oil film formation
6) Temperature including effects on viscosity and seal material properties
7) External environment

sections.text: When using standard test results to predict actual seal performance, all these factors and their potential effects on seal performance must be considered.

Author's note: 1. Without control of factors affecting installation and operation of reciprocating seals, devices, or systems, test results for reciprocating seals will be unpredictable and cannot be used for performance comparison.

sections.text: 4. Measurement Method and Instruments
(1) Leakage

Before each test, a measuring cylinder with a range of 10 mL and an accuracy of 0.1 mL should be prepared. If the test leakage exceeds 10 mL, a measuring cylinder with a larger range and an accuracy of 1 mL should be prepared.
(2) Friction Force

1) Force Sensor. The force sensor should be installed between the linear driver of the test device and the test piston rod to measure the pulling force and pressure caused by the friction of the sealing element. The force sensor should be connected to a suitable adjustment device and a chart recorder to retain the friction force record. The chart recorder should have appropriate frequency response to measure the amplitude of the friction force.
2) Determination of Dynamic Friction Force.
① At the beginning of each test, the inherent friction force F₁ of the sliding bearing ring and dust seal should be measured.
② From the curve of the chart recorder (see Figure 2-9 and Figure 2-10 in GB/T 32217-2015), calculate the average friction force of the test sealing element, as shown in Equation (2-56).

Where: Fs — Average value of the friction force of a single test sealing element during the forward stroke and return stroke; F₁ — Sum of the inherent friction forces of the test device during the forward stroke and return stroke; Ft — Sum of the friction forces of the two test sealing elements and the test device during the forward stroke and return stroke.
Note: Fs is an average value and cannot be used as the actual friction force of a specified stroke of a single sealing element.
3) Steps for Measuring Starting Friction Force.
① Set the test circuit pressure and start the static test cycle (e.g., 16 h).
② After completing the static test cycle, adjust the drive circuit pressure to zero.
③ Set the test speed.
④ Set the direction of the piston rod movement, and move the test sealing element A in the forward direction.
⑤ Start the chart recorder, see 4.(2)1).
⑥ Gradually increase the drive circuit pressure to make the piston rod start moving.
⑦ Record the friction force at the instant when the piston rod starts moving, see Figure 10 in GB/T 32217-2015.
⑧ Increase the drive circuit pressure to overcome the friction force during movement and perform dynamic tests.
(3) Pressure Measurement
1) Pressure Gauge. A pressure gauge with an appropriate range should be installed and ensure it is reliable under cyclic pressure conditions.

2) Pressure Sensor. Select a suitable pressure sensor and install it according to the requirements shown in Figure 2-10 to record the test pressure cycle. The pressure sensor should have temperature compensation function to ensure the measurement error is within ±0.5% (relative) at 65°C.
(4) Surface Roughness
The surface roughness measurement should comply with GB/T 6062-2009 and be equipped with a filter.
(5) Temperature Measurement
The thermocouple should be installed according to the requirements shown in Figure 2-10 and be able to withstand the maximum circuit pressure. The thermocouple should be calibrated to ±0.25°C.

The instruments and measuring equipment used to complete the test should be calibrated annually according to traceable national standards. 6. Test Procedure
(1) Test Steps

items: Measure the surface roughness Ra and Rt of the piston rod along the axial direction of the piston rod according to GB/T 10610-2009. Take a sample length of 0.8 mm each time, and the evaluation length is 4 mm.
Use a non-contact measuring instrument with a resolution of 0.02 mm to measure the dimensions of the new test sealing element: d₁, d₂, S₁, S₂, and h.
Install the new test sealing element and two new leak-collecting dust seals.
Raise the oil temperature to the test temperature.
The test device reciprocates at a linear speed v under stable medium pressure p₁ for 1 h.
Before the end of the reciprocating motion, record the friction force curve of at least one cycle and record the friction force Ft.
Stop the reciprocating motion, maintain the test pressure p₁ and test temperature for 16 h.
Measure the starting friction force according to 4.(2)3).
The test device continues to reciprocate at a linear speed v according to the cycle requirements of 2.(6), with the pressure alternating between the forward stroke p₁ and the return stroke p₂.
Complete 200,000 uninterrupted cycles (complete 60,000 cycles when the linear speed is 0.05 m/s). If the cycle is interrupted, ignore the restart.

GB/T 3227-2015 "Hydraulic Transmission - Sealing Device - Test Method for Evaluating the Performance of Hydraulic Reciprocating Motion Seals" was issued on December 10, 2015, and implemented on January 1, 2017

The author has interpreted and discussed it many times, and has also used this standard to evaluate the performance test bench of a domestic seal company. Now some issues that need attention in the application process of this standard are explained:
Some Issues Regarding the Standard

1) Hydraulic reciprocating motion seals or sealing devices undoubtedly include hydraulic cylinder piston dynamic sealing devices and hydraulic cylinder piston rod dynamic sealing devices. This can be proved from the normative references of the standard, because it cites GB/T 15242.2-2017 "Hydraulic Cylinder Piston and Piston Rod Dynamic Sealing Device Dimensional Series Part 2: Support Ring Dimensional Series and Tolerances". In GB/T 3227-2015, only the schematic diagram of the hydraulic cylinder piston rod dynamic sealing test device is given (see Figure 1), but the schematic diagram of the hydraulic cylinder piston dynamic sealing test device is not given, that is, the test device for evaluating the hydraulic cylinder piston dynamic sealing device (or seal) is missing.
It is recommended that all parties speed up research and provide test devices and test methods for hydraulic cylinder piston dynamic sealing devices (or seals).

2) The test medium temperature specified in GB/T 3227-2015 has only one temperature, which is inconsistent with some hydraulic cylinder standards. This will lead to the test results obtained according to this standard cannot be used as a reference when the hydraulic cylinder actually applies this type of seal, and it loses the engineering significance that the test should have. It is recommended that, like other test parameters, the test temperature should also provide "series standard values", among which at least one test temperature value should be adapted to the current hydraulic cylinder standard.

3) The starting friction force test specified in GB/T 3227-2015 is also different from the hydraulic cylinder starting pressure characteristic test specified in general standards. For example, JB/T 10205-2010 stipulates: "The pressure in the rodless chamber (double rod hydraulic cylinder, either chamber can be used) is gradually increased until the hydraulic cylinder starts, and the recorded starting pressure is the minimum starting pressure." The seal is subjected to gradually increasing pressure, rather than "maintaining the test pressure p₁" to measure the starting friction force. The "starting pressure characteristic" test specified in JB/T 10205-2010 is basically the same as the working conditions of the actual application of the hydraulic cylinder, while the test specified in GB/T 3227-2015 does not match the actual working conditions of the hydraulic cylinder, and the consistency of the test results of the two cannot be evaluated, and the test may not be able to "provide a basis for the design and selection of seals".

4) It can be determined from Figure 5 given in GB/T 3227-2015 that the so-called dust ring 1 (see Figure 6) does not have the structural characteristics of "a device used on a reciprocating rod to prevent contaminants from intruding", because it does not have a sealing lip to prevent contaminants from intruding, and its structural shape is consistent with the Y-shape or U-shape specified in the current standards. In this regard, hydraulic cylinders should generally have dust protection devices, and piston rod sealing systems or devices without dust seals have no practical application value; at the same time, test devices without dust protection devices are also very dangerous in tests.

In addition, this standard does not specify the cleanliness of the test environment. It is recommended to use a double-lip dust ring (such as a C-type dust ring), which can play the role of dust prevention and auxiliary sealing.
5) Judging from the test steps specified in GB/T 3227-2015, some issues affect the specific operation of the test:

items: In "The test device reciprocates at a linear velocity v and stable medium pressure p₁ for 1 h", v and p₁ are not specified, so it is not easy to operate and it is easy to cause disputes.

According to the test steps specified in GB/T 3227-2015, the test is mainly divided into three stages: reciprocating motion for 1 h and maintaining test pressure p₁ and test temperature for 16 h, and measuring starting friction force is the first stage; completing 200,000 uninterrupted cycles (at a linear velocity of 0.05 m/s, completing

202.page_header: Chapter 2  Design of Hydraulic Cylinders and Basic Components  191

sections.text: 6 million cycles) is the second segment; completing a total of 300,000 uninterrupted cycles (at a linear speed of 0.05 m/s, completing 100,000 cycles) is the third segment. There is a problem here: in addition to the linear speed of 0.05 m/s, the standard values for the speed series also include two other speeds of 0.15 m/s and 0.5 m/s, so how to choose the speed in the latter two stages of the test is an issue.

③ In the above three stages of tests, the friction force (under constant pressure) was recorded or measured respectively, but how to deal with these three friction force values is not clearly specified in Appendix B (normative appendix) of GB/T32217-2015.
④ Similarly, in the latter two stages of tests, "starting friction force" measurements were also performed, so how to deal with these two starting friction force values is also an issue.
⑥ There are also some statements, algorithms, or practices in this standard that are worth discussing:

items: In the introduction of this standard, "key variables" are proposed, and it is required that "tests on sealing elements should strictly control these key variables," but no subsequent text specifies what the key variables are.

In "At the beginning of each test, the inherent friction force F₁ of the sliding bearing ring and dust seal ring should be measured," the "sliding bearing ring" and "inherent friction force F₁" are unknown as to which standard they come from, and it is also unclear how to measure the inherent friction force F₁.

Due to the issue of "inherent friction force F₁," the calculation formula (2-56) for the average friction force of the tested sealing element also has problems. Of course, the calculation result (average friction force of the tested sealing element) is also worth discussing.

In "Fs -- the average value of the friction force during the forward stroke and return stroke of a single tested sealing element," the "forward stroke" and "return stroke" are unknown as to which standard they come from, and their specific meanings are also unclear.

In the "steps for measuring starting friction force," the "drive circuit pressure" is unclear because there is no drive circuit in the test device schematic diagram (original figure 1), only a "linear driver."

Since this standard includes both "starting friction force" and "kinetic friction force," the original formula (1) should be for calculating the average kinetic friction force of the tested component, rather than "calculating the average friction force of the tested component." There are also situations elsewhere where "kinetic friction force" and "friction force" are mixed.

sections.text: 2.10.5  Hydraulic Cylinder Sealing Elements and Their Grooves
1. O-ring Rubber Sealing Elements and Their Grooves
(1) Characteristics and Functions of O-rings

As shown in Figure 2-17, O-ring rubber sealing elements (abbreviated as O-rings) are rubber rings with a ring shape and a circular cross-section (or cross-sectional shape of O-ring), which are the most widely used and produced sealing elements. They can be used for both static and dynamic sealing, and are also the basic components of many combined sealing devices. The O-rings currently in use are basically molded from synthetic rubber. Ordinary O-rings for hydraulic systems are divided into two categories, I and II, based on their working temperature range, and each category is further divided into four levels based on hardness. Category I has a working temperature range of -40 to 100°C, while category II has a working temperature range of -25 to 125°C; the applicable working medium is petroleum-based hydraulic oil and lubricating oil. O-rings for other working conditions and working media different from those mentioned above need to be selected from other suitable rubber materials. If ordinary O-ring molds are still used for pressing, it may result in incorrect inner diameter dimensions and cross-sectional diameter dimensions of the O-ring; in this case, it is necessary to redesign the sealing groove or open a new molding mold to achieve the O-ring corresponding to the standard groove. Since the design and manufacturing of O-ring molding molds are relatively simple, O-rings are chosen for sealing in many special occasions. Therefore, there are many situations where O-ring grooves need to be designed.
For the design and manufacturing of O-rings, readers can further refer to Reference [102] and its references.
O-rings have the following advantages compared to other sealing rings:

items: The sealing groove is simple and has small dimensions.
It can achieve bidirectional sealing and can be used for both dynamic and static sealing.
It has good static sealing performance.
It has small dynamic friction resistance and can also be used in situations with alternating pressure.
Both O-rings and their grooves have current standards, making them easy to select and use.
They are easy to manufacture and inexpensive.

sections.text: It should be noted that O-rings are now rarely used alone for dynamic sealing in hydraulic cylinders in China - reciprocating motion sealing, while static sealing in hydraulic cylinders still frequently uses them, so readers should pay attention.
(2) Sealing Design of O-rings

After selecting an O-ring, the compression rate and elongation rate of the O-ring and its working state are determined by the groove (or sealing groove). The design and selection of the sealing groove have a great impact on the sealing performance and service life. The design of the sealing groove is the main content of O-ring sealing design. The design of the sealing groove mainly includes determining the shape (structural type), dimensions and tolerances, surface roughness, etc. of the sealing groove. It should be emphasized that the design of chamfers or fillets, geometric tolerances, etc. at various parts of the groove is particularly important; determining the fitting clearance for reciprocating motion sealing is also very important. In summary, the O-ring
The design of seal groove should follow: reasonable dimension design, easy processing and manufacturing, guaranteed precision, and convenient assembly and disassembly during maintenance.

1) Seal groove shape. The common seal groove for O-ring rubber seals used in hydraulic and pneumatic systems is the rectangular groove, as shown in Figure 2-18. GB/T 3452.3-2005 "O-ring Rubber Seals for Hydraulic and Pneumatic Systems - Groove Dimensions" stipulates the groove dimensions and tolerances for O-ring rubber seals for general hydraulic and pneumatic applications. This type of groove has the advantages of easy processing and manufacturing, convenient measurement, and good dimension and precision guarantee. In addition to rectangular grooves, there are also some other shaped special O-ring seal grooves, but they are generally not commonly used in hydraulic cylinder seals, as shown in Figure 2-19.

To ensure sufficient sealing under normal conditions, the compression rate should be determined when designing O-rings, which is often given by experience. The size of the compression rate is achieved by modifying the depth of the sealing groove.

⑤ O-ring swelling. When O-rings come into contact with hydraulic working medium, they absorb a certain amount of hydraulic working medium and expand. The size of the expansion varies with different sealing materials and hydraulic working media. The volume of the O-ring sealing groove should be able to accommodate the swelling of the O-ring and the expansion of the O-ring due to temperature rise.

⑥ Groove depth. The depth of the groove is determined based on working conditions and experience to determine the compression rate of the O-ring. The extreme values of the groove depth and the corresponding range of compression rate for piston seals and piston rod seals generally applied should comply with the provisions of Table 2-72. The extreme values of the axial seal groove depth and their corresponding range of compression rate should comply with the provisions of Table 2-73.

sections.text: Note: 1. The table gives the extreme values. The groove depth value for piston rod seals and their corresponding compression rate should be selected according to actual needs.
Note 2. The extreme values with background color are debatable, and t should be the radial depth of the groove, t=t'+g, where t' is the groove depth; g is the unilateral radial clearance.

sections.text: ⑦ Groove width. The width of the sealing groove in GB/T 3452.3—2005 "O-rings for hydraulic and pneumatic use" is given based on the volume swelling value of 15% of O-ring material. When purchasing O-rings, it is required to request the volume swelling rate parameter from the seal manufacturer.

⑧ Rounded corners at all parts of the groove. Practice has proved that the rounded corners at all parts of the groove are very important and directly related to the service life of the O-ring. Proper rounded corners at the edges of the groove can ensure that the O-ring is not scratched during assembly and not cut (squeezed) when pressed. Generally, they are processed into R0.1~R0.3. Proper rounded corners at the bottom of the groove can not only avoid stress concentration here but also prevent excessive deformation and squeezing at the bottom corner when the O-ring is pressed. When the cross-section diameter of the O-ring is φ1.8, φ2.65, the radius of the rounded corner at the bottom of the groove is R0.2~R0.4; when the cross-section diameter of the O-ring is φ3.55~φ5.30, the bottom radius is R0.4~R0.8; when the cross-section diameter of the O-ring is φ7, the bottom radius is R0.8~R1.2. However, the rounded corner at the bottom of the groove should not be too large, as it is easy for the O-ring to extrude if it is too large.

⑨ Clearance. There must be clearance between the mating surfaces of reciprocating motion, and the size of the clearance is related to factors such as the pressure, viscosity of the hydraulic working medium, the cross-section size of the O-ring, and the hardness of the sealing material. Attention should also be paid to the working temperature when designing and selecting the clearance. Generally speaking, the higher the working pressure, the smaller the clearance should be; the higher the hardness of the sealing material, the larger the clearance can be.

The following reference materials can be referred to during design: When no retaining ring is used, the extrusion of the O-ring will significantly affect the service life of the O-ring. The clearance between mating parts (2g) has a special influence on the extrusion of the O-ring groove, and other factors such as the pressure of the fluid and the hardness of the rubber material also have an influence on it.

In JIS B 2406, when the value exceeds that in Table 2-74, it is recommended to use a retaining ring together. Table 2-74 gives the extreme values of the clearance for extrusion from the O-ring groove, which are determined by test. So far, this value has been used as a reference value in China.
