Hydraulic cylinders, especially proportional/servo-controlled hydraulic cylinders, should clearly state environmental requirements and the standards to which environmental test methods should adhere or refer in their relevant technical documents. This should be included in the contract and technical documents signed by both parties, becoming an important part of the contract, to evaluate or determine the safety, integrity, and impact on the performance (such as reliability, see Section 5.7) of hydraulic cylinders in this environment, or to evaluate the quality and effectiveness of hydraulic cylinders and their material protective coatings and decorative layers, identify potential problem areas, discover quality control deficiencies and design defects, and optimize materials. Even when testing proportional/servo-controlled hydraulic cylinders according to GB/T 32216—2015 (Hydraulic Transmission - Test Methods for Proportional/Servo-Controlled Hydraulic Cylinders), the following environmental test methods (such as high temperature test, salt spray test, etc.) are also of important reference value.
5.6.1 High Temperature Test

Although GJB 150.3A—2009 (Environmental Test Methods for Military Equipment - Part 3: High Temperature Test) stipulates that this standard is applicable to high temperature testing of military equipment, it has reference value for high temperature testing of hydraulic cylinders in other fields.
1. Purpose and Application
(1) Purpose
The purpose of this test is to obtain relevant data to evaluate the impact of high temperature conditions on the safety, integrity, and performance of equipment.
(2) Application
This test is applicable to evaluating equipment used in high temperature environments.
(3) Limitations

This test is only applicable to evaluating thermal effects with shorter evaluation times (months rather than years) and uniform heat distribution throughout the test piece, and is generally not suitable for: a) Evaluating the effect of performance degradation over time during long-term stable exposure to high temperature conditions (storage or operation) (because this may include some superimposed effects). Such high temperature degradation effects should be evaluated through natural environment. b) Evaluating thermal effects caused by solar radiation, as solar radiation will produce significant temperature gradients in equipment. The direct effect of solar radiation should be evaluated using procedure I of GJB 150.7A—2009. c) Evaluating photochemical effects (photochemical effects should be evaluated using procedure II of GJB 150.7A—2009). d) Evaluating aerodynamic heating effects.
2. Tailoring Guide
(1) Selection of Test Method

1) Overview. Analyze the requirements of relevant technical documents, apply the results obtained from implementing GJB 4239—2001 (General Requirements for Equipment Environmental Engineering) during the equipment (product) ordering process, determine the equipment life cycle.

phase occurring during period of high temperatures. Determine whether to perform this test according to the following environmental effects. When it is determined that this test needs to be performed, and this test uses the same specimen as other environmental tests, it is also necessary to determine the order of this test and other tests.
Note: This test will also have a significant impact on the results of low pressure tests of sealed products [see 2.(1)2)d)～f)].
(2) Selecting the Test Procedure
1) Overview
This test includes two test procedures: Procedure I—Storage and Procedure II—Operation. The test procedure to be used should be determined before the test.
2) Factors to consider when selecting the test procedure
When selecting the test procedure, the following should be considered:

items: a) The purpose of the equipment.
b) Natural exposure environment.
c) Test data consistent with the actual use of the equipment.
d) The order of procedures. If both of the above procedures are selected, Procedure I is performed first, followed by Procedure II.

sections.text: e) Other major heat sources that affect the equipment, such as electric motors, engines, power supplies or exhaust gases.
3) Differences between procedures

① Overview. The difference between the two procedures is the time of performance testing, which is performed after high temperature exposure in Procedure I and during high temperature exposure in Procedure II. Procedure I is applicable to evaluate the effect of high temperature storage on equipment performance, and Procedure II is applicable to evaluate the effect of high temperature on equipment during operation.

② Procedure I—Storage. Procedure I is used to examine the effect of high temperature during storage on the safety, integrity and performance of the equipment. In this procedure, the specimen is first exposed to high temperatures (and low humidity if applicable) that may be encountered during equipment storage, and then performance is tested under standard atmospheric conditions.
③ Procedure II—Operation. Procedure II is used to examine the effect of high temperature on performance when the equipment is operating. There are two implementation methods:

items: a) Expose the specimen to the conditions of the test chamber temperature cycle, so that the specimen works continuously, or works during the maximum temperature response (when the specimen reaches the highest temperature).
b) Expose the specimen to a constant temperature, so that the specimen works when its temperature reaches stability.

sections.text: (3) Determining test conditions

1) Overview. After selecting this test and the corresponding procedure, it is also necessary to select the test conditions and test techniques for the procedure according to the provisions of the relevant documents and the information provided for the procedure. When determining the test conditions, the contents of 2.(3)2)～2.(3)6) should be considered.

2) Climate conditions. The high temperature cycle data of basic heat and heat climate types worldwide are shown in Tables 5-21 and 5-22. China's ground high temperature conditions are shown in GJB1172.2-1991 "Climatic extremes for military equipment: Ground temperature", and the temperature daily variation corresponding to the national 1% working extreme of high temperature is shown in Table 1 of GJB1172.2-1991. The climate conditions of the region where the equipment is stored and used should be determined. When determining high temperature conditions

Considerations should include:
a) The climate zone involved.
b) Whether the equipment is exposed to solar radiation, and whether solar radiation directly acts on the equipment, transport packaging, protective packaging cover, etc.
c) The path of heat transfer from ambient air and solar radiation to the equipment.

3) Exposure conditions.

① Overview. Before determining the test temperature values, the thermal exposure method of the equipment in normal storage and operating environments should be determined. At least the exposure states in 2.(3)3)② ~ 2.(3)3)③ should be considered.
② Technical state of equipment. The technical state of the equipment is as follows:

items: a) Open exposure state. The most severe conditions experienced by equipment without any protective covering.

b) Sheltered state. The presence or absence of shading objects, etc., can have a significant impact on the temperature of the air surrounding the covered equipment. Examples of sheltered equipment include:
Inside unventilated housings
Inside enclosed vehicle bodies
Inside compartments of aircraft with surfaces exposed to solar heating
Inside tents
Under waterproof tarpaulins
Above ground, on ground, or below ground

sections.text: ③ Special conditions. High temperature tests usually only consider the average temperature of the air surrounding the equipment. However, special heating conditions can produce significant localized heating, causing local temperatures to be noticeably higher than the average temperature of the surrounding air, thereby significantly affecting the evaluation of the equipment's thermal characteristics and performance. When the following conditions exist, these conditions should be included or simulated in the high temperature test setup as much as possible:

items: a) Enhanced solar radiation. When equipment is located below glass or transparent material panels, or in enclosed, unventilated compartments below thin metal skins, direct solar irradiation may temporarily raise local air temperatures. Due to increased risk of damage, caution should be exercised when applying extreme temperature values. In this case, tests should be based on field measurement data (in this case, solar radiation tests can be conducted separately or both tests can be performed).

b) Artificial heat sources. Artificial heating devices (motors, engines, power supplies, high-density electronic packaging, etc.) can significantly increase the local air temperature around equipment through radiation, convection, or impact of exhaust airflow.

sections.text: ④ Test duration.

① Overview. Determine the exposure duration that equipment must undergo under the specified various exposure conditions. Exposure can be constant or cyclic. In cyclic cases, the number of occurrences of exposure must also be determined.
② Constant temperature exposure. After the test specimen is exposed to a high temperature environment until temperature stabilization is achieved, maintain the test temperature for at least 2 hours.

③ Cyclic exposure. The test duration for cyclic exposure should be determined based on the required number of cycles to meet design requirements and the following guidelines. Both Procedure I and Procedure II expose the test specimen to cyclic temperatures, so the number of cycles is very critical. Unless otherwise specified, each cycle period is 24 hours.

a) Procedure I - Storage. Storage tests should be conducted for at least 7 cycles, corresponding to the number of hours during the most severe month of a normal year in the most severe region when extreme temperatures occur at a rate of 1%. In each cycle, the highest temperature occurs for approximately 1 hour. If storage time for critical materials or high-temperature sensitive materials needs to be extended, the number of cycles should be increased to ensure design requirements are met.

b) Procedure II - Operation. Operational exposure tests should be conducted for at least 3 cycles. This is usually sufficient for the test specimen to reach its highest response temperature. When temperature response is difficult to reproduce, it is recommended to use up to 7 cycles.

⑤ Technical state of the test specimen. The technical state of the test specimen should be determined based on the expected actual state of the equipment during storage and operation, and should at least consider the following technical states:

items: a) Enclosed in a transport/storage container or transfer box.
b) With or without protective conditions (with a roof, shelter).
c) Normal operating state.
d) State after modification for special purposes.
e) Technical state of stacked or pallet-stacked configuration.

sections.text: ⑥ Operation of the test specimen. When the test specimen must operate, prepare the test operation procedure according to the following requirements:

items: General requirements are given in GJB150.1A-2009, 3.9.2.
Special requirements are as follows:
a) Include the operating state with maximum power (generating the most heat).

b) When voltage changes affect the thermal consumption or temperature response of the test specimen (such as power generation and fan speed), include the required range of input voltage condition variations.

c) Introduce cooling media (such as forced cooling air or coolant) that are typically used during operation. When using cooling media, consider the temperature and flow rate at the inlet of the cooling media to reflect typical and worst-case temperature and flow conditions.

d) For constant temperature tests, when the temperature of internal critical operating parts is relatively constant, it is considered that the temperature has stabilized (in reality, due to the periodic nature of the test specimen's operation or the operating characteristics of the test specimen, the operating temperature cannot be constant).

e) For cyclic temperature tests, the temperature of the test specimen is related to the cyclic temperature and the characteristics of the test specimen, so the temperature cannot be stabilized. In this case, the temperature response of the test specimen is also cyclic, i.e., the peak response temperature is within 2°C compared to the peak response temperature of the previous cycle.

sections.text: 3. Information Requirements
⑴ Information needed before the test

items: General information. See GJB150.1A-2009, 3.8.
Special information. Humidity control requirements (if applicable) are given in 2.(3)6).

sections.text: ③ Location of temperature sensors. Location of temperature sensors used to measure temperature response and temperature stabilization (indicating which part, component, and/or structure of the test specimen).
⑵ Information needed during the test
General information is given in GJB150.1A-2009, 3.11. Special information is as follows:

items: a) Test chamber temperature (and humidity, if applicable)-time data.
b) Temperature-time data of the test specimen during the test.

sections.text: ⑶ Information needed after the test
4. Test Requirements
(1) Test Equipment

items: The test chamber should be equipped with auxiliary instruments that can maintain and monitor high-temperature air conditions around the test piece (and humidity when applicable).

Except when the platform environment has proven it reasonable to use other speeds and to prevent heat transfer in the test piece that would not occur in practice, the wind speed near the test piece should not exceed 1.7 m/s.
The temperature measurements in the test chamber should be continuously recorded, and if necessary, the temperature measurements of the test piece should also be continuously recorded.

sections.text: (2) Test Control

items: Temperature. Except as otherwise specified in the technical documentation, if any action other than the operation of the test piece (such as opening the chamber door) causes a significant change (greater than 2°C) in the test temperature or the chamber temperature, the test piece should be allowed to stabilize again to the specified temperature before continuing the test. If performance checks cannot be completed within 15 minutes, the test piece should be restored to the specified conditions before continuing the inspection.
Temperature Change Rate. Except as otherwise specified, the temperature change rate should not exceed 3°C/min to avoid temperature shock.

sections.text: (3) Test Interruption

items: General Requirements. See GJB150.1A-2009 Section 3.12.
Special Requirements.

① Insufficient Test Interruption. a) Cyclic Test. If a high-temperature cyclic test is interrupted unexpectedly during the test such that the test conditions drop to standard atmospheric conditions and exceed the tolerance, the test should be resumed from the point where the last successful cycle was completed. b) Constant Test. If a constant test is interrupted unexpectedly during the test such that the test conditions drop to standard atmospheric conditions and exceed the tolerance, the test piece should be stabilized again at the specified test temperature, and the test should continue from the point where the test conditions deviated. The time when the temperature exceeds the tolerance during the interruption is not included in the total test time. The duration of the test segments before and after the interruption should be recorded.

② Excessive Test Interruption (such as chamber malfunction). a) Physical Inspection and Performance Check. If the interruption of a cyclic or constant test exposes the test piece to an environment more severe than specified in the product standard, a comprehensive physical inspection and performance check should be conducted after the interruption (if possible), and then a decision should be made whether to continue the test based on the inspection and check results. b) Safety, Performance, and Material Issues. When safety, performance, and material issues are found after an excessive test, the best course of action is to terminate this test and repeat it with new test pieces. If this is not done and the test piece fails during the remaining tests, the test results will be considered invalid due to the excessive test conditions. If no safety, performance, or material issues are found, the following measures should be taken:

sections.text: ● For constant temperature tests, the previous conditions should be restored, and the test should continue from the point where the test tolerance was exceeded, with the time during the test interruption included in the total test time.

● For cyclic temperature tests, the test should be resumed from the point where the last successful cycle was completed, and the incomplete cycle during the excessive test interruption is not included in the total number of cycles.
(4) Installation and Debugging of Test Pieces

items: General Requirements. See GJB150.1A-2009 Section 3.9.
Special Requirements. The installation and debugging of test pieces should include all additional heat sources or appropriate simulated heat sources.

sections.text: 5. Test Process
(1) Test Preparation

items: Pre-test Preparation. Before the test begins, determine the test procedure, technical status of the test piece, number of cycles, test duration, and the values of the storage/operating environmental parameters of the test piece based on relevant documents.

Initial Inspection. All test pieces need to be inspected under standard atmospheric conditions before the test to obtain baseline data. The inspection is conducted in the following steps: a) Visually inspect the test piece, paying special attention to stress areas (such as corners of castings), and record the inspection results. b) Install temperature sensors on, in, or around the test piece according to the technical documentation. For Program II, to ensure the measurement of the maximum temperature response of the test piece, the temperature sensors should be installed on the functional components. c) Place the test piece in the test chamber under standard atmospheric conditions. d) Perform performance checks according to the technical documentation and record the results. If the test piece operates normally, proceed with Program I or Program II based on the specific situation.

sections.text: (2) Test Program

items: Program I - Storage.

① Cyclic Storage. The steps for cyclic storage testing are as follows: a) Place the test piece in the storage technical state. b) Adjust the environment in the test chamber to the test conditions for the start of the test, and stabilize the temperature of the test piece under these conditions. c) Expose the test piece to the temperature (and humidity if applicable) conditions of the storage environment for a duration of at least 7 cycles (or a total of 168 hours if using a 24-hour cycle) or the number of cycles specified in the technical documentation. If required by the technical documentation, record the temperature response of the test piece. d) After the end of the cyclic temperature exposure, adjust the air temperature in the test chamber to standard atmospheric conditions and maintain it under standard atmospheric conditions until the temperature of the test piece stabilizes. e) Visually inspect and perform performance checks on the test piece, record the results, and compare them with the pre-test data.
② Constant Temperature Storage. The steps for constant temperature storage testing are as follows:

sections.text:
a) Put the test piece into storage technical state.
b) Adjust the environment in the test chamber to the specified test conditions, and keep the test piece at stable temperature under these conditions.
c) After the test piece reaches stable temperature, continue to maintain the test temperature for at least 2 hours to ensure that the temperature of internal components/parts that cannot be measured truly reaches stability. If the temperature of internal components/parts cannot be measured, additional thermal soaking time should be determined based on thermal analysis to ensure the temperature of the entire test piece reaches stability.
d) After the end of constant temperature exposure, adjust the air temperature in the test chamber to standard atmospheric conditions, and maintain these standard atmospheric conditions until the test piece temperature stabilizes.
e) Perform visual inspection and functional performance testing on the test piece, record the results, and compare them with pre-test data.

2) Procedure II - Operation.
① Constant temperature operation. The test steps for constant temperature operation are as follows:
a) Install the test piece according to the operational technical state.
b) Adjust the air temperature in the test chamber to reach the required constant temperature (and humidity if applicable).
c) After the test piece temperature reaches stability, continue to maintain the conditions in the test chamber for at least 2 hours. If the temperature of internal components/parts cannot be measured, additional thermal soaking time should be determined based on thermal analysis to ensure the temperature of the entire test piece reaches stability.
d) Inspect the test piece visually as much as possible, record the inspection results, and compare them with pre-test data.
e) Operate the test piece and allow it to reach stable temperature again. Perform performance testing on the test piece according to the technical document requirements, record the test results, and compare them with pre-test data.
f) Stop the operation of the test piece, adjust the air temperature in the test chamber to standard atmospheric conditions, and maintain these conditions until the test piece temperature stabilizes.
g) Perform comprehensive visual inspection and functional performance testing on the test piece according to the technical document requirements, record the inspection and test results, and compare them with pre-test data.
② Cyclic operation. The test steps for cyclic operation are as follows:
a) Install the test piece according to the operational technical state.
b) Adjust the air temperature (and humidity if applicable) in the test chamber to reach the initial conditions of the operational cycle specified in the technical document, and maintain these conditions until the test piece temperature stabilizes.
c) Expose the test piece for at least 3 cycles or the number of cycles required to ensure the highest response temperature of the test piece is reached. During the cyclic exposure period, perform comprehensive visual inspection of the test piece as much as possible, and record the inspection results.
d) Operate the test piece during the highest temperature response period of the exposure cycle (due to the thermal lag effect of the test piece, the highest temperature response period may not coincide with the highest temperature period of the temperature cycle). Repeat this step until all functional performance testing of the test piece is completed according to the technical document.

Record the test results.
e) Stop the operation of the test piece, adjust the air temperature in the test chamber to standard atmospheric conditions, and maintain these conditions until the test piece temperature stabilizes.
f) Perform comprehensive visual inspection and functional performance testing on the test piece according to the technical document requirements, record the inspection and test results, and compare them with pre-test data.
6. Result Analysis

In addition to the guidelines provided in 3.1.7 of GJB150.1A-2009, the following information is also helpful for evaluating test results. Any data that does not meet the product specification requirements can be used for analysis in this test. Consider the following relevant information at the same time:
a) Results of non-destructive inspection after storage testing under extreme temperatures (if applicable).
b) Degradation or changes in operational performance under extreme high temperatures.
c) The necessity of special tooling or specific operating procedures during high temperature exposure.
d) Evidence of inadequate lubrication and proof of using lubricants under specified environmental conditions.
5.6.2 Low Temperature Test

Although GJB150.4A-2009 "Military Equipment Laboratory Environmental Test Methods Part 4: Low Temperature Test" stipulates that this standard is applicable to low temperature testing of military equipment, it has reference value for low temperature testing of hydraulic cylinders used in other fields.
1. Purpose and Application

(1) Purpose
The purpose of this test is to evaluate the impact of low temperature conditions on the safety, integrity, and performance of equipment during storage, operation, and disassembly.
(2) Application
This test is applicable to evaluating equipment used in low temperature environments.
(3) Limitations
This test is not applicable to equipment installed and operated on non-pressurized aircraft, which is usually tested according to the provisions of GJB150.24A-2009.
2. Tailoring Guide
(1) Selection of Test Method

1) Overview. Analyze the requirements of the relevant technical document, apply the results obtained from implementing GJB4239-2001 "General Requirements for Equipment Environmental Engineering" during the equipment (product) ordering process, determine the stages in the equipment life cycle when low temperature environments occur, and determine whether this test is necessary based on the following environmental effects. When it is determined that this test is necessary and the same test piece is used for this test and other environmental tests, also determine the sequence of this test and other tests.

2) Environmental Effects. Low temperatures have an adverse effect on almost all substrate materials. For equipment exposed to low-temperature environments, since low temperatures will alter the physical properties of the constituent materials, they may cause temporary or permanent damage to their operational performance. Therefore, as long as the equipment is exposed to temperatures below standard atmospheric conditions, consideration should be given to conducting low-temperature testing. Considering the following typical low-temperature environmental effects helps determine whether this test is applicable to the equipment under test:

items: Hardening and embrittlement of materials
Differential shrinkage of different materials in response to temperature transients, and different expansion rates of different components, causing components to seize
Reduced lubrication and fluidity of lubricants due to increased viscosity
Performance changes in electronic components (resistors, capacitors)
Performance changes in transformers and electromechanical components
Increased rigidity of vibration isolators
Cracking of solid explosive charges or columns (such as ammonium nitrate)
Rupture and crazing, brittle fracture, changes in impact strength, and strength reduction
Static fatigue in constrained glass
Condensation and freezing of water
Reduced flexibility, hearing, and vision of personnel wearing protective clothing
Changes in burning rate

sections.text: 3) Selection of test sequence.
① General requirements. See GJB150.1A-2009 "Military Equipment Laboratory Environmental Test Methods Part 1: General Requirements" 3.6.
② Special requirements. The selection of test sequence should at least follow the following two principles:

items: Life saving. First apply environmental stresses that cause the least damage to the test item, so that the test item can undergo more test items. To this end, this test should be conducted early in the test sequence.
The applied environment should maximize the display of superposition effects. To this end, this test should be conducted after mechanical environment tests such as vibration and shock.

sections.text: Although not explicitly specified, this test can be combined with vibration and shock tests to evaluate the effect of mechanical events (i.e., transportation, loading/unloading, impact) on materials at low temperatures. At the same time, this test will also significantly alter the sealing performance of the product during the low-pressure test in GJB150.2A-2009.
(2) Selection of test procedures

1) Overview. This test includes three test procedures: Procedure I - Storage, Procedure II - Operation, and Procedure III - Assembly/Disassembly Operations. Determine the applicable test procedure, combination of test procedures, or the order of implementation of each procedure based on the demand for test data. In most cases, all three procedures should be used.
2) Factors to consider when selecting test procedures. When selecting test procedures, the following should be considered:

items: Purpose of the equipment. According to the requirements of relevant documents, determine the functions that the equipment should achieve under low-temperature environments and any other restrictive conditions (such as storage).
Natural exposure environment.
The following test data that matches the actual use of the equipment: ● Expected temperature in the deployment area. ● Expected duration in the deployment area. ● Technical status of the equipment.

Sequence of procedures. When determining the sequence of the three low-temperature tests, the following should be considered: ● Procedure II can be performed after Procedure I/Procedure III. If the equipment needs to be stored at low temperatures before use, Procedure I should be performed before Procedure II; if assembly/disassembly operation testing is required, Procedure III can be performed before the operational test; if the equipment is not intended to be stored at low temperatures or disassembled/reassembled before use, proceed directly to Procedure II. ● If necessary, assembly/disassembly operation testing can be performed after storage testing/operational testing.

sections.text: 3) Differences between procedures. Although all procedures involve low temperatures, they differ fundamentally in the timing of performance testing and performance aspects.

items: Procedure I is used to check the safety of the equipment during storage and after storage under low-temperature conditions, as well as the impact on the equipment's performance after storage.

Procedure II is used to check the operational status of the equipment under low-temperature environments. The "operation" in this section refers to the startup and operation of the equipment with minimal personnel contact.
Procedure III is used to detect whether it is easy for operators to assemble and disassemble the equipment while wearing heavy cold-weather clothing.

sections.text: (3) Determination of test conditions

1) Overview. After selecting this test and the corresponding procedure, the test conditions and test techniques for that procedure should also be selected according to the provisions of relevant documents and the information provided for that procedure. The determination of test conditions should consider the contents of 2.(3)2) to 2.(3)4).

2) Climatic conditions. It is best to select specific test temperatures according to relevant documents. If there is no such information, the test temperatures should be determined based on the area where the equipment will be used and other factors. Although low-temperature environments usually vary cyclically, in many cases it is acceptable to conduct tests using constant low temperatures. Only in cases where exposure to changing low-temperature environments is considered important in design evaluation should low-temperature cyclic testing be selected. The low-temperature conditions for low-temperature cyclic testing should be determined according to relevant documents. The following are separately used in specific regions (climate types):
The following provides a guide for selecting test temperatures for equipment stored and used worldwide, as well as equipment stored long-term (two years or more) worldwide:

a) Equipment used in specific regions. When equipment is only used in a specific region, Table 5-23 can be used to determine the test temperature. The extreme air temperature values shown in Table 5-23 are based on the frequency of occurrence of 20% for the coldest hour in the coldest month at the coldest location within the climate region (excluding extremely cold regions). Table 5-23 shows the range of daily temperature cycles. In this test, only the lowest value of each range is usually considered.

sections.text: b) Equipment stored and used worldwide. When equipment will be stored or operated worldwide, the selection of temperature should consider not only the extreme low temperature but also the frequency of occurrence of this extreme low temperature. Without considering the frequency of occurrence, the test conditions may be excessive. This frequency is the percentage of the total number of hours in the most extreme area and month worldwide, also known as the time risk rate. Within the corresponding number of hours at this ratio, the lowest temperature that occurs will be equal to or lower than the given test low temperature. In most cases, a frequency of 20% is used; other values may be selected to meet specific applications and test requirements (see Table 5-24).

c) Equipment stored and used worldwide for a long time. If equipment is stored for a long time (measured in years) in areas with extremely low temperatures without cover or protection (such as northeastern Siberia or the "Pole of Cold" in the center of Greenland), the opportunity for the equipment to be subjected to very low temperatures (close to -65°C) will increase. Long-term exposure at such extremely low temperatures may affect the safety of items such as ammunition and life support equipment. Therefore, this temperature should be selected as the test temperature.

3) Duration of exposure. The duration of low temperature exposure affects the safety, integrity and performance of equipment, and can be selected based on the material, structural characteristics and usage of the equipment itself:

a) Non-hazardous or non-safety-related (non-life support) equipment. Most of this type of equipment (in a non-operating state) (except for those with organic plastics) will not exhibit performance degradation after reaching temperature stability at low temperatures. If there is no other suitable time, the storage time can be 4 hours after the test piece reaches temperature stability.

b) Equipment containing explosives, ammunition, organic plastics and other products. The performance of such products in this type of equipment may continue to deteriorate after temperature stabilization, so they need to be subjected to long-term low temperature testing. After the test piece reaches temperature stability, at least 72 hours of storage testing should be performed, as this is the typical low temperature exposure duration for such products.

c) Equipment containing products such as limit glass. Glass, ceramics and glass products that need to be installed or restricted to a specific position, or equipment (such as optical systems, laser systems and electronic systems) that need to be installed or restricted to a specific position, often cause damage to the equipment due to static fatigue of such products. Therefore, a longer low temperature test time may be required to induce this phenomenon. If there is no other reference data, an exposure time of 24 hours is recommended.

4) Technical status of the test piece. The technical status of the test piece is an important factor in determining the degree of temperature impact. Therefore, the test should be conducted using the technical status that the equipment is expected to have during storage or use. At least the following technical statuses should be considered:

items: Installed in a transport/storage container or transport box.
Protected or unprotected state.
Normal use status.
Status after modification for specific use.

sections.text: 3. Information Requirements
(1) Information Required Prior to Testing

items: General information: see GJB150.1A-2009, Section 3.8.
Special information: test temperature, required types of protective clothing, and other information.
Location of temperature sensors: Position of temperature sensors for measuring temperature response and temperature stabilization (indicate which component or assembly/structure of the specimen).

sections.text: (2) Information Required During Testing
General information see GJB150.1A-2009, Section 3.11. Special information as follows:

items: a) Temperature-time record of the test chamber.
b) Protective clothing used during installation/removal operations.

sections.text: (3) Information Required After Testing
General information see GJB150.1A-2009, Section 3.14. Special information as follows:

items: a) Time required for each functional test.
b) Temperature-time data of specimen and test chamber.
c) Protective clothing and special equipment used for assembling and disassembling specimen.
d) Anthropometric data of necessary operators for performing installation/removal operations.

sections.text: 4. Test Requirements
(1) Test Equipment

items: Required equipment, including test chamber and auxiliary instruments capable of maintaining and monitoring (see GJB150.1A-2009, Section 3.8) the low temperature conditions required around the specimen.

Except where the platform environment of the equipment has proven it reasonable to use other speeds, and to prevent heat transfer in the specimen that is not representative, the wind speed near the specimen should not exceed 1.7 m/s.

sections.text: (2) Test Control

items: Temperature: Except as otherwise specified in the technical document, if any action other than operation of the specimen (e.g., opening the chamber door) causes a significant change in the specimen temperature (greater than 2°C), the specimen temperature should be allowed to stabilize at the specified value before continuing the test. If functional testing cannot be completed within 15 minutes, the specimen temperature should be allowed to stabilize before continuing testing.
Rate of temperature change: Except as otherwise specified, to prevent the effects of temperature shock, the rate of temperature change should be controlled to not exceed 3°C/min.
Temperature measurement: Install temperature sensors in or on the specimen to measure temperature stabilization data.
Temperature recording: If required, continuously record the temperatures of the test chamber and specimen.

sections.text: (3) Test Interruption
General requirements see GJB150.1A-2009, Section 3.12. Special requirements as follows:

items: a) Under-test interruption: For test interruptions that cause the test temperature to change toward the ambient temperature and exceed the tolerance range, perform a comprehensive physical inspection and functional test of the specimen (if possible). If no problems are found, allow the specimen to stabilize at the test temperature again and continue the test from the interruption point. Any problems that occur due to not encountering extreme conditions should be considered as problems with the specimen itself. The time during which the temperature exceeds the tolerance during the interruption is not counted in the total test time.

b) Over-test interruption: For test interruptions that expose the specimen to more severe conditions than required by the product specification, perform a comprehensive physical inspection and functional test of the specimen (if possible) before continuing the test. This is especially necessary when safety issues exist (e.g., ammunition). If problems are found, the best approach is to end this test and redo it with a new specimen; otherwise, if the specimen fails during subsequent tests, the test results are considered invalid due to the occurrence of over-test conditions. If no problems are found, continue the test under the conditions before the interruption. The time during the test interruption is counted in the total test time.

sections.text: (4) Installation and Debugging of Specimen
See GJB150.1A-2009, Section 3.9.
5. Test Procedure
(1) Test Preparation

items: Pre-test preparation: Before the test begins, determine the test procedure, technical status of the specimen, number of cycles, duration, and nominal values of specimen storage/working environment parameters according to relevant documents.

Initial inspection: All specimens must be inspected under standard atmospheric conditions before the test to obtain baseline data. The inspection is carried out in the following steps (the order of steps may need to be changed for large specimens):
a) Perform a comprehensive visual inspection of the specimen, paying particular attention to stress areas such as corners of castings. Record the inspection results.
b) If it is necessary to measure the test temperature, install temperature sensors in or on the specimen as required.

c) Prepare the specimen according to the technical status requirements of GJB150.1A-2009, Section 3.9.1, and place the specimen in the test chamber to allow it to reach a stable temperature under standard atmospheric conditions.

d) Perform functional testing of the specimen according to the technical document and record the test results. If the specimen is functioning normally, proceed with the test according to the provisions of the technical document.

sections.text: (2) Test Procedure

items: Procedure I - Storage: The test steps for Procedure I are as follows:
a) Place the specimen in the storage technical state.
b) Adjust the air temperature in the test chamber to the low-temperature storage temperature specified in the technical document.
c) After the specimen temperature stabilizes, maintain this storage temperature for the duration specified in the technical document.
d) Perform a visual inspection of the specimen and compare the inspection results with the pre-test data. Record the inspection results.

sections.text: e) If low temperature operation tests are required, proceed with 5.(2)(2)(c) next; otherwise, proceed with f) next.
f) Adjust the air temperature inside the test chamber to the temperature under standard atmospheric conditions and maintain this temperature until the test piece reaches temperature stability.
g) Conduct a comprehensive visual inspection of the test piece and record the inspection results.
h) If necessary, perform operational performance tests on the test piece and record the inspection results.
i) Compare these data with those obtained before the test.
2) Procedure II - Operation. The test steps for Procedure II are as follows:

a) After loading the test piece into the test chamber, adjust the air temperature inside the test chamber to the low temperature operating temperature specified in the technical documentation. Maintain this temperature for at least 24 hours after the test piece reaches temperature stability.
b) If the conditions of the test chamber permit, conduct a comprehensive visual inspection of the test piece and record the inspection results.
c) Perform operational performance tests on the test piece according to the technical documentation and record the test results.
d) If disassembly and assembly operation tests under low temperature are required, proceed with 5.(2)(3)(d) next; otherwise, proceed with e) next.
e) Adjust the air temperature inside the test chamber to the temperature under standard atmospheric conditions and maintain this temperature until the test piece reaches temperature stability.
f) Conduct a comprehensive visual inspection of the test piece and record the inspection results.
g) If necessary, perform operational performance tests, record the inspection results, and compare them with the data obtained in 5.(1)(2)(d).
3) Procedure III - Disassembly and Assembly Operations. The test steps for Procedure III are as follows:

a) After loading the test piece into the test chamber, adjust the air temperature inside the test chamber to the low temperature operating temperature specified in the technical documentation. Maintain this temperature for 2 hours after the test piece reaches temperature stability.
b) While maintaining the low temperature operating temperature, place the test piece in its normal operational technical state according to the selection scheme in d).
c) Restore the temperature to that in a).
d) Select the appropriate operation method according to the type of test chamber used:

● When using a walk-in laboratory, operators should dress and equip themselves as they would in a low temperature combat state and disassemble the test piece as they would on the battlefield. Then, repack the test piece using normal transportation/storage containers, transport boxes, or other packaging forms and technical states.

● When using a small test chamber, follow the method in (1), except that when performing disassembly and packaging operations, operators should wear thick gloves as required in natural environments, with their hands reaching into the test chamber through inspection holes or an open chamber door. Perform assembly or disassembly according to the requirements of the disassembly and assembly operation test, limiting each operation to 15 minutes, and restore the temperature in a) between two operations.
Note: Opening the test chamber door will cause the test piece to gradually warm up and frost to form on it.
e) If operational tests on the test piece under low temperature are required, repeat b), then proceed with 5.(2)(2)(a); otherwise, proceed with f) next.
f) Conduct a comprehensive visual inspection of the test piece, record the inspection results, and compare them with the data before the test.
g) Adjust the air temperature inside the test chamber to the temperature under standard atmospheric conditions and maintain this temperature until the test piece reaches temperature stability.
h) Conduct a comprehensive visual inspection of the test piece and record the inspection results.
i) If necessary, perform operational performance tests on the test piece, record the inspection results, and compare them with the data obtained in 5.(1)(2)(d).
6. Result Analysis

In addition to the guidelines provided in 3.17 of GJB150.1A-2009, the following information also helps in evaluating test results. Any data related to test piece failures can be used to analyze whether the product meets specification requirements, considering the following relevant information:

items: Results of non-destructive tests/inspections performed on the test piece at low test temperature after low temperature exposure.
Permissible decrease in operational performance under low temperature conditions.
Necessity of using special tool sets or specific cold climate procedures.
Evidence of improper lubrication and proof of using lubricants under specified environmental conditions.
For engine starting failures, whether the used fuel and antifreeze are suitable and related evidence.
Condition and suitability of the power source.

sections.text: 5.6.3 Humid Heat Test

Refer to GJB 150.9A—2009 (Environmental Test Methods for Military Equipment Part 9: Humid Heat Test) for the standard test method applicable to equipment under test. However, the hydraulic pressure test methods for other fields shall refer to this standard.
1. Purpose and Application
(1) Purpose
The purpose of this test is to verify that the equipment (including hydraulic pressure, as described below) can withstand the effects of high temperature and humidity.
(2) Application
This test method is applicable to:

items: Equipment that may be stored in a humid heat environment.
Equipment that may be used in a high temperature and high humidity environment or stored in such an environment.

sections.text: c) Display potential problems related to damp heat that equipment may encounter.
Of course, it is more effective to conduct tests on equipment in a suitable self-heating environment.
(3) Limitations

This test cannot reproduce all humidity effects related to natural environments, such as long-term effects; nor can it reproduce humidity effects related to low humidity environments. This test does not reproduce complex temperature and humidity environments, but rather provides a general stress (usage) environment to expose potential problems that may occur in equipment. Therefore, this test does not include natural or induced temperature and humidity cycles. This test does not evaluate the interior of airtight sealed components (such as hydraulic cylinders), nor does it consider the following situations:

items: a) Condensation inside airborne and ground equipment caused by changes in pressure and temperature.
b) Condensation caused by blackbody radiation (such as night sky effect).
c) Combined effects of biological and chemical pollutants with moisture or condensation.
d) Accumulation of liquid water inside equipment or packaging and retention for a considerable period of time.

sections.text: 2. Tailoring Guidelines
(1) Selection of Test Method

1) Overview. Analyze the requirements of relevant technical documents, apply the results obtained from implementing GJB4239-2001 "General Requirements for Equipment Environmental Engineering" during the equipment (product) ordering process, determine the stages in which damp heat environments occur during the equipment's service life (cycle), and determine whether this test is necessary based on the following environmental effects. When it is determined that this test is necessary and this test is to be conducted on the same sample as other tests, it is also necessary to determine the sequence of this test and other tests.

2) Environmental Effects. Dampness can have physical and chemical effects on equipment; changes in temperature and humidity can cause condensation inside equipment. Physical phenomena related to humidity are described in 7 (i.e., Appendix A of GJB150.9A-2009). Considering the following typical problems (not including all problems) can help determine whether this test is applicable to the equipment under test:

items: a) Surface effects, such as:
① Metal oxidation/electrochemical corrosion.
② Accelerated chemical reactions.
③ Chemical or electrochemical destruction of organic or inorganic surface coatings.
④ Corrosion layers produced by the interaction of surface moisture and foreign adhesions.
⑤ Changes in friction coefficient leading to bonding or adhesion.
b) Changes in material properties, such as:
① Material expansion due to absorption effects.

② Other property changes, such as reduced physical strength, changes in electrical insulation and thermal insulation properties, delamination of composite materials, changes in plasticity or elasticity, reduced performance of moisture-absorbing materials, reduced performance of lubricants, etc.
c) Effects of condensation and free water, such as:
① Electrical short circuits.

sections.text: ② Changes in thermal conductivity, etc.
3) Selection of Test Sequence.
① General Requirements. See 3.6 in GJB150.1A-2009 "Environmental Test Methods for Military Equipment Part 1: General Requirements".

② Special Requirements. If the damp heat test affects other subsequent tests on the same sample, the damp heat test should be arranged after these tests. Similarly, since potential combined environmental effects are not representative, it is generally not advisable to conduct this test on the same sample that has undergone salt spray test, sand and dust test, or fungus test.
(2) Selection of Test Procedure
This test has only one test procedure.
(3) Determination of Test Conditions

1) Overview. After selecting this test, it is also necessary to select the test conditions and test techniques for this procedure based on the provisions of relevant documents and the information provided for this procedure. Test parameters such as the number of temperature and humidity cycles, test duration, temperature and humidity values, and technical status of the sample should be determined. The requirements for equipment operation and performance testing, as well as ventilation requirements for the test, should also be considered. The content of 2.(3)2) ~ 2.(3)4) should be taken into account when making determinations.

2) Test Duration. This test uses a 24-hour cycle, with at least 10 cycles. Generally, 10 cycles are sufficient to demonstrate the potential effects of damp heat environments on most equipment. To make the results of the damp heat test more truly reflect the ability of equipment to withstand damp heat environments, the test duration can be extended according to the provisions of relevant documents.

3) Temperature and Humidity Values. Temperature and humidity values are shown in Figure 1 of GJB150.9A-2009, i.e., the Damp Heat Cycle Control Chart (one cycle period is 24 hours). Although the combination of 60°C temperature and 95% relative humidity will not occur in natural environments, this combination of temperature and relative humidity values can reveal potential problem areas in equipment.

4) Test Description. This test procedure is designed to reproduce the main effects of damp heat environments on equipment, without reproducing the temperature and humidity changes over time that occur in nature or are induced during use, nor the damp heat effects after solar radiation. This procedure may induce failures that indicate long-term effects.
3. Information Requirements
(1) Information Required Before the Test
General information is described in 3.8 of GJB150.1A-2009, and special information is as follows:

items: a) Whether sealed parts of the sample should be opened or closed during the test.
b) Number of equipment operation times or prescribed visual inspections.
c) Information on test procedure operation (if applicable).

sections.text: (2) Information Required During the Test
General information is described in 3.11 of GJB150.1A-2009, and special information is as follows:

sections.text:
a) Record of temperature and humidity changes in the test chamber over time.
b) Performance parameters of the specimen and the timing of inspections and their duration.
(3) Information Required After Testing
Refer to 3.1.4 of GJB150.1A-2009 for general information. Special information includes:

items: a) Tests previously conducted on the specimen.
b) Results of each performance test (before, during, and after the test) and visual inspections (photographs should be taken when applicable).
c) Time required for each performance test.
d) Duration of exposure or number of test cycles completed.
e) Technical status of the specimen and specifications of special equipment.

sections.text: 4. Test Requirements
(1) Test Equipment

1) Test Chamber. Unless otherwise specified, the test chamber should prevent condensation from dripping onto the specimen from the chamber walls. The test chamber should be equipped with an exhaust vent to prevent pressure buildup inside the chamber and should prevent external contamination.

2) Sensors and Test Instruments. Use solid-state sensors unaffected by condensation to measure relative humidity, or use fast-response wet-bulb and dry-bulb sensors or dew point testers for measurement. This test is a high relative humidity test and should not use sensors sensitive to condensation, such as lithium chloride sensors. A data acquisition system is needed to measure test conditions, and this system should be equipped with appropriate recording devices. The data acquisition system is generally separate from the chamber controller. If using recording paper with scales, the paper should be accurate to at least ±0.6°C. If using wet-bulb control method, the wet-bulb and container should be kept clean, and new wet-bulb wick should be replaced before each test and at least every 30 days. The wet-bulb wick used should be as thin as possible to facilitate water evaporation and keep the sensor surface moist. The water used in the wet-bulb system should be of the same quality as the water used for humidification. If possible, visual inspection of the water container, wet-bulb wick, sensors, and other components of the relative humidity measurement system should be conducted at least every 24 hours during the test to ensure proper functioning.

3) Air Velocity. The air velocity passing over the wet-bulb sensor should not be less than 4.6 m/s, and the wet-bulb wick should be on the intake side of the fan to avoid the influence of fan heat. The air velocity at any point around the specimen should be maintained at 0.5–1.7 m/s.

4) Humidification Method. Use steam or spray water to humidify the air around the specimen. The water used for humidification should meet the requirements of 3.2 in GJB150.1A-2009. Water quality should be checked regularly (not more than every 15 days) to ensure it meets the requirements. If using spray water for humidification, adjust the water temperature before spraying to avoid disrupting test conditions, and do not spray water directly into the test area. During the test, condensate generated inside the test chamber should be removed from the chamber.

5) Prevention of Contamination. Except for water, no other substances should come into direct contact with the specimen to prevent deterioration or affect test results. No rust, corrosive contaminants, or other substances should be introduced into the test chamber. The methods used for dehumidification, humidification, heating, and cooling around the specimen should not alter the chemical composition of air, water, and water vapor in the test chamber.
(2) Test Control
Test control should meet the following requirements:

items: a) The test chamber should be equipped with measurement and recording devices, which should be separate from the chamber controller.

b) Unless otherwise specified, temperature and relative humidity should be continuously measured during the test. If digital measurement is required, the measurement interval should not exceed 15 minutes.
c) The instruments and test chamber used should meet the tolerance requirements of 3.3 in GJB150.1A-2009.

sections.text: (3) Test Interruption
Refer to 3.1.2 of GJB150.1A-2009 for general requirements. Special requirements are as follows:

items: a) Under-test interruption. If the test is unexpectedly interrupted, causing test conditions to fall below specified values and exceed tolerances, the test should be restarted from the end point of the last valid cycle before the interruption.
b) Over-test interruption. See 6.3b) of GJB150.9A-2009.

sections.text: (4) Installation and Debugging of Specimens
1) General Requirements. See 3.9.1 of GJB150.1A-2009.
2) Special Requirements. Check whether the sensor type used for monitoring test conditions is appropriate and whether the installation position is correct to obtain the required test data.
5. Test Procedure
(1) Overview
Perform humidity and heat tests using the following steps individually or in combination to collect necessary information about specimens in humid and hot environments.
(2) Test Preparation
1) Pre-test Preparation. Before the test begins, determine the technical status, temperature, humidity, duration, and number of test cycles of the specimen according to relevant documents.
2) Initial Inspection. All specimens should be inspected under standard atmospheric conditions before the test to obtain baseline data. The inspection should be conducted in the following steps:

items: a) Install the specimen in the test chamber.
b) Prepare the specimen according to the specified technical status.
c) Conduct a comprehensive visual inspection of the specimen.
d) Record the inspection results.
e) Perform operational inspection according to technical documents (if applicable) and record the results.

sections.text: 3) Test Procedure. The steps of the test procedure are as follows:
a) After completing the initial inspection, adjust the temperature of the test chamber to 23°C±2°C and relative humidity to 50%±5%, and maintain for 24 hours.
b) Adjust the temperature of the test chamber to 30°C and relative humidity to 95%.

c) Expose the test specimens according to the test conditions shown in Figure 1 of GJB150.9A-2009. The test cycle is determined by 2.(3)2). Perform performance testing on the specimens, recommended at the end of the 5th or 10th cycle period, within the time period shown in Figure 1 of GJB150.9A-2009, with the time required to complete the testing being the minimum time needed to verify the specimen's performance. Performance testing of the specimens can also be conducted according to relevant documents. Record the test results. If the specimen malfunctions, terminate the temperature and humidity cycling and proceed to step d). If the specimen functions normally, continue the test.

If the specimen's working performance needs to be tested by opening the test chamber door, or if the specimen needs to be removed from the test chamber, and the specimen's working performance test cannot be completed within 30 minutes, to prevent false drying, keep the specimen at a temperature of 30°C and relative humidity of 95% for 1 hour, then conduct the test until it is completed.

If the specimen's working performance test is conducted inside the test chamber and the test time exceeds 4 hours as shown in Figure 1 of GJB150.9A-2009, subsequent cycles cannot be conducted as shown in Figure 1 of GJB150.9A-2009, but the time should be extended until the test is completed. Once the test is completed, continue with subsequent cycles as shown in Figure 1 of GJB150.9A-2009.
d) Adjust the temperature and humidity conditions to standard atmospheric conditions. Perform performance testing for comparison with pre-test results.
e) Conduct a comprehensive visual inspection of the specimen and record any changes caused by exposure to temperature and humidity conditions.
6. Result Analysis
In addition to the guidelines provided in 3.1.7 of GJB150.1A-2009, the following information is helpful for evaluating test results:

items: Permissible or acceptable decline in working performance.
Potential effects caused by specific operational procedures or special devices required for the test.
Whether the effects of temperature and humidity can be considered separately.

sections.text: 7. Physical Phenomena Related to Moisture
(1) Condensation

The phenomenon of water vapor condensing on surfaces with temperatures lower than the surrounding air's dew point is called condensation. Condensation causes water vapor to transform into liquid water.

The amount of water vapor in the air determines the dew point's height. The dew point, absolute humidity, and water vapor pressure are interrelated. When the surface temperature of specimens placed in the test chamber is lower than the dew point of the air inside the chamber, condensation will occur. Therefore, to prevent condensation, specimens should be preheated.

Usually, condensation is only determined by visual inspection, but this does not include all situations, especially small specimens with rough surfaces, which are difficult to judge by visual inspection. If the specimen's thermal capacity is very small, condensation will only occur when the air temperature rises rapidly or the relative humidity is close to 100%. Slight condensation can be observed on the surfaces inside the chamber due to the decrease in temperature around the specimen.
(2) Adsorption

The phenomenon of water molecules adhering to surfaces with temperatures higher than the dew point is called adsorption. The amount of water molecules adhering to the specimen's surface depends on the material type, surface structure, and the water vapor pressure of the surrounding air. It is not easy to evaluate the effects of adsorption alone, as the effects of absorption, which usually occur simultaneously with adsorption, are usually more pronounced.
(3) Absorption

The accumulation of water molecules inside a material is called absorption. The amount of absorbed water vapor partially depends on the water content in the surrounding air. The absorption process continues until equilibrium is reached. The rate of water molecule penetration increases with rising temperature.
(4) Diffusion

The movement of water molecules within a material due to local pressure differences is called diffusion. Examples of diffusion phenomena commonly encountered in electronic products include: water vapor penetrating through organic coatings on capacitors or semiconductors, or through sealing putty into the interior of electronic products.
(5) Breathing

The phenomenon of air exchange between the inside and outside of a specimen's cavity due to temperature changes is called breathing. Breathing usually causes condensation inside the specimen's cavity.
5.6.4 Mold Test

Although GJB150.10A-2009 "Military Equipment Laboratory Environmental Test Methods Part 10: Mold Test" specifies that this standard is applicable to mold testing of military equipment, it has reference value for mold testing of hydraulic cylinders in other fields.
1. Purpose and Application
(1) Purpose
The purpose of this test is to evaluate the degree of mold growth on equipment (including hydraulic cylinders, hereinafter the same) and the extent of its impact on equipment performance or use.
(2) Application

items: This test is used to determine:
① Whether the equipment or component grows mold.
② The growth rate of mold on the equipment.
③ The impact of mold growth on the equipment and the completion of its tasks and usage safety.
④ Whether the equipment can be effectively stored in the environment.
⑤ If mold grows, whether there are simple removal methods.
This test involves highly specialized techniques and contains potential risks.

sections.text: hazardous microorganisms. Only personnel with professional technical qualifications (such as microbial experts) may conduct this test. The test location must comply with safety requirements specified in GB/T 2423.16—2008.
(3) Limitations

This test is not applicable to the detection of matrix materials. Detection of matrix materials should be performed using other material testing methods, such as soil burial, pure culture, mixed culture, and plate tests.
2. Test Selection Guidelines
(1) Selection of Test Method

1) Overview. Analyze the requirements of relevant technical documents and the results obtained from implementing GJB4239-2001 "General Requirements for Equipment Environmental Engineering" in equipment procurement to determine the stages of mold growth environment that may occur during the equipment's service life (period). Based on the following environmental effects, determine whether this test is needed. When it is determined that this test is needed and the same specimen is used for this test and other environmental tests, the sequence of this test relative to other tests must also be determined.
2) Effects of Mold Growth

Since the degradation effect of microorganisms varies with temperature and humidity and is closely related to conditions in tropical and temperate regions, it should be considered during equipment design. Mold growth can change the physical properties of equipment, thereby weakening its function or affecting its use.
① Harmful Effects. The harmful effects caused by mold growth are summarized as follows:
a) Direct erosion of materials. Non-mold-resistant materials are susceptible to direct erosion because molds can decompose materials and use them as nutrients. This leads to degradation of the equipment's physical properties. Non-mold-resistant materials include:
• Natural materials: plant fiber materials (wood, paper, natural fiber fabrics, and ropes, etc.), animal-based and fabric-based adhesives, fats, oils, and many hydrocarbons, leather.
• Synthetic materials: polyvinyl chloride products (such as products plasticized with fatty acid esters), certain polyurethanes (such as polyesters and certain polyethers), plastics with organic fillers, and coatings and varnishes containing mold-sensitive components.
b) Indirect erosion of materials. The destruction of mold-resistant materials comes from indirect erosion, which occurs in the following situations:
• Even if the underlying material can resist direct erosion by mold, mold growing on deposited dust, grease, sweat stains, and other contaminants (formed during manufacturing or use) can damage the underlying material.
• Metabolic products secreted by molds (such as organic acids) can cause metal corrosion, glass etching, and discoloration or degradation of plastics and other materials.
• Molds growing on materials sensitive to direct erosion can produce erosion when their metabolic products come into contact with nearby mold-resistant materials.
② Physical Effects. The possible physical effects are as follows:
a) Electrical or electronic systems: Both direct and indirect erosion can lead to damage to electrical or electronic systems. For example, mold can form unwanted conductive paths on insulating materials or negatively affect the electrical characteristics of precision adjustment circuits.
b) Optical systems: Damage to optical systems is mainly caused by indirect erosion. Mold can negatively affect the propagation of light in optical systems, block precision moving parts, make dry surfaces moist, and reduce performance.
③ Health and Aesthetic Factors
Mold growth on equipment can cause physiological problems (such as allergies) or affect the appearance of the equipment, leading users to be unwilling to use the equipment.
3) Selection of Test Sequence

① General Requirements. See 3.6 in GJB150.1A-2009 "Laboratory Environmental Test Methods for Military Equipment, Part 1: General Requirements".
② Special Requirements. This test is generally not suitable for specimens that have undergone salt spray, dust, or damp heat tests. If necessary, the mold test can be performed before the salt spray or dust test. A large amount of accumulated salt can affect the germination and growth of mold, and dust can provide nutrients for mold, which may create false impressions of the specimen's biological sensitivity.
(2) Selection of Test Procedure

This test has only one procedure. Since the combination of temperature and humidity is critical for microbial growth, the temperature and humidity conditions specified in this test must be maintained during the test.
(3) Determination of Test Conditions

1) Test Duration. The minimum duration of the mold test is 28 days (the minimum time required for mold germination, decomposition of carbon molecules, and degradation of materials is 28 days). Since indirect erosion and physical effects caused by mold growth on specimens may not occur within a shorter test duration, if a higher degree of certainty or lower risk is required to determine the effects of mold on specimens, the test duration should be extended to 84 days.
2) Selection of Mold Strains. Table 5-25 lists two commonly used groups of mold strains. One group should be selected for the test, and the strains may be adjusted according to 2.(3)2)② if necessary. These strains are selected based on their ability to degrade materials, their distribution on Earth, and their stability. The strains listed in Table 5-25 indicate the types of materials they erode. If necessary, additional strains may be added to the selected group.
① Since the specimens do not need to be sterilized before the test, other microorganisms may be present on the surface of the specimens. During the test, these microorganisms will compete with the test strains for nutrients, so non-test strains may grow on the specimens at the end of the test.
