sections.text: 4. Test Requirements
(1) Test Equipment

1) Test chamber. The structure of the test chamber and accessories should prevent condensation water from dripping onto specimens. The test chamber is connected to the atmosphere through filtered vents, which prevent pressure buildup in the chamber while preventing release of fungal spores to the atmosphere. 2) Sensors. Use a humidity measurement system or sensor unaffected by condensation to monitor and control humidity in the test chamber (see GJB 150.1A—2009, section 3.18). Separate sensors should be used for controlling the chamber environment and for recording humidity and temperature. 3) Air velocity. Air velocity through the humidity sensor should be at least 4.5 m/s. Air velocity through and near specimens and control strips should be controlled between 0.5-1.7 m/s. If necessary, deflectors or filters should be installed around specimens. Humidity sensors should be installed where they are not affected by heat from fan motors.

788.page_header: Chapter 5 Test Methods for Hydraulic Cylinders 777

sections.text: (2) Test Control
1) Overview. In addition to the information provided in Section 3.1.8 of GJB150.1A-2009, the controls in Sections 4.2.2-4.2.5 are also (appropriate) applicable to this test.

2) Relative Humidity. Use a solid-state sensor not affected by water condensation or an equivalent method (such as a rapid-response wet and dry bulb sensor) to determine relative humidity. Do not use lithium chloride sensors sensitive to condensation, while also noting:

items: a) When using the wet bulb control method, clean the wet bulb assembly and install new gauze strips for each test.
b) To obtain the evaporation necessary to measure wet bulb temperature on the sensor, ensure the air velocity through the wet bulb is not less than 4.5 m/s.

c) Since heat from the fan motor may affect temperature readings, do not install the wet bulb and dry bulb sensors near the fan used to meet the requirements of Section 4.2.2b) or the heat dissipation of the air supply.

sections.text: 3) Air Flow. Ensure free air flow around the specimen and maintain minimal contact area between the specimen support frame and the specimen.
4) Water Vapor. Do not directly introduce water vapor into the test chamber workspace as it may have adverse effects on the specimen and microbial activity.
5) Reagents and Water. The requirements for reagents and water in this section are as follows:

items: a) Use qualified reagents.
b) The water mentioned in this section refers to distilled water or water of equal purity as specified in Section 3.2 of GJB150.1A-2009.

sections.text: (3) Test Interruption
1) General Requirements. See Section 3.1.2 of GJB150.1A-2009.
2) Special Requirements.

items: ① Different from other environmental tests, mold tests involve living microorganisms. If the test is interrupted, consider the actual situation involving active microorganisms.
② If the interruption occurs in the first 10 days of the test, repeat the test using new specimens or cleaned specimens of the same type.

③ If the interruption occurs in the later stage of the test, check the mold growth on the specimens. If the specimens have grown mold, there is no need to repeat the test; if the cotton control strip shows active microorganisms but there are no signs of mold growth on the specimens, handle according to the guidance below:

a) Temperature Reduction. Generally, reducing the temperature of the test chamber will slow down mold growth. If the relative humidity remains unchanged, re-establish the test conditions and continue the test from the time point below the specified tolerance for temperature reduction; otherwise, proceed as specified in c).

b) Temperature Increase. Increased temperature may significantly affect mold growth. If any of the following occurs, the test must be repeated from the beginning; otherwise, re-establish the test conditions and continue the test from the interruption point:
c) Humidity Reduction. If any of the following occurs, repeat the test from the beginning; otherwise, re-establish the test conditions and continue the test from the interruption point:
• Temperature exceeds 40°C.
• Temperature exceeds 31°C for 4 hours or more.
• The mold growing on the control strip shows signs of decline.
• Relative humidity is below 50%.
• Relative humidity is below 70% for 4 hours or more.
• The mold growing on the control strip shows signs of decline.

sections.text: (4) Decontamination
Test equipment and specimens exposed to mold should be decontaminated (see Appendix A of GJB150.10A-2009).
5. Test Procedure
(1) Test Preparation
1) Pre-test Preparation. Before the test begins, determine the technical status of the specimen, duration, strains, storage/working parameter values, etc., according to relevant documents.

2) Specimen Pretreatment. Preferably use new specimens, or specimens that have undergone other tests. If specimen cleaning is required, the test should start at least 72 hours after cleaning is completed to allow volatile substances to evaporate. Clean specimens should be cleaned using typical methods.
3) Guidance Information. The following guidance information is helpful for implementing this test:

items: a) Select strains that have the ability to corrode most materials on the equipment. If necessary, add other strains [see Section 2.3.2].
b) It should be performed by professionals in professional laboratories.

c) Spore germination and growth require a moist environment. When the relative humidity of the ambient air exceeds 70%, mold spores begin to germinate and grow; when the relative humidity is higher than this value, such as 90%-100%, mold germination and growth will be faster.

sections.text: d) The test temperature is 30°C±1°C, which is most favorable for the growth of test mold.
e) The cotton control strip specified in Section 5.1.6 is used to:

items: • Verify the activity of mold spores in the inoculum.
• Verify the extent to which the environment in the test chamber is suitable for mold growth.

sections.text: f) Mold tests on materials and components cannot fully represent the mold growth of the equipment they constitute; therefore, if comprehensive information on mold growth of the equipment is required, use the entire equipment for testing.
g) Strain preservation at 6°C±4°C should not exceed 4 months, during which time re-inoculation should be performed and used as a new preserved strain.
h) It is best to use freshly prepared spore suspension for each test. If the spore suspension is not freshly prepared, its preservation time at 6°C±4°C should not exceed 14 days.
4) Preparation of Inorganic Salt Solution. Using clean containers, prepare the inorganic salt solution according to Table 5-27, and maintain the pH of the solution between 6.0-6.5.

sections.caption: Table 5-27 Components of inorganic salt solution

sections.text: 5) Preparation of mixed spore suspension. The requirements and procedures for preparing mixed spore suspension are as follows:

items: a) Prepare spore suspension containing at least two test strains specified in 2.(3)2) using aseptic techniques.

b) Cultivate pure strains separately on appropriate media (such as potato dextrose agar), while Aspergillus glaucus should be cultivated on filter paper placed on the surface of inorganic salt agar. Preparation method for inorganic salt agar: dissolve 15.0 g agar in 1 L of inorganic salt solution specified in 5.(1)4).
c) Check the purity of strains before the test.
d) Prepare primary culture of preserved pure strains, and cultivate at 30°C±1°C for 10~21 d.

sections.text: Note: Most molds require a cultivation period of 10~21 d, and may show signs of degeneration after extended cultivation. Certain strains such as Aspergillus glaucus require 21 d or longer cultivation.

items: e) Add 10 mL of aqueous solution containing 0.05 g of non-toxic wetting agent (such as sodium dioctyl sulfosuccinate or sodium dodecyl sulfate) per liter to each test tube of secondary culture.
f) Gently scrape the surface of test strains with sterile glass rod, platinum wire, or nichrome wire.
g) Transfer the spore extract to a 125 mL stoppered Erlenmeyer flask containing 45 mL water and 50~70 solid glass beads with a diameter of 5 mm.
h) Vigorously shake the Erlenmeyer flask to break up spores and release them from the mycelia.
i) Filter the mold spore suspension through a glass funnel containing 6 mm thick glass wool into an Erlenmeyer flask to remove large mycelial fragments and agar pieces.
j) Centrifuge the filtered spore suspension and discard the supernatant.
k) Add 50 mL water to the remaining precipitate and resuspend, then centrifuge again. Centrifuge each mold spore in this manner at least 3 times (until the supernatant becomes clear).
l) Dilute the final precipitate with inorganic salt solution, and through counting, adjust to achieve a final concentration of 10000000×(1±20%) spores per liter in the spore suspension.
m) Repeat steps c)~l) for each strain used in the test.

sections.text: n) Perform viability test on spores of each strain according to 5.(1)6).
6) Verification test.

items: ① Overview. Two verification tests should be conducted in this test to check the viability of spore suspension and whether the test chamber environment is suitable for mold growth.
② Viability of spore suspension. The test procedure is as follows:
a) Before preparing mixed spore suspension, inoculate 0.2~0.3 mL of each mold spore suspension onto sterile potato dextrose or other agar plates, using separate agar plates for each strain.
b) Spread the inoculum evenly over the entire surface of the agar plates.
c) Incubate the inoculated agar plates in an incubator at 30°C±1°C for 7~10 d.
d) Check mold growth after incubation.

sections.text: Note: If any test strain shows no substantial growth over the entire surface of the plates, the test using spores of these strains is invalid.
③ Test chamber environment. The test procedure is as follows:

items: a) Prepare the solution according to Table 5-28, and adjust the final solution pH to 5.3 using HCl and NaOH.

b) Prepare control strips by cutting unbleached plain 100% cotton cloth into strips about 3 cm wide. Only use cotton strips free from antimold agents, water repellents, and sizing additives. To remove any treatment materials from the cotton strips, it is recommended to boil them in distilled water, then immerse the cotton strips in the solution from Table 5-28, ensuring the strips are thoroughly wetted. After soaking, remove excess liquid from the strips, hang to dry before placing them in the test chamber for inoculation.

c) In the test chamber, hang the control strips vertically near the test specimens, ensuring the control strips and specimens are subjected to the same test environment. The length of the control strips should be at least equal to the height of the specimens.
d) To ensure proper conditions in the test chamber to promote mold growth, place 3 control strips with the specimens for inoculation.

Non-toxic wetting agent (such as sodium dioctyl sulfosuccinate or sodium dodecyl sulfate)

sections.text: 7) Initial inspection. Before the test, all specimens should be inspected under standard conditions.
Verification should be conducted under normal atmospheric conditions to obtain baseline data. The detection should be performed according to the following steps:

items: Record the atmospheric conditions inside the laboratory.
Conduct a comprehensive visual inspection of the specimen and record the inspection results (photographs may be taken if necessary).

If functional testing of the specimen is required according to technical documents, record the test results. If the specimen functions normally, proceed with the subsequent test procedures; if the specimen does not function normally, resolve the issues and retest the specimen until normal operation is achieved.

sections.text: (2) Test Procedure
The test procedure should be conducted according to the following steps:

items: Install the specimen in the appropriate bracket inside the test chamber or suspend it according to the required technical state.
Place the specimen in the working test chamber (temperature 30°C±1°C, relative humidity 95%±5%) for at least 4 hours before inoculation.

Use a sprayer to apply the mixed spore suspension as a fine mist to the cotton cloth control strip, as well as the surface and interior of the specimen (if not permanently sealed or hermetically sealed). With the assistance of personnel familiar with the specimen, expose the internal surfaces of the specimen and inoculate them.
To allow air to enter the interior of the specimen, do not fully tighten the fasteners when resetting the specimen's housing.
Begin the test culture immediately after inoculation.

sections.text: Note: When spraying the mixed spore suspension on the specimen and control strip, ensure the spray covers all exposed external and internal surfaces of the specimen during use or maintenance. If the surface is not wetted, continue spraying until droplets begin to form on the surface.

items: f) Except for steps g) and h), conduct the test under constant conditions of temperature 30°C±1°C and relative humidity 95%±5% (for at least 28 days).

g) After 7 days of testing, check the mold growth on the control strip to confirm that the environmental conditions inside the test chamber are suitable for mold growth. At this point, at least 90% of the surface of each control strip at the same horizontal level as the specimen should be covered by mold. Otherwise, adjust the test chamber to the required conditions suitable for mold growth and restart the entire test. The control strips remain in the test chamber during the test.

h) If mold growth covers more than 90% of the control strip surface after 7 days of testing, continue the test until the required test time is reached. If the mold growth on the control strip does not increase compared to the 7-day mark at the end of the test, the test is considered invalid.

i) Immediately inspect the specimen at the end of the test. If possible, conduct the inspection inside the test chamber. If inspection outside the test chamber cannot be completed within 8 hours, return the specimen to the test chamber or a similar humid environment for at least 12 hours. Except for airtight equipment, open the specimen's housing and inspect both the interior and exterior. Record the inspection results.

sections.text: j) If functional testing of the specimen (such as electronic equipment) is required after the test, operate the specimen during the inspection specified in i). Inspection should be conducted with personnel familiar with the specimen present to assist in exposing the interior for inspection and operating the specimen. Any disturbance to mold growth during functional inspection must be kept to a minimum.
6. Result Analysis
In addition to the guidelines in 3.1.7 of GJB150.1A-2009, the following information also helps in evaluating the test results:

items: Any mold growth on the specimen must be analyzed to determine whether it is growing on the specimen material or on contaminants.
Any mold growth on the specimen material, whether from the inoculation solution or other sources, must be evaluated by qualified personnel as follows:
a) The extent of mold growth on sensitive components or materials. Use Table 5-26 to guide the evaluation, but any mold growth must be fully described.
b) The direct impact of mold growth on the equipment's physical properties.
c) The long-term effects of mold growth on the equipment.
d) The specific materials (nutrients) that support mold growth.

sections.text: 5.6.5 Salt Spray Test
1. National Standard Salt Spray Test

In the introduction of GB/T 10125-2012 "Artificial Atmosphere Corrosion Test - Salt Spray Test," it is stated that due to the many factors affecting metal corrosion, single salt spray resistance cannot replace resistance to other media. Therefore, the test results obtained from this test cannot be used as a direct guide for the corrosion resistance of the tested material in all usage environments. Similarly, the performance of various materials in the test cannot be used as a direct guide for their corrosion resistance in actual use.
Nevertheless, the method specified in this standard can still be used as a method to determine whether the tested material has corrosion resistance.

The salt spray test can be used as a rapid method to evaluate defects such as discontinuities, pores, and damage in organic and inorganic coatings, and can also be used to compare the process quality of samples with similar coatings.

It is unreliable to draw conclusions about the long-term corrosion behavior of different coating systems from salt spray test comparisons, as the corrosion resistance of these coating systems in actual environments is significantly different from their corrosion resistance in salt spray tests.

Author's note: Based on the use of terms such as "salt spray resistance," "corrosion resistance," "anticorrosive performance," and "corrosion resistance," this standard clearly shows signs of translation (this standard adopts the translation method equivalent to ISO 9227:2006 "Artificial Atmosphere Corrosion Test - Salt Spray Test"). Readers should take note when citing.
(1) Scope
In GB/T 10125-2012 "Artificial Atmosphere Corrosion Test - Salt Spray Test," the scope is defined as follows:

"Neutral Salt Spray Test" specifies the equipment, reagents and methods for neutral salt spray (NSS) test, acetic acid salt spray (AASS) test and copper-accelerated acetic acid salt spray (CASS) test, and is applicable to the evaluation of corrosion resistance of metal materials and coatings.
The test object can be either with permanent or temporary corrosion protection performance, or without permanent or temporary corrosion protection performance.
This standard also specifies the method for evaluating the corrosion severity of the test chamber environment.
This standard does not specify the specimen size, special product test period and result interpretation, which should be referred to the corresponding product specifications.
This test is applicable to detect discontinuities, pores and other defects of metals and their alloys, metal coatings, organic coatings, anodic oxide films and conversion films.

items: Neutral salt spray test is applicable to:
① Metals and their alloys.
② Metal coatings (anodic or cathodic).
③ Conversion films.
④ Anodic oxide films.
⑤ Organic coatings on metal substrates.

sections.text: 2) Acetic acid salt spray test and copper-accelerated acetic acid salt spray test are applicable to copper+nickel+chromium or nickel+chromium decorative plating layers, and also to anodic oxide films of aluminum.
This test is applicable to compare the performance of metal materials with or without corrosion protection, but not applicable to rank different materials in terms of corrosivity.
(2) Test conditions

items: Test conditions are shown in Table 5-29.

sections.caption: Table 5-29  Test conditions
headers: Copper-accelerated acetic acid salt spray (CASS) test
rows: Average settling rate of 80 cm² horizontal area/(mL/h)
Concentration of sodium chloride solution (collected solution)/(g/L)

sections.text: 2) Before the test, the salt spray chamber should be left empty or filled with simulated specimens, and it can only be put the specimens into the salt spray chamber and start the test after confirming that the salt spray settling rate and other test conditions are within the specified ranges.

3) The sodium chloride concentration and pH value of the collected liquid of each collecting device should be within the ranges given in Table 5-29. The settling rate of salt spray should be measured after continuous spraying for at least 24 h.
4) The used spray solution should not be reused.

Note: 1. If "Before the test, the salt spray chamber should be left empty or filled with simulated specimens", the specimens will not be able to be put into the salt spray chamber and start the test. 2. "Average settling rate of 80 cm² horizontal area" should be understood as "settling rate of salt spray".
(3) Test period

1) The test period should be selected according to the relevant standards of the test material or product. If there is no standard, it can be determined through consultation with relevant parties. The recommended test periods are 2h, 6h, 24h, 48h, 72h, 96h, 144h, 168h, 240h, 480h, 720h and 1000h.
Note: If the test period of 2h, 6h or 24h is selected, the settling rate of salt spray cannot be measured.
2) Spraying should not be interrupted during the specified test period, and the salt spray chamber can only be opened when it is necessary to briefly observe the specimens.

3) If the test is terminated depending on the time when corrosion starts to occur, the specimens should be checked frequently. Therefore, these specimens cannot be tested together with the specimens that require a predetermined test time.

4) The specimens of the predetermined test period can be checked regularly by visual inspection, but the surface of the test specimens should not be damaged during the inspection, and the time and frequency of opening the chamber for inspection should be minimized.
(4) Treatment of specimens after test

After the test, take out the specimens. In order to reduce the shedding of corrosion products, the specimens should be left to dry naturally indoors for 0.5-1h before cleaning, and then gently cleaned with clean flowing water with a temperature not higher than 40°C to remove the residual salt spray solution on the surface of the specimens, and then immediately blown dry with air at a distance of about 300mm from the specimens and an air pressure not exceeding 200kPa.
Note: The method specified in ISO 8407 can be used to treat the specimens after the test.
In the test specification, how to treat the specimens after the test should consider work practicability.
(5) Evaluation of test results
The evaluation criteria for test results should generally be proposed by the standards of the test material or product. Generally, the test only needs to consider the following aspects:

items: 1) Appearance after the test.
2) Appearance after removing the surface corrosion products.

3) The number and distribution of corrosion defects (i.e. the extent of pitting, cracking, bubbling, corrosion or corrosion spreading from scratches on organic coatings, etc.), which can be carried out according to the methods specified in ISO 8993 and ISO 10289 and ISO 4628-1, ISO 4628-2, ISO 4628-3, ISO 4628-4, ISO 4628-5,

sections.text: ISO 4628-8 specifies the evaluation method for the protective value of coatings.

items: The time when corrosion begins to appear.
Mass change.
Changes in microscopic morphology.
Changes in mechanical properties.

sections.text: The appropriate evaluation of the tested coating or product is determined in good engineering practice.
(6) Test Report

1) The test report must clearly state the evaluation criteria used and the obtained test results. If necessary, there should be test results for each sample, the average test results for each group of identical samples, or test photographs.
2) According to the purpose of the test and its requirements, the test report should include the following contents:

items: The standard number of this standard and the relevant standards referenced.
The type of salt and water used in the test.
Description of the material or product being tested.
Dimensions, shape, area, and surface condition of the sample.
Preparation of the sample, including cleaning before the test and protective measures for the edges or other special areas of the sample.
Description of the known characteristics of the coating and surface treatment.
Number of samples.
Cleaning method of the sample after the test, if necessary, the weight loss caused by cleaning should be explained.
Angle at which the sample is placed.
Frequency and number of sample displacements.
Test cycle and intermediate inspection results.
Special reference samples placed in the salt spray chamber to check the accuracy of test conditions.
Test temperature.
Salt spray settling rate.
pH value of the test solution and collected solution.
Density of the collected liquid.
Corrosion rate of the reference sample (weight loss, unit: g/m²).
Unexpected situations that affect the test results.
Time intervals for inspection.

sections.text: 2. National Military Standard Salt Spray Test

Although GJB 150.11A-2009 "Laboratory Environmental Test Methods for Military Equipment Part 11: Salt Spray Test" stipulates that this standard is applicable for salt spray testing of military equipment, it has reference value for salt spray testing of hydraulic cylinders in other fields.
(1) Purpose and Application
1) Purpose. The purpose of this test is to:

items: Determine the effectiveness of material protective layers and decorative layers.
Measure the impact of salt deposits on the physical and electrical performance of equipment.

sections.text: 2) Application. This test is applicable to:

items: Evaluate the quality and effectiveness of equipment (including hydraulic cylinders, hereinafter the same) and its material protective layers and decorative layers, identify potential problem areas, and discover quality control defects and design defects.
Optimize materials and evaluate equipment.
Equipment mainly exposed to atmospheres with high salt content.

sections.text: 3) Limitations. This test:

items: Does not reproduce the effects of marine atmospheric environment because the chemical composition and concentration of marine and other corrosive environments differ from this test.
Cannot demonstrate a direct relationship between salt spray corrosion and corrosion caused by other media.
Cannot prove that equipment that has passed this test can withstand corrosion in all corrosive environments.
Has been proven unreliable for predicting the service life of different materials and coatings.
Cannot replace the evaluation of corrosion caused by humidity and mold.
Cannot use the test of samples or sample parts to replace the test of components.

sections.text: (2) Tailoring Guidelines
1) Selection of test method.

items: Overview. Analyze the requirements of the relevant technical documents, apply the results obtained from implementing GJB 423.9-2001 "General Requirements for Equipment Environmental Engineering" during the equipment (product) ordering process, determine the stage of atmospheric corrosion that appears during the equipment's (product's) service life (cycle), and determine whether this test is needed based on the following environmental effects. When it is determined that this test is needed and this test is used with other environmental tests using the same specimen, it is also necessary to determine the order of this test relative to other tests.

sections.text: 2) Environmental effects.

items: a. Corrosion effects. Salt spray environment may cause the following corrosion effects on equipment (product):
a) Corrosion caused by electrochemical reactions.
b) Accelerated stress corrosion.
c) Salt ionizing in water to form acidic or alkaline solutions.
b. Electrical effects. Salt spray environment may cause the following electrical effects on equipment (product):
a) Damage to electrical equipment caused by salt deposits.
b) Formation of conductive coating.
c) Corrosion of insulating materials and metals.
c. Physical effects. Salt spray environment may cause the following physical effects on equipment (product):
a) Blocking or jamming of moving parts of mechanical parts and components.
b) Blistering of coatings due to electrolysis.
3) Selection of test sequence.
a. General requirements. See GJB 150.1A-2009 "Laboratory Environmental Test Methods for Military Equipment Part 1: General Environmental Test Methods"

sections.text: Environmental test method Part 1 Section: General requirements) in 3.6.

b. When using one test specimen to complete multiple types of tests, under large temperature differences, it is recommended to use other test specimens for salt spray testing to avoid affecting the results of other tests. Generally, do not use the same test specimen for sand and dust testing and salt spray testing, but if necessary, salt spray testing should be performed after sand and dust testing.
The test procedure has a sequence.
3) Determination of test conditions

① Overview. After selecting this test and the corresponding procedure, the test conditions and test techniques for the procedure should be determined according to the relevant documents and the information provided for the procedure. The test parameters such as the concentration and pH value of the salt solution, the test duration, the deposition rate of salt spray, the test temperature, etc., and the technical state of the test specimen should be determined, considering the contents of 2.(3)2) to 2.(3)7).

② Salt solution. Except as otherwise specified, the concentration of the salt solution should be 5%±1%. The water used should conform to the provisions of 3.2 in GJB150.1A-2009 to avoid introducing pollution or changes in acid-base conditions that may affect the test results.

③ Test duration. This test recommends a test procedure of 96 hours (two wet spray salt spray stages and two dry stages) consisting of 24 hours of salt spray and 24 hours of drying alternately. It has been proven that this alternating method and test time can provide salt spray test results that are closer to the actual exposure situation than continuous salt spray for 96 hours, and have greater potential destructiveness, because the corrosion rate is higher during the transition from wet state to dry state. If it is necessary to compare the corrosion levels between multiple tests, in order to ensure the repeatability of the test, the drying rate of each test drying process should be strictly controlled, and the equipment should be dried for 24 hours. In order to give a higher confidence evaluation of the equipment's ability to resist the corrosive environment, the number of test cycles can be increased; it is also possible to use a test procedure of 48 hours of salt spray and 48 hours of drying.
④ Temperature. The test temperature during the salt spray stage is 35°C±2°C. This temperature does not simulate the actual exposure temperature. If appropriate, other temperatures can also be used.
⑤ Wind speed. During the test, the wind speed in the test box should be kept as close to zero as possible.
⑥ Settling rate. Adjust the settling rate of salt spray so that the collection amount of each collector in the horizontal collection area of 80cm² (diameter 10cm) is 1~3mL of solution per hour.

⑦ Technical state of the test specimen. The technical state and orientation of the test specimen in the salt spray test are important parameters for determining the effect of the environment on the test specimen. Except as otherwise specified, the test specimen should be placed according to its technical state and orientation during intended storage, transportation, or use. The following contents provide the technical states that are most likely to be assumed by equipment exposed to a corrosive atmosphere, and the technical state that should be selected during the test should be the one that can bring the most severe test results:

items: a. In a storage/transportation container or transportation box.
b. Outside the storage/transportation container, but with an effective environmental control system that can partially exclude the salt spray environment.
c. Outside the storage/transportation container and installed in its normal working state.
d. In a state after being modified for special purposes.

sections.text: (3) Information requirements
1) Information required before the test. General information is given in 3.8 of GJB150.1A-2009, and the special information is as follows:

items: The scope of visual inspection and performance inspection of the test specimen, and the description of including or excluding these scopes.
The concentration of the salt solution (if not 5%).
The resistivity and type of water.

sections.text: 2) Information required during the test. General information is given in 3.11 of GJB150.1A-2009, and the special information is as follows:

items: The record of temperature changes in the test box over time.
The settling rate of the salt solution [mL/(80cm²·h)].
The pH value of the salt spray.

sections.text: 3) Information required after the test. General information is given in 3.14 of GJB150.1A-2009, and the special information is as follows:

items: The scope of visual inspection and performance inspection of the test specimen, and the description of including or excluding these scopes.
Test variables:
a. The pH value of the salt solution.
b. The settling rate of the salt solution [mL/(80cm²·h)].
The detection results of corrosion effects, electrical effects, and physical effects.
The observation results used for failure analysis.

sections.text: (4) Test requirements
1) Test equipment.

items: Test box. Use a support frame (sample rack) that does not affect the characteristics of salt spray. All parts in contact with the test specimen cannot cause electrochemical corrosion. Condensate cannot drip onto the test specimen. Any test solution that has been in contact with the test box or test specimen cannot return to the salt solution tank. The test box should have an exhaust port to prevent the pressure in the test space from rising. The waste liquid should be treated according to the relevant regulations of our country.
Salt solution tank. Use materials that do not react with the salt solution to prepare the salt solution tank, such as glass, hard rubber, or plastic.

Salt solution injection system. a. Filter the salt solution and transport it to the test box. The test box is equipped with an atomizer that can produce dispersed, fine, and wet dense fog. The atomizer nozzle and pipeline system should be made of materials that do not react with the salt solution. Prevent salt precipitation from clogging the nozzle.

sections.text:
b. Under the following conditions, suitable salt spray can be obtained in a test chamber with a volume less than 0.34 m³:
a) The nozzle pressure is as low as possible to achieve the required salt spray rate.
b) The nozzle diameter is between 0.5-0.76 mm.
c) In each 0.28 m³ test chamber, approximately 2.8 L of salt solution is atomized every 24 hours.
When using a test chamber with a volume much larger than 0.34 m³, the conditions mentioned in a) to c) need to be modified.

④ Salt spray collector. Use at least two salt spray collectors to collect salt solution samples. One should be placed at the edge of the test piece closest to the nozzle, and the other should also be placed at the edge but farthest from the nozzle. If multiple nozzles are used, the same principle applies. The installation position of the collector should not be shielded by the test piece, nor should it collect salt water dripping from the test piece or other places.

2) Test control. After the compressed air is removed of oil and dirt, it should be preheated and humidified. The purpose of preheating is to compensate for the cooling effect when compressed air expands to atmospheric pressure. Table 5-30 provides the recommended compressed air pressure values and corresponding preheating temperature requirements.

sections.caption: Table 5-30 Compressed Air Pressure and Corresponding Preheating Temperature Requirements

sections.text:
3) Test interruption. General requirements are as specified in 3.1.2 of GJB150.1A-2009, with special requirements as follows:
① Insufficient test interruption. If an unexpected test interruption occurs, causing the test conditions to fall below the specified values and exceed the tolerance, the test piece should be comprehensively visually inspected, and a technical evaluation should be made on the impact of the test interruption on the test results. Stabilize the test piece under test conditions and restart the test from the interruption point.
② Excessive test interruption. If an unexpected test interruption occurs, causing the test conditions to exceed the specified values and exceed the tolerance, the test conditions should be stabilized within the tolerance range and maintained at this level until a comprehensive visual inspection and technical evaluation can be conducted to determine the impact of the test interruption on the test results. If the visual inspection or technical evaluation concludes that the test interruption has not adversely affected the final test results, or confirms that the impact of the interruption is negligible, the test conditions before the interruption should be re-stabilized, and the test should continue from the moment when the tolerance is exceeded. Otherwise, the test should be restarted with new test pieces.

4) Installation and debugging of test pieces.
① General requirements. See 3.9.1 of GJB150.1A-2009.
② Special requirements. Ensure that the position where the settling amount collector is placed in the test chamber will not collect droplets dripping from the test piece.

(5) Test process
1) Test preparation.
① Preparatory steps.
a. Overview. Before the test starts, determine the program variables, technical status of the test piece, number of cycles, duration, order of magnitude of storage/working parameters, etc., according to relevant documents.
b. Pretreatment and technical status of the test piece. The surface of contaminated test pieces should be pretreated to ensure that there are no contaminants on the surface, such as oil, grease, or dirt (dust), as they can cause the surface water film to rupture. No corrosive solvents should be used in any cleaning method, solvents that form a corrosion layer or protective layer on the test piece surface should not be used, and abrasives other than pure magnesium oxide should not be used. The pretreatment of the test piece should be minimized as much as possible.
c. Preparation of test solution. The salt used in this test is sodium chloride, and this sodium chloride (in dry state) should not contain more than 0.1% sodium iodide, and the total amount of impurities should not exceed 0.5%. Sodium chloride containing an anti-caking agent should not be used, as the anti-caking agent will have a corrosion inhibition effect.
Except as otherwise specified, a 5%±1% sodium chloride solution should be prepared by the following method:
Dissolve 5 parts by weight of sodium chloride in 95 parts by weight of water.
Adjust and maintain the relative density of the salt solution by adjusting the temperature and concentration. If necessary, borax (Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O) can be added to the salt solution as a pH buffer, with no more than 0.7 g of borax added to 75 L of salt solution. The pH value of the salt solution should be maintained so that the pH value of the settled salt solution collected in the test chamber remains between 6.5 and 7.2 at a temperature of 35±2°C. Only dilute chemically pure hydrochloric acid or sodium hydroxide can be used to adjust the pH value. The pH value can be measured by electrochemical or colorimetric methods.
d. Operation check of the test chamber. If the test chamber has not been used within 5 days before the test or the nozzle is not blocked, all test parameters of the test chamber should be adjusted under no-load conditions before the test starts to meet the requirements of this test. Maintain this test condition for at least 24 hours, or maintain the test condition until normal operating conditions and salt spray settling rate are confirmed. To ensure the normal operation of the test chamber, the salt spray settling rate should still be monitored after 24 hours. The temperature of the test chamber should be continuously monitored and recorded, or monitored every 2 hours until the test starts.
② Preliminary inspection. Before the test, all test pieces should be inspected under standard atmospheric conditions to obtain baseline data. The inspection should be carried out in the following steps:
a. Record the atmospheric conditions in the laboratory.
b. Conduct a comprehensive visual inspection of the test piece, paying attention to the following contents:
a) High-stress areas.
b) Areas where different types of metals are in contact.
c) Electrical and electronic components—especially those that are close to each other and have no

Coated or exposed circuit elements.
d) Metal surfaces.
e) Enclosed areas where condensation has occurred or may occur.
f) Surfaces or components with coatings or surface anti-corrosion treatments.
g) Cathodic protection systems.
h) Mechanical systems that fail due to blockage or coverage by salt deposits.
i) Insulators for electricity and heat.
Note: If a more thorough visual inspection is required, partial or complete disassembly of the specimen should be considered. However, care must be taken not to damage any protective covering, etc.
c. Record inspection results (photos may be taken if necessary).
d. Install the specimen in the test chamber and ensure it meets the required technical state.
e. Perform operational testing according to relevant documents and record test results as required by 3.10 of GJB150.1A-2009.
f. If the specimen is not functioning properly, solve the problem and restart the pre-test detection under standard atmospheric conditions from the most appropriate step above.
2) Test procedure.
The steps of the test procedure are as follows:
① Adjust the temperature of the test chamber to 35°C and keep the specimen in this condition for at least 2 hours before spraying salt mist.
② Spray salt mist for 24 hours or the time specified in relevant documents. During the entire salt mist spraying process, the salt mist settling rate and pH value of the settling solution should be measured at least every 24 hours to ensure the salt mist settling rate is 1-3 mL/(80cm²·h).
③ Dry the specimen for 24 hours or the time specified in relevant documents under standard atmospheric conditions (15-35°C) and relative humidity not exceeding 50%. During drying, the technical state of the specimen cannot be changed or its mechanical state adjusted.
④ At the end of the drying stage, unless otherwise specified, the specimen should be returned to the salt mist chamber and repeat b) and c) at least once.
⑤ Perform physical and electrical performance testing, record test results (photos may be taken if necessary). If helpful for subsequent corrosion inspection, the specimen can be gently rinsed with flowing water under standard atmospheric conditions, then tested and test results recorded.
⑥ Perform visual inspection on the specimen according to 5.(1)2) and record inspection results.

(6) Result analysis
In addition to the guidelines provided in 3.17 of GJB150.1A-2009, the following information (also) helps evaluate test results:
1) Physical. Salt deposits can cause blockage or adhesion of mechanical parts or components. Any salt deposits produced by this test may represent results caused by the expected environment.
2) Electrical. After the 24-hour drying stage, residual moisture will cause electrical performance failures. Such failures should be considered in relation to failures in actual use.
3) Corrosion. Analyze the impact of corrosion on the normal function and structural integrity of the specimen from both short-term and potential long-term perspectives.
5.6.6 Acceleration Test

Although GJB150.15A-2009 "Military Equipment Laboratory Environmental Test Methods Part 15: Acceleration Test" stipulates that this standard is applicable to acceleration testing of military equipment, it has reference value for acceleration testing of hydraulic cylinders in other application fields.
1. Purpose and Application
(1) Purpose

The purpose of this test is to verify:
a) The equipment's ability to withstand steady-state inertial loads caused by platform acceleration, deceleration, and maneuvering in the use environment, and that its performance will not degrade during and after these loads.
b) The equipment will not become dangerous after experiencing crash inertia.
(2) Application
This test is applicable to equipment installed on aircraft, helicopters, manned spacecraft, aircraft external stores, and ground-launched missiles.
(3) Limitations

items: Other accelerations. The accelerations mentioned in this test are overload coefficients, whose application is slow enough and maintained constant for a long enough time that the equipment has sufficient time to disperse the generated internal loads without exciting the equipment's dynamic response. If the loads do not meet this definition, other complex analysis, design, and test methods are needed.

Aerodynamic loads. When the platform is flying, equipment surfaces exposed to airflow, in addition to bearing inertial loads, also bear aerodynamic loads. This test is generally not applicable in this situation. Equipment bearing aerodynamic loads should be designed and tested according to the most severe combination of these loads. This usually requires more complex structural (static and fatigue) test methods.

Impact. Impact is a rapid movement that can excite the equipment's dynamic (resonance) response, but the total deformation (stress) generated is small. Impact test criteria and test methods cannot replace acceleration criteria and test methods, and vice versa.

sections.text: 2. Tailoring Guide
(1) Selection of test method

items: Overview. Analyze the requirements of relevant technical documents, apply the results derived from implementing GJB4239-2001 "General Requirements for Equipment Environmental Engineering" during the equipment (product) ordering process, determine the stages during the equipment's service life (cycle) when acceleration environment occurs, and determine based on the following environmental effects.

sections.text: Whether this test is necessary. When it is determined that this test is necessary and this test uses the same specimen as other environmental tests, it is also necessary to determine the sequence of this test and other tests.

2) Environmental effects. Acceleration typically produces inertial loads on the equipment mounting bracket and inside the equipment. Attention should be paid to the fact that all parts of the equipment (including liquids) are subjected to loads. The following lists some of the damages caused by high-value acceleration, and equipment that may have any of the following situations should undergo an acceleration test.

items: a) Structural deformation that affects the operation of the equipment.
b) Permanent deformation and fracture that cause the equipment to malfunction or be damaged.
c) Fracture of fasteners or brackets that cause the equipment to fall apart.
d) Fracture of the mounting bracket that causes the equipment to become loose.
e) Short circuit and open circuit of electronic circuit board.
f) Changes in inductance and capacitance values.
g) Relay disconnection or closing.
h) Jamming of actuators or other mechanisms.
i) Seal leakage.
j) Changes in pressure and flow regulation values.
k) Pump cavitation.
l) Displacement of the spool of the servo valve causes incorrect and dangerous control system response.

sections.text: 3) Selection of test sequence. ① General requirements. See 3.6 in GJB150.1A-2009 "Military Equipment Laboratory Environmental Test Methods Part 1: General Requirements". ② Special requirements. High temperature test before acceleration test.
(2) Selection of test procedure
1) Overview. This test includes three test procedures: Procedure I - Structure Test, Procedure II - Performance Test, and Procedure III - Crash Safety Test.

2) Factors to consider when selecting test procedures. Except as otherwise specified, the equipment should undergo both Procedure I and Procedure II tests. For manned aircraft, equipment installed in the work area or at the inlet and outlet passages should undergo Procedure III test.

3) Differences between procedures. ① Procedure I - Structure Test. Procedure I is used to verify the ability of the equipment structure to withstand the loads generated by the use of acceleration. ② Procedure II - Performance Test. Procedure II is used to verify that the performance of the equipment under and after bearing the loads generated by the use of acceleration will not be reduced. ③ Procedure III - Crash Safety Test. Procedure III is used to verify that the equipment will not break or fall off the fixed frame under the action of crash acceleration.
(3) Determination of test conditions

1) Overview. The test varies with the acceleration value, acceleration axis, duration, test equipment and the working state of the specimen. The test acceleration value of each equipment should be obtained from the platform structure load analysis. If the platform used is unknown, the test conditions can be estimated using the values in Table 5-31, Table 5-32 and Table 5-33, as well as the following content.

2) Test axis. For these tests, the forward acceleration direction is always the direction of the platform's forward acceleration. For each test procedure, the specimen should be tested along each axis of the three mutually perpendicular axes. One axis is consistent with the platform's forward acceleration (forward and backward, X), another axis is consistent with the platform's wingspan direction (lateral, Z), and the third axis is perpendicular to the plane composed of the above two axes (up and down, Y). Figure 1 in GJB150.15A-2009 gives the definitions of the three linear and three rotational axes of typical aircraft acceleration.

3) Test values and conditions - General. Tables 5-31, 5-32, and 5-33 list the test values for Procedure I - Structure Test, Procedure II - Performance Test, and Procedure III - Crash Safety Test, respectively. When the orientation of the equipment relative to the operating platform is unknown, the maximum value corresponding to each axis in the table should be selected for the test of each axis.

4) Test values and conditions - Fighters and Attack Aircraft. The test values determined from Tables 5-31 and 5-32 are based on the acceleration at the center of gravity of the platform. For fighters and attack aircraft, considering the loads generated by roll, pitch and yaw maneuvers, the test values of equipment far from the center should be increased. When determining the test conditions of a specific aircraft, consider the influence of the additional angular acceleration caused by the maneuver on the linear acceleration. See GJB150.15A-2009 for details.
(4) Special considerations

1) Measurement of swing amplitude. If the equipment is installed on a shock absorber, the equipment should be installed on the shock absorber for the test together, and the swing amplitude of the equipment should be measured to determine its potential impact on adjacent equipment (determine the swing clearance requirements).

2) Acceleration simulation. Since different test equipment produce acceleration loads in different ways, when selecting acceleration test equipment, the function and characteristics of the specimen should be carefully analyzed. There are two types of commonly used equipment: centrifuges and rocket sleds with tracks.
3) Centrifuge. See GJB150.15A-2009.
4) Rocket sled with track. See GJB150.15A-2009.
3. Information requirements
(1) Information required before the test
General information is given in 3.8 of GJB150.1A-2009, and special information is as follows:
1) Orientation of the specimen relative to the fixture.
2) Orientation of the fixture relative to the direction of acceleration.
(2) Information required during the test
1) General information. See 3.11 in GJB150.1A-2009.

2) Special Information. Special information includes information on the failure criteria of the test specimen under the acceleration of the selected program. Test sensors, test equipment, and test methods should be carefully considered. For example, it should be determined how to collect the test signals of the test specimen on the centrifuge, whether through the centrifuge to lead out the signals, or telemetry signals, or record the signals with a recorder installed on the centrifuge, and also consider the influence of acceleration on the recorder.

items: Orientation of the test specimen relative to the fixture.

sections.text: 4. Test Requirements
(1) Test Equipment

A centrifuge of appropriate size or a rocket sled with a slide rail can be used. It is recommended to use a centrifuge for Program I (Structural Test), Program III (Crash Safety Test), and most Program II (Performance Test). For Program II (Performance Test) when linear acceleration is strictly required, it is recommended to use a rocket sled with a slide rail. Verification of the correct application of acceleration to the test specimen is carried out according to the test equipment regulations.
(2) Test Control

items: Calibration. Correctly calibrate the measurement amplitude and frequency range of the test instrument to ensure reliable acceleration measurement.
Tolerance. The tolerance of the acceleration value at all points of the test specimen is ±10% of the specified value.
Test Interruption. General requirements are in 3.1.2 of GJB150.1A-2009, and special requirements are as follows:

If the test specimen is unexpectedly interrupted at the specified test quantity, it can be restarted to complete the test. If interrupted several times, the fatigue damage of the test specimen should be evaluated (each application of acceleration is a load cycle, and the duration of one cycle will not affect the test result).

If the test specimen is subjected to an acceleration load exceeding the test specified value, the test should be stopped, and the test specimen should be inspected and functionally tested. Based on the inspection and functional test results, an engineering judgment should be made to decide whether to continue the test with the original test specimen or replace it with a new one.

sections.text: 5. Test Process
(1) Test Preparation

1) Initial Inspection. All test specimens need to be inspected under atmospheric conditions before the test to obtain baseline data, and additional inspections and performance inspections need to be carried out during and after the test. The inspection is carried out in the following steps:

items: Check the physical damage of the test specimen, etc.
Install the test specimen according to the technical status required by the technical documents.
Measure the accurate dimensions of the test specimen to provide a reference baseline for evaluating the physical damage generated during the test.
Check whether the installation of the test specimen, fixture, centrifuge, or slide sled is consistent with the requirements of the test specimen and technical documents.
If possible, perform performance inspection according to the technical documents and record the results.
Record the inspection results.

sections.text: 2) Installation of Test Specimen.

items: Overview. Place the test specimen in working condition, and install the test specimen on the test equipment using the support frame for normal installation of the equipment.
Installation on Centrifuge. The steps for installing on the centrifuge are in GJB150.15A-2009.
Installation on Rocket Sled with Slide Rail. The steps for installing on the rocket sled with a slide rail are in GJB150.15A-2009.

sections.text: See GJB 150.15A—2009 for steps.
(2) Test Procedure
1) Procedure I — Structural test. The steps for Procedure I are as follows:

items: a) Install the specimen according to the orientation specified in 5.(1)2), and place it in the working mode.

b) Accelerate the centrifuge to the rotational speed that enables the specimen to generate the g-values specified in 2.(3) and Table 5-31. After the centrifuge reaches a stable speed, maintain this speed for at least 1 minute.
c) Perform functional testing and inspection of the specimen as specified in 5.(1)1).
d) Repeat the test process for the remaining five test directions specified in 5.(1)2).
e) After completing all six test directions, perform functional testing and inspection of the specimen as specified in 5.(1)1).

sections.text: 2) Procedure II — Performance test.

items: ① Centrifuge test. The steps are as follows:
a) Install the specimen according to the orientation specified in 5.(1)2), and place it in the working mode.
b) Perform functional testing and inspection of the specimen as specified in 5.(1)1).

c) Keep the specimen in the working state, and accelerate the centrifuge to the rotational speed that enables the specimen to generate the g-values specified in 2.(3) and Table 5-32. After the centrifuge reaches a stable speed, maintain this speed for at least 1 minute. Perform performance testing and record the results.
d) Repeat steps a) to d) for the remaining five test directions specified in 5.(1)2).
e) After completing all six test directions, perform functional testing and inspection of the specimen as specified in 5.(1)1).

sections.text: ② Rocket sled test with slide rails. The steps are as follows:

items: a) Install the specimen according to the orientation specified in 5.(1)2), and place it in the working mode.
b) Perform functional testing and inspection of the specimen as specified in 5.(1)1).

c) Keep the specimen in the working state, and accelerate the rocket sled to the speed that enables the specimen to generate the g-values specified in 2.(3) and Table 5-32. When the specimen reaches the specified g-value, perform performance testing and record the results.

d) Evaluate the test run parameters to confirm whether the required test acceleration has been achieved. If necessary, repeat the test run under the specified test acceleration to verify the performance of the specimen. Record the test run parameters.

e) Repeat the test process for the remaining five test directions specified in 5.(1)2). After completing all six test directions, perform functional testing and inspection of the specimen as specified in 5.(1)1).

sections.text: 3) Procedure III — Crash installation test. The steps for Procedure III are as follows:

items: a) Install the specimen according to the orientation specified in 5.(1)2), and place it in the working mode.

b) Accelerate the centrifuge to the rotational speed that enables the specimen to generate the g-values specified in 2.(3) and Table 5-33. After the centrifuge reaches a stable speed, maintain this speed for at least 1 minute.
c) Inspect the specimen as specified in 5.(1)1).
d) Repeat the test process for the remaining five test directions specified in 5.(1)2).
e) After completing all six test directions, perform functional testing and inspection of the specimen as specified in 5.(1)1).

sections.text:
6. Result Analysis
See 3.17 in GJB 150.1A—2009 for general requirements. Special requirements are as follows:

items: a) Structural test. If the specimen is undamaged and functions properly after the test, the test is considered qualified.
b) Performance test. If the specimen functions normally during the test and is undamaged with proper functionality after the test, the test is considered qualified.
c) Crash installation test. If the specimen's structure remains connected to the mount after the test, with no parts or fragments separated from the specimen, the test is considered qualified.

sections.text: Author's note: In the result analysis, should "the test is qualified" be expressed as "the specimen test is qualified" or "the specimen is qualified"?
5.6.7 Vibration Test

Although GJB 150.16A—2009 "Military Equipment Laboratory Environmental Test Methods - Part 16: Vibration Test" specifies that this standard is applicable to vibration testing of military equipment, its provisions for vibration testing of hydraulic cylinders in other fields are of reference value.
GJB 150.16—1986 "Military Equipment Environmental Test Methods - Vibration Test" is a normative reference document for CB 1374—2004 "Specification for Reciprocating Hydraulic Cylinders for Ships."
1. Purpose and Application

(1) Purpose
The purpose of this test is to:

items: Enable the developed equipment to withstand vibration and other environmental factors during its lifecycle and operate normally. When considering the superposition of vibration and other environmental factors, refer to other relevant parts of GJB 150.1A—2009 and GJB 150.16A—2009.
Verify whether the equipment can withstand vibration conditions during its lifecycle and operate normally.

sections.text: The term "lifecycle (life cycle)" is defined in GB/T 2900.99 as: The series of stages that a product goes through from conception to disposal. Examples include: A typical system lifecycle includes: concept and definition; design and development; manufacturing, installation, and commissioning;

operation; use lifting and protection; ensure smooth lifting or extension; remove rust and dirt. (2) Application 1) Overview: except as specified in 1.(3), this test method is applicable to various types of tests. Vibration tests combined with other environmental tests shall also be conducted according to other applicable technical documents. This test method can be used to determine the level of vibration test, duration, data processing, and test procedures. 2) Test Purpose: The test procedures and guidelines in this test method can be adjusted according to different test purposes such as development test, reliability test, and identification test (see Appendix B of GJB150.16A-2009). 3) Vibration Experienced in Life Cycle: Table 5-34 provides the categories of vibration environment that equipment may experience in different life cycle stages. Appendix A of GJB150.16A-2009 provides guidelines for estimating vibration level, duration, and selecting test procedures. Appendix B of GJB150.16A-2009 provides definitions and engineering guidelines for describing and applying these tests.
