items: Manufacturing. Equipment will experience vibration environment during manufacturing and acceptance. Assuming that the test piece to be subjected to environmental test and the product to be delivered have the same manufacturing and acceptance process, the test piece will accumulate the same damage as the product before delivery before the test, so that the environmental test can verify the field life of the delivered product. If the manufacturing process changes, resulting in an increase in vibration environment, the influence of this increase in vibration level should be evaluated to ensure that the field life of the subsequent products is not shortened. For example, the prototype may be assembled on the same site, while the delivered equipment is sub-assembled on one site and then transported to another site for final assembly. Such vibration environment can be incorporated into the test plan as pre-treatment.

Environmental Stress Screening (ESS). Before delivery, many equipments have to undergo environmental stress screening, aging or other product acceptance tests. As with the basic production process, it is assumed that the equipment under test and the field equipment are subjected to the same vibration environment, so that the results of environmental tests are valid for field equipment. For equipment that does not have to experience the same vibration environment (such as multiple environmental stress screening), the maximum allowable vibration environment can be applied to the equipment as pre-treatment test for environmental test (see GJB150.16A-2009 Appendix A.2.1.4 and B.2.1.9).

sections.text: (3) Limitations

items: Safety tests. After consultation with the departments responsible for safety, this method can be used as specific safety test requirements, and the vibration level and duration of specific safety tests are not discussed and provided here.

Coupling of platform/equipment. In this test method, the vibration requirements are usually described in terms of the input to the equipment, and the equipment relative to the vibration excitation device (platform, vibration table, etc.) will be regarded as a rigid body. Although this simplification is usually not accurate enough, it is acceptable for smaller equipment; but for larger equipment, the equipment and the excitation device should be combined to consider the vibration of a flexible system. There is no simple rule to determine the validity of this assumption (see GJB150.16A-2009 Appendix B.2.4). For a given equipment, the correct test method should be determined according to the platform. When the impedance between the platform/equipment and the laboratory vibration table/test piece is inconsistent, the force limit method or acceleration limit control method should be adopted to prevent unrealistic strong vibration response (see 6.2 in GJB150.16A-2009). This control limit depends on the measurement data of the field and laboratory. For sensitive equipment that cannot adopt overly conservative test methods, force limit or acceleration limit control can be selected. Sometimes, for some small components, if the response measurement data in the field can be described very specifically and the vibration lasts for a short time, vibration test with open-loop waveform control can be carried out in the laboratory according to the field measurement data.

Manufacturing and maintenance. The vibration experienced during the processing in the factory or during the maintenance process is not mentioned in this method. The guidelines for transport environment can be used to determine the transport environment during manufacturing or maintenance.
Environmental Stress Screening (ESS). This method does not include guidelines for selecting environmental stress screening, and some discussions are made in Appendix A.2.1.4 of GJB150.16A-2009.

sections.text: 2. Tailoring Guide
(1) Selection of test method

Analyze the requirements of relevant technical documents, and use the results obtained by implementing GJB4239-2001 "General Requirements for Equipment Environmental Engineering" in the process of ordering equipment (product) to determine the stage of vibration environment occurrence in the life (cycle) of equipment, and determine whether this test is necessary according to the following environmental effects. When it is determined that this test is necessary and this test uses the same test piece as other environmental tests, it is also necessary to determine the order of this test and other tests.
(2) Selection of vibration test method

1) Overview. The test method selects the vibration environment category and test procedure according to Table 5-34, and determines the corresponding test level and test duration from Appendix A of GJB150.16A-2009. The selection of vibration test method should also consider:

a) Conservatism in test level selection: The vibration test conditions usually contain additional margins to represent those factors that cannot be covered when the conditions are formulated. These factors usually include the worst conditions that cannot be determined, the superposition effect with other environmental stresses (temperature, acceleration, etc.), and the difference between the three-dimensional vibration of orthogonal axes and the vibration of three axes respectively. In order to reduce weight and cost, these margins are often not considered, but it should be realized that this may increase the risk of equipment life and function.

b) Conservatism of measurement data: Specific equipment measurement data should be used as the basis for vibration conditions as much as possible. Due to the limitation of the number of sensors, the accessibility of measurement points, the linearity of data under extreme conditions and other reasons, the measurement may not cover all extreme conditions. In addition, the test is also limited by the implementation conditions, such as using single-axis vibration instead of multi-axis vibration, and using test fixtures to simulate the support platform. When using measured data to determine test conditions, additional margins should be added to represent these factors. If there is enough measurement data, the statistical method given in GJB150.18A-2009 should be used.

c) Conservatism of estimated data: When measured data cannot be obtained, estimated data of test conditions can be obtained from Appendix A and Appendix D of GJB150.16A-2009. The data in Appendix A of GJB150.16A-2009 is based on the envelope of various conditions, which is conservative for any condition, so no additional margin is recommended.

2) Environmental effects. Vibration causes dynamic displacement of equipment and its internal structure. These dynamic displacements and their corresponding velocities and accelerations may cause or aggravate structural fatigue, and mechanical wear of structures, components and parts. In addition, dynamic displacement can also lead to collision/damage of components. Some typical phenomena caused by vibration problems are as follows:

items: a) Wire wear.
b) Fastener/component loosening.
c) Intermittent electrical contact.
d) Electrical short circuit.

802.page_header: Chapter 5  Test Methods of Hydraulic Cylinders  791

items: e) Seal failure.
f) Component failure.
g) Optical or mechanical misalignment.
h) Structural cracks or fractures.
i) Displacement of particles and failed components.
j) Particles or failed components falling into circuits or mechanical devices.
k) Excessive electrical noise.
l) Bearing abrasion.

sections.text: 3) Selection of test sequence. Use the expected life cycle (phase) event sequence as the general test sequence, while considering the following factors:

a) The cumulative effects of vibration stress may affect the performance of equipment under other environmental conditions (such as temperature, altitude, humidity, leakage, or electromagnetic interference/compatibility). If you want to evaluate the cumulative effects of vibration and other environmental factors, use one specimen for all environmental tests, usually starting with vibration tests. However, if damage from other environmental factors (such as temperature cycling) is expected to make the equipment more sensitive to vibration, this environmental factor test should be performed before the vibration test. For example, temperature cycling may produce initial fatigue cracks, which will expand under vibration.

b) Generally, each specimen should undergo various vibration tests in the order of the life cycle. For most tests, the test sequence can be adjusted to accommodate the scheduling of the test equipment or for other reasons. However, certain tests must be performed in the order of their life cycle. For example, pretreatment related to the manufacturing process (including environmental stress screening) should be completed before vibration tests, pretreatment related to the maintenance process (including stress screening) should be completed before environmental tests representing the mission, and finally, critical environmental tests representing the final stage of the mission should be performed. Sometimes a low integrity test (see Appendix A.2.4.1 of GJB150.16A-2009) is used instead of transportation and maintenance vibration tests.

c) Comparison of transportation and usage states: When evaluating the relative severity of environments, the differences between the transportation state (packaging, support, folding, etc.) and the usage state (installed on the platform, deployment of components when working, etc.) should be included. In addition, the environment of the transportation state is usually defined by the input to the packaging, while the environment of the usage state is described by the input on the equipment installation structure or the response of the equipment to the environment.
3) Differences between procedures.

① Procedure I - General vibration. Procedure I applies to cases where the specimen is fixed on the vibration table, and vibration acts on the specimen through the fixture/specimen interface. According to test requirements, steady-state vibration or transient vibration can be applied.

② Procedure II - Bulk cargo transportation. Procedure II is used for equipment transported by trucks, trailers, or tracked vehicles without fixed installation (binding) to the transportation tools. The test values cannot be tailored, as they represent the transportation vibration experienced by bulk items when military vehicles pass through rough roads.

③ Procedure III - Large component transportation. Procedure III is used to reproduce the vibration and shock environment experienced by large components installed or transported on wheeled or tracked vehicles. It applies to large equipment or cargo piles that account for a large proportion of the vehicle's total mass, as well as equipment that becomes an internal part of the vehicle. In this procedure, vibration excitation is applied to the equipment by a vehicle of a specified type. The vehicle travels on roads in typical service conditions, truly simulating the vibration environment and the dynamic response of the tested equipment to the environment. Generally, measured data is not used to determine the severity of this test, but measurement data is often collected during the test to verify whether the vibration and shock conditions of the equipment components are realistic.

④ Procedure IV - Combination of external suspension and free flight of aircraft. Procedure IV is used for external suspension and free flight of aircraft suspended on fixed-wing aircraft, as well as free flight of ground or sea-launched missiles. For other parts of the external suspension life cycle, procedures I, II, and III can be used. If appropriate, steady-state vibration or transient vibration can be applied. Procedure I is not applicable to the external suspension and free flight of fixed-wing aircraft.
(4) Determination of test conditions

1) Overview. The selection of excitation form (steady-state or transient), excitation level, control scheme, duration, and laboratory conditions should simulate the vibration environment during the equipment's life cycle as realistically as possible. The above parameters should be based on measured data as much as possible. The typical situations of various stages in the life cycle environment, discussions on important parameters, and guidelines for selecting test parameters are provided in
See Appendix A of GB/T 15150.16A—2009. Appendix B provides instructions for engineering information related to resonance testing.

2) Climatic conditions. Most laboratory vibration tests are conducted under standard atmospheric conditions specified in GB/T 15150.1A—2009, but when it is necessary to simulate actual climatic conditions during the life cycle that differ significantly from standard atmospheric conditions, these environmental factors should be considered during vibration testing. The single-stress climatic test methods in GB/T 15150.16A—2009 can be used to determine the corresponding climatic environmental conditions. Special guidelines for comprehensive environmental testing are provided in GB/T 15150.24A—2009 and GB/T 15150.25A—2009. For tests that need to be conducted under temperature conditions, especially high-temperature tests of energetic materials or explosives, consideration should be given to the aging of materials at extreme temperatures, and the total climatic exposure of the test program should not exceed the material's lifespan.

3) Technical status of the test item. The test should simulate the technical status corresponding to the life cycle stage. When simulating transportation, all packaging, supports, fillers, and other special transportation methods should be included in the technical status modifications. The technical status of transportation may vary depending on the mode of transportation:

items: a) Bulk cargo: The methods in Table 5-34 are a combination of experience and measurements, and their conditions cannot be trimmed (see Appendix A.2.2.3 of GB/T 15150.16A—2009). For trucks, trailers, and other ground transportation, the most realistic method is Procedure III. Note that Procedure III requires a transport vehicle and fully loaded cargo.

b) Fastened cargo: Procedure I assumes that there is no relative motion between the vehicle cargo box or aircraft cargo hold and the cargo. This procedure is directly applicable to bundled equipment or equipment fixed in other forms, which should not have relative displacement under the effects of vibration, shock, and acceleration. When the cargo is not fixed or allows limited relative displacement, a certain gap should be left in the test fixture and vibration excitation system to account for this motion. For ground transportation equipment, Procedure III can also be used.

c) Stacked cargo: For grouped stacked or bundled equipment, it may affect the vibration transmitted to each cargo item. Ensure that the technical status of the test item includes the appropriate number of equipment and groups.

sections.text: (5) Operation of the test item. Whenever possible, the test item should be operated during vibration testing, monitoring and recording its performance, and collecting as much data as possible to determine the equipment's sensitivity to vibration. When conducting vibration functional testing, the test item should operate; in other cases, whether the test item operates should be determined based on the actual situation. In most cases, equipment does not operate during transportation, but there are also situations where the functional technical status of the equipment varies with different mission stages, or high-level vibration does not require operation, otherwise it may lead to equipment damage.
3. Information Requirements
(1) Overview

To better conduct and document vibration testing, the following information is needed, and the listed items should be trimmed according to the actual situation. If possible, the modes of the fixture and equipment should be measured. These mode measurement data can be used to evaluate the test results. When the technical requirements of the equipment change or the equipment is used for new purposes, the equipment's adaptability can also be evaluated. If the future focus is on using existing equipment for new purposes, this data is particularly important. When modal measurement is canceled for some reason, a simple resonance search can also provide useful information.
(2) Information needed for testing

items: 1) General information. General information can be found in sections 3.8 and 3.10 of GB/T 15150.1A—2009, and specific information is as follows:
a) Requirements for test fixtures.
b) Modal test method for test fixtures.
c) Modal test method for test item/fixture.
d) Vibration table control scheme.
e) Test tolerances.
f) Requirements for comprehensive environment.
g) Test sequence and duration.
h) Axial direction of vibration.
i) Technical status of measuring instruments.
j) Test safety shutdown procedures when test equipment or test items malfunction or fail.
k) Recovery procedures after test interruption.
l) Test end conditions.

sections.text: 2) Special information for procedures. Special information for procedures is as follows:

items: a) Procedure II—Vibration of bulk cargo: Determine the orientation of the test item relative to the throwing axis of the test table.
b) Procedure III—Transportation of large components: Determine the test vehicle, load, road conditions, distance, and vehicle speed.

sections.text: Note: Modal determination of test fixtures and test items is very important. Large test items on large complex fixtures often exhibit fixture resonance phenomena within the test frequency range. These resonances can lead to over-testing or under-testing of the test item at specific frequencies or positions. When the fixture and test item resonate together, the results can be catastrophic. Even with well-designed vibration table and fixture systems, similar problems can occur with small test items. This is because the lowest resonance frequency of the fixture is difficult to exceed 2000 Hz. If fixture and test item resonance coupling is unavoidable, special vibration control schemes such as acceleration limit or force limit control should be considered.
(3) Information needed during testing
See section 3.11 of GB/T 15150.1A—2009.
(4) Information needed after testing
General information can be found in section 3.14 of GB/T 15150.1A—2009, and specific information is as follows:

items: a) Overview and record of the test, test interruption, and test failure.
b) Discussion and analysis of the test.
c) Functional verification data.
d) Modal analysis data of the test specimen.
e) Modal analysis data of the fixture.
f) All vibration measurement data.

sections.text: 4. Test Requirements
(1) Test Equipment

1) Overview. The test equipment (including all auxiliary facilities) shall be capable of achieving the vibration environment, control scheme, and test tolerance requirements specified in 4.(2). Measurement sensors, data recording, and data processing equipment shall meet the requirements for data measurement, recording, analysis, and display. Unless otherwise specified, vibration tests and measurements shall be conducted under standard atmospheric conditions as specified in 3.1 of GJB150.1A-2009.

2) Procedure I - General Vibration. This procedure utilizes a general-purpose laboratory vibration table (shaker), sliding table, and fixture. The selection of the vibration table is based on the required test frequency range, low-frequency stroke (displacement), and the size and mass of the test specimen and fixture.

3) Procedure II - Transportation of Bulk Cargo. This environment requires the use of a transportation vibration table (see Figure C.5 in GJB150.16A-2009) to simulate, which can produce a circular motion with a frequency of 5 Hz and a double amplitude of 25.4 mm in the vertical plane of the table. The motion occurs in a vertical plane, and the figure shows the required fixture. The fixture is not used to fix the test specimen on the table surface of the transportation vibration table; the size of the transportation vibration table should be sufficient to accommodate the specific test specimen (size and weight). The requirements for the test table surface and baffle plate are specified in GJB150.16A-2009.

4) Procedure III - Transportation of Large Components. The test equipment used in this procedure is a test road and vehicle that can represent the vibration environment experienced by the equipment during transportation and service phases. Other requirements are specified in GJB150.16A-2009.

5) Procedure IV - Combined External Mounting of Aircraft. This procedure uses a general-purpose laboratory vibration table (shaker) to directly or through a fixture drive the test specimen. The test specimen is supported by an independent test frame of the shaker [see 4.(4)4)]. The selection of the vibration table is based on the required test frequency range, low-frequency stroke (displacement) of the table surface, and the size and mass of the test specimen and fixture.
(2) Test Control

1) Overview. The accuracy of generating and measuring the vibration environment is largely related to the installation of the test fixture and test specimen, the measurement system, and the control scheme of the shaker. Ensure that all instruments are maintained in optimal condition. To achieve the tolerances specified in 4.(2)3), careful design of the test apparatus, fixture, sensor installation and wiring, and comprehensive quality control are necessary.
2) Control Scheme.

① Description. The selected control scheme should be able to produce the required vibration level at the required test specimen location. This selection depends on the required vibration characteristics and the dynamic vibration coupling between the platform/equipment, see [1.(3)2) and Appendix B.2.4 of GJB150.16A-2009]. Generally, a single control scheme is adopted, but multiple control schemes can also be used simultaneously.

② Acceleration Input Control Method. Acceleration input control is a traditional method of vibration testing. The control accelerometer is installed on the fixture connected to the test specimen. The motion of the vibration table is controlled by the feedback from the control accelerometer to ensure that the fixture/test specimen interface achieves the specified vibration level. Depending on the test requirements, the control signal can be the average of the output signals of several accelerometers installed at the test specimen/fixture interface. This control scheme is suitable for simulating the input from the platform to the equipment and assumes that the equipment will not affect the vibration of the platform.

③ Force Limit Control Method. A dynamic force sensor is installed between the vibration table/fixture and the test specimen. The motion of the vibration table is controlled by the feedback from the force sensor to reproduce the interface force measured in the field. This method should be used when there is a significant difference in dynamic coupling between the field (platform/equipment) and the laboratory (vibration table/test specimen). This control method can ensure that the correct field-measured dynamic force is input at the interface between the laboratory vibration table and the test specimen. Using this method can avoid over-testing or under-testing the equipment at its lowest structural resonance frequency, which may not be avoidable with other control methods.

④ Acceleration Limit Control Method. Input vibration as specified in 4.(2)2). Additionally, the vibration acceleration response limit at specific points on the equipment should also be specified (determined based on field measurement data), and monitoring accelerometers should be installed at these specific points. Excite the test specimen as specified in 4.(2)2), and use the accelerometer signals at the test specimen mounting points to control the vibration table. When the response values of the monitoring accelerometers exceed the pre-set response limits in certain frequency bands, the input spectrum can be modified to limit the response of the monitoring accelerometers within the pre-set response limits. In the case of satisfying the specified response limits, such modification to the input spectrum (bandwidth and level) should be minimized.

⑤ Acceleration Response Control Method. Use the state of specific points on or within the test specimen to specify the vibration conditions. The control accelerometer is installed at the interface between the vibration table/fixture, and the monitoring accelerometer is installed at specific points on the test specimen. At the beginning of the test, apply a random low-level vibration to the test specimen, controlled by the feedback signal from the control sensor, and then adjust the input vibration experientially during the test until the vibration level of the monitoring accelerometer reaches the specified vibration level. This method is commonly used for combined external mounting of aircraft when there are already measured or evaluated data on the dynamic environment response of the external mounting. This method is also suitable for equipment that already has field-measured response data.

⑥ Open-Loop Waveform Control Method. The monitoring accelerometer is installed on the test specimen at the same location as in the actual measurement. The vibration table is driven by an appropriately compensated time/voltage waveform, which is directly obtained from field measurement data or specific digitized waveforms. During the test, measure the response of the monitoring accelerometer and compare it with the given conditions. Generally, the method for determining the above-compensated voltage waveform is similar to that used in shock testing.

The method of determining the waveform is the same, i.e., the convolution of the required response waveform with the impulse response function of the inverse system. This method is generally not applicable to the test procedures in this part, but is more suitable for controlling transient or short-duration time-varying random vibration in the impact test of GJB150.18A-2009.
3) Tolerance

① Overview. Unless otherwise specified, the tolerance in 4.(2)3)②~4.(2)3)⑤ should be used. If these tolerances cannot be met, achievable tolerances should be proposed and confirmed by the development unit and the user before the test. Protect the measuring sensor to prevent it from contacting surfaces other than the installation surface.
② Acceleration Spectral Density

Carefully analyze the non-Gaussian distribution characteristics in the probability density information of the response data measured at the external site. In particular, determine the relationship between the response data measured at the external site and the reproduced data after the peak 3σ limit clipping technique is often used in the laboratory. The tolerance requirements for acceleration spectral density are: a) Vibration environment: Within the given frequency range, keep the acceleration spectral density on the control sensor within +2.0dB or -1.0dB. For small, compact specimens (such as square electronic devices with small to medium dimensions), well-designed fixtures, and advanced control equipment, this tolerance is usually easy to achieve. When the specimen is large or heavy, or it is impossible to eliminate the resonance of the fixture, or when there are very steep slopes (greater than 20dB/Oct) in the spectrum, it may be necessary to increase this tolerance. In this case, try to ensure that the selected tolerance is the smallest and compatible with the test purpose. In any case, the tolerance within the entire test frequency range should not exceed ±3dB; above 500Hz, it can be +3dB, -6dB. The cumulative bandwidth exceeding these tolerances should be limited to within 5% of the entire test frequency band, otherwise the test, fixture, or test device should be modified to meet the test purpose. For procedure IV - Combined External Suspension of Aircraft, the allowable deviation is ±3dB.
③ Sinusoidal Peak Acceleration

The tolerance requirements for sinusoidal peak acceleration are: a) Vibration environment: Ensure that the deviation of sinusoidal peak acceleration on the control sensor within the specified frequency range does not exceed ±10% of the specified value. b) Vibration measurement: Ensure that the vibration measurement system provides sinusoidal peak value measurement data on the sensor installation surface (or the sensor connector block installation surface) within the test frequency range, with a deviation within ±5% of the vibration level. c) Root mean square (RMS) acceleration value: The RMS acceleration of sinusoidal vibration is equal to 0.707 times the peak acceleration. It has no relationship with the RMS acceleration of random vibration spectrum (g²/Hz), and do not use it to compare sinusoidal conditions (g) and random conditions (g²/Hz).
④ Frequency Measurement

Within the test frequency range, the deviation of the frequency provided by the vibration measurement system on the sensor installation surface (or the sensor connector block installation surface) should be within ±1.25%. ⑤ Transverse acceleration. At any frequency, the vibration acceleration on two axes that are mutually perpendicular and perpendicular to the test drive axis should not exceed 0.45 times (or 0.2 times the acceleration spectral density) of the acceleration on the test axis. In random vibration tests, there are often some high and narrow spikes in the transverse acceleration spectral density, and these factors should be considered when trimming the transverse tolerance.
(3) Test Interruption

See 3.12 in GJB150.1A-2009, with the following special requirements: a) If the test is interrupted due to the failure of the specimen, analyze the cause of the failure. Based on the analysis results, decide whether to restart the test, replace the specimen, continue the test after repairing the failed component, or end the test. b) If the qualification test is interrupted due to component failure, the test continued from the interruption point after replacing the failed component cannot guarantee that the replaced component meets the test requirements. Before making the test pass decision, each replaced component should undergo a complete vibration test. Further explanation is provided in 6b).
(4) Installation and Debugging of the Specimen

items: General requirements: See 3.9 in GJB150.1A-2009.

Procedure I - General Vibration. ① Overview. The technical status of the specimen should be consistent with the equipment status of the life cycle stage to be simulated. ② Transportation. The technical status of the specimen should be the same as during transportation, with a protective box, protective device/packaging. Fix/bond the specimen to the fixture according to the transportation method during the life cycle. ③ Operation. The technical status of the specimen should be the same as during operation. Use the same type of fixing device as during operation in the life cycle to fix the specimen at the test fixture installation position. Provide all mechanical, electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic, or other connections that will be used when the equipment is running. Unless otherwise specified, ensure that these connections can dynamically simulate service.

sections.text: The connection status at the time is completely consistent with the function.
3) Program II — Bulk Cargo Transportation

① Overview. Select the baffle facilities according to the following two types of specimens (if multiple specimens are used, it refers to the same specimen rather than a mixture of unrelated specimens):

items: a) Specimens that are prone to sliding on the test surface or "rectangular cross-section specimens" (typical packaged specimens).
b) Specimens that are prone to rolling on the test surface or "circular cross-section specimens".

sections.text: ② For rectangular cross-section specimens, 4 or more circular cross-section specimens, and 3 or fewer circular cross-section specimens, see GJB150.16A-2009 for the selection of baffle facilities.
4) Program III — Large Component Transportation. See GJB 150.16A—2009.
5) Program IV — Combined External Mounting of Aircraft, External Mounting and Free External Mounting. See GJB 150.16A—2009.
5. Test Process
(1) Overview
The following steps, whether performed individually or in combination, provide a basis for collecting data related to the durability and functionality of specimens in a vibration environment.
(2) Test Preparation

1) Preparation before the test. Before the test begins, determine the test program, technical status of the specimen, test level, test duration, vibration table control method, failure criteria, specimen function requirements, measurement instrument requirements, test equipment capabilities, and fixtures according to relevant documents. Additionally, the following is required:

items: a) Select a suitable vibration table and fixture.
b) Select a suitable data acquisition system (instruments, cables, signal conditioners, recorders, and analysis equipment, etc.).
c) Perform a pre-debugging of the vibration equipment without installing the specimen to confirm that it is working properly.
d) Ensure that the functionality of the data acquisition system meets the technical requirements.

sections.text: 2) Initial Inspection. All specimens should undergo a pre-test inspection under standard atmospheric conditions to obtain original baseline data. The inspection is carried out in the following steps:

items: a) Check the specimen for physical damage and record the results.
b) Prepare the specimen according to the technical state of operation as specified in the technical document, if required.
c) Check whether the combination of the specimen, fixture, and vibration table meets the requirements of the specimen and technical document.

d) If applicable, perform a working check of the specimen under the working state as specified in the technical document and record the inspection results for comparison with the data obtained during and after the test.

sections.text: (3) Test Program
1) Program I — General Vibration. The steps of Program I are as follows:
a) Perform an appearance inspection and functional inspection of the specimen. If a failure is found, handle it according to 4.(3).
b) If required, perform a modal test of the fixture to verify whether it meets the requirements.
c) Install the specimen on the fixture in the actual state of use in the life cycle.

d) Install a sufficient number of sensors near or at the connection between the specimen/fixture/vibration table to measure the vibration data of the specimen/fixture interface, control the vibration table according to the control scheme, and measure other necessary data. Install the control sensor as close as possible to the interface between the specimen/fixture. Ensure that the overall accuracy of the measurement system is sufficient to verify that the vibration level is within the tolerance specified in 4.(2)3) and meets the additional specific accuracy requirements.
e) If required, perform a modal test of the specimen.
f) Perform an appearance inspection of the specimen, and if applicable, a functional inspection. If a failure is found, handle it according to 4.(3).
g) Apply low-level vibration at the connection between the specimen and fixture. If required, apply other environmental stresses as well.
h) Check whether the vibration table, fixture, and measurement system meet the specified requirements.
i) Apply the required vibration level and other required environmental stresses at the connection between the specimen/fixture.

j) Check whether the vibration level at the connection between the specimen/fixture meets the specified requirements. If the test duration is not more than 0.5 h, perform this step immediately after the first application of full-level vibration and before the end of the entire test. Otherwise, perform this step immediately after the first actual full-level vibration, then every 0.5 h thereafter, and before the end of the entire test.

k) Monitor the vibration level throughout the entire test process. If feasible, continuously monitor the performance of the specimen. If the vibration level changes or a failure occurs, terminate the test according to the shutdown procedure in 3.(2)1)j). Determine the cause of the change in vibration level, and then handle it according to the test interruption recovery procedure in 3.(2)1)k.

l) Stop the vibration when the required test duration is reached. According to the test purpose, the technical document may require additional vibration of different levels before the end of the test. If so, repeat steps f) to l) according to the requirements of the technical document.

m) Check the specimen, fixture, vibration table, and measuring instrument. If a failure, wear, loosening, or other abnormality occurs, handle it according to the test interruption recovery procedure in 3.(2)1)k.
n) Check the functionality of the measuring equipment and perform a functional check of the specimen. If a failure occurs, handle it according to 4.(3).
o) Repeat steps a) to n) in each required excitation direction.
p) Repeat steps a) to o) in each required vibration environment.
q) Remove the specimen from the fixture and check the specimen, installation hardware, packaging, etc. If a failure occurs, handle it according to 4.(3).
Author's Note: In the standard GJB150.16A-2009, the above steps k) and
m) The description may not be accurate. The interruption and recovery procedure should be 4.(3) instead of 3.(2)1)k).
2) Procedure II — Bulk Cargo Transportation. The steps of Procedure II are as follows:

items: a) Perform visual and functional inspection of the specimen.
b) If required, perform modal testing of the specimen.
c) Place the specimen inside the restraining panels on the transport vibration table according to the requirements of 4.(1)3) and 4.(4)3).
d) Install sufficient sensors to measure all required data. Ensure that the accuracy of the measurement system meets the specified requirements.
e) Operate the transport vibration table for half of the predetermined test duration.
f) Perform visual and functional inspection of the specimen. If failure occurs, handle it according to 4.(3).
g) Adjust the orientation of the specimen and the panels/walls according to the requirements of 4.(4)3).
h) Operate the transport vibration table for half of the specified test duration.
i) Perform visual and functional inspection of the specimen. If failure occurs, handle it according to 4.(3).

sections.text: 3) Procedure III — Large Component Transportation. The steps of Procedure III are given in GJB150.16A-2009.
4) Procedure IV — Combination External Mounting and Free Drop of Aircraft. The steps of Procedure IV are given in GJB150.16A-2009.
6. Result Analysis
In addition to the guidelines provided in 3.17 of GJB150.1A-2009, the following information also helps in evaluating the test results:

1) Failure Mechanism. The failure analysis related to vibration should correlate the failure mechanism with the dynamic characteristics and dynamic environment of the failed equipment. Simply determining that the equipment was damaged due to high-cycle fatigue or wear is insufficient. The failure must be correlated with the dynamic environment and the dynamic response of the equipment. Therefore, the failure analysis should include not only the usual material properties and crack initiation location data, but also the determination of resonant frequencies, modes, damping values, and dynamic strain distribution (see B.2.5 in GJB150.16A-2009).
2) Qualification Tests. When the test is used to determine compliance with contractual requirements, the following definitions are recommended:

items: a) Failure: If the equipment exhibits permanent deformation or fracture, if fixed parts or components become loose, if the moving or actuated parts of a component become uncontrollable or unresponsive during operation, if the moving parts or controlled quantities drift during setting, positioning, or adjustment, or if the equipment's performance cannot meet the specified requirements after functional vibration and durability tests, the equipment is considered to have failed.

b) Test Completion: The vibration qualification test is considered complete when all elements of the specimen have successfully passed the entire test. If a failure occurs, the test should be terminated, the cause of failure analyzed, and the specimen repaired. The test should continue until all repairs have undergone the entire test. An element is considered qualified only after it has successfully passed the entire test. A qualified element failing during the test extension period is not considered a failure. It can be repaired and the test completion acknowledged.

sections.text: 3) Other Tests. For tests other than qualification tests, corresponding test purposes/failure criteria and test completion criteria should be established.
5.6.8 Impact Test

Although GJB150.18A-2009 "Military Equipment Laboratory Environmental Test Methods Part 18: Impact Test" stipulates that this standard is applicable to impact testing of military equipment, it has reference value for impact testing of hydraulic cylinders in other fields.
GJB150.18-1986 "Military Equipment Environmental Test Methods - Impact Test" is a normative reference document for CB1374-2004 "Specification for Reciprocating Hydraulic Cylinders for Ships".
1. Purpose and Application
(1) Purpose
The purpose of this test is to:

items: a) Evaluate the structural and functional capability of the equipment to withstand non-repetitive impacts that occur infrequently during handling, transportation, and use.
b) Determine the fragility of the equipment for use in packaging design to protect the integrity of the equipment's structure and function.
c) Test the strength of the equipment's mounting devices when the equipment is installed on platforms that may experience collisions.

sections.text: (2) Application

This test is applicable to evaluating the structural and functional characteristics of the equipment under mechanical shock environments that the equipment may experience during its lifetime (cycle). The frequency range of mechanical shock environments is generally not more than 10,000 Hz, and the duration does not exceed 1.0 s. Under most mechanical shock environments, the main response frequency of the equipment does not exceed 2000 Hz, and the response duration does not exceed 0.1 s.
(3) Limitations
This test does not include:

items: a) The impact effects on the equipment caused by the action of pyrotechnic devices (such impact tests are covered in GJB150.27-2009).

b) The impact effects on the equipment caused by high-speed local impacts (such as ballistic impacts) (for such impact tests, they should be specially designed based on test data, and refer to GJB150.29-2009).
c) The strong impact effects on shipboard equipment (impact testing of shipboard equipment should be conducted according to relevant standards for ship impact test methods).
d) The impact effects on fuze systems (safety and functional impact testing of fuzes and their components should be conducted according to GJB573A-1998).

e) The impact effects on the equipment caused by high-pressure wave impacts (such as the pressure wave impacts on the equipment surface caused by artillery fire) (for such impact tests, they should be specially designed based on test data).

sections.text: For such impact tests and their resulting equipment responses, special design based on test data should be applied, and refer to GJB 150.20A—2009.

f) Impact effects on large deployed equipment (such as building pipeline distribution systems). Different parts of such equipment will experience different and unrelated impacts (for such impact tests, special design based on test data should be applied).

g) Special provisions for impact tests under high and low temperature conditions. If there are no special requirements, tests are generally conducted at room temperature. However, the content of GJB 150.18A—2009 helps in the design and implementation of impact tests under high and low temperature environments.

h) Engineering guidelines for unexpected test interruptions caused by test equipment failure or other malfunctions. (If an interruption occurs during impact pulse input, it is generally necessary to re-input the impact pulse, but it should be determined whether the stress caused by the interrupted impact pulse will invalidate subsequent test results. Before continuing the test, data generated due to the interruption should be recorded and analyzed for all test equipment. Additionally, the equipment should be inspected to ensure its integrity before the impact test).
2. Tailoring Guidelines
(1) Selection of Test Method

1) Overview. Analyze the requirements of relevant technical documents, apply the results obtained from implementing GJB 4239—2001 "General Requirements for Equipment Environmental Engineering" during the equipment (product) ordering process, determine the stages of impact environment occurrence during the equipment service life (period), and determine whether this test is needed based on the following environmental effects. When it is determined that this test is needed and the same specimen is used for this test and other environmental tests, it is also necessary to determine the order of this test relative to other tests.

2) Environmental Effects. Generally, impacts may adversely affect the structural and functional integrity of the entire equipment. The degree of adverse effects generally changes with the increase or decrease of the magnitude and duration of the impact. When the duration of the impact is consistent with the reciprocal of the equipment's natural frequency, or the main frequency component of the input impact environment waveform is consistent with the equipment's natural frequency, it will increase the adverse effects on the structural and functional integrity of the equipment. The response of equipment to mechanical impact environment has the following characteristics: high-frequency oscillation, short duration, significant initial rise time, and high magnitude positive and negative peak values. The peak response of mechanical impact is generally enveloped by an exponential function that decreases with time. For equipment with complex multimodal characteristics, its impact response includes the following two frequency response components: the forced frequency response component of the external excitation environment applied to the equipment, and the natural frequency response component of the equipment during or after the application of excitation. These responses lead to:

items: Increased or decreased friction between parts, or equipment failure caused by mutual interference.
Changes in equipment insulation strength, decrease in insulation impedance, and changes in magnetic field and electrostatic field strength.

Equipment circuit board failures, damage, and electrical connector failures (sometimes, under the action of impact, the equipment may cause excess material on the circuit board to shift and cause a short circuit).

sections.text: d) Permanent mechanical deformation of the equipment caused by excessive stress on the equipment's structural or non-structural parts.
e) Damage to mechanical parts of the equipment due to exceeding the limit strength.
f) Accelerated fatigue of materials (low-cycle fatigue).
g) Potential piezoelectric effects of the equipment.
h) Equipment failure caused by the rupture of crystal, ceramic, epoxy resin, or glass packaging.
3) Selection of Test Sequence

items: General Requirements. See 3.6 in GJB 150.1A—2009.

Special Requirements. The test sequence when using the same specimen for other tests depends on the type of test (such as development test, appraisal test, durability test, etc.) and the versatility of the specimen. Generally, the impact test should be arranged as early as possible in the test procedure, but after the vibration test. The specific requirements are as follows:

a) If the impact environment is particularly severe, and there is little possibility for the equipment to pass the test without major structural or functional failure, the impact test should be arranged first in the test sequence. This allows for redesigning the equipment before other environmental tests to meet the impact technical requirements and save costs.

b) If the impact environment is severe but there is a high possibility for the equipment to pass the test without major structural or functional failure, the impact test should be conducted after vibration and temperature tests, which can expose faults under the combined environment of vibration and temperature impact.
c) If the severity of the impact test is not as severe as the vibration test, the impact test can be deleted from the test sequence.

d) It is generally beneficial to conduct the impact test before the climatic test (if this order represents the actual usage conditions). Test experience shows that after conducting the impact test, the equipment's defects sensitive to climatic conditions are often more clearly revealed. However, internal or external thermal stresses may permanently weaken the equipment's ability to withstand vibration and impact. If the impact test is conducted before the climatic test, these defects cannot be detected.

sections.text: (2) Selection of Test Procedure

items: Overview. This test includes eight test procedures:
a) Procedure I—Functional Impact.
b) Procedure II—Packaged Equipment.
c) Procedure III—Fragility.
d) Procedure IV—Transportation Drop.
e) Procedure V—Crash Safety.
f) Procedure VI—Workbench Operation.
g) Procedure VII—Railway Impact.
h) Procedure VIII—Ejection Takeoff and Arresting Landing.

sections.text: 2) Factors to Consider When Selecting Test Procedures. Based on test requirements, consider the equipment's service life (period) (including logistics support and work

All expected impact environments in the test status) shall be determined to use the test program, combination of programs, and the order of programs. When selecting a test program, the following should be considered:
a) Purpose of the equipment. According to the technical document requirements, determine the operation or function of the equipment before, during, and after the impact.

b) Subjected environment. Programs I to VII refer to single impacts caused by momentum exchange between the equipment or its supporting structure and other objects. The ejection takeoff in Program VIII includes a sequence of two impacts separated by a relatively short-duration vibration (such as transient vibration). The arresting landing in Program VIII can be considered as a single impact followed immediately by a transient vibration.
c) Data requirements. Requirements for recording test environment data and test data used to verify the equipment's performance before, during, and after the test.
d) Test sequence, see 2.(1)3).
3) Differences between programs

① Program I - Functional Impact. Conduct impact tests on equipment in working condition (including mechanical, electrical, hydraulic, and electronic) to evaluate the structural integrity and functional consistency of the equipment under impact. Generally, it is required that the equipment can operate during the impact and will not be damaged when subjected to typical impacts that may be encountered during actual use.

② Program II - Packaged Equipment. Used for equipment that requires container transportation. It specifies the minimum critical impact capability as the loading and unloading drop height, providing a basis for packaging design. This program is not suitable for testing extremely fragile equipment (such as missile guidance systems, precision calibration test equipment, gyroscopes, and inertial guidance platforms). For particularly fragile equipment, the quantification of impact resistance should consider using Program III.

③ Program III - Fragility. Used to determine the fragility level of the equipment, providing a basis for packaging design or redesign of the equipment to meet transportation or handling requirements. This program is used to determine the critical impact conditions of the equipment, under which the structural and functional integrity of the equipment may degrade. If more realistic ultimate capability is to be obtained, this program should be conducted at extreme environmental temperatures.

④ Program IV - Transportation Drop. Used to determine whether the equipment can withstand the impact caused by normal loading and unloading, which is usually moved in or out of the transport box or combined box, or used in the field (transported to the battlefield by manpower, trucks, trains, etc.). Such impacts are accidental but may impair the function of the equipment. This program is not applicable to the impacts encountered in normal logistics transportation environments, such as the impacts experienced by equipment in containers and determined in the equipment's life cycle profile (see Program II - Packaged Equipment).

⑤ Program V - Crash Safety. Used for equipment installed on air and ground vehicles, which may detach from mounting brackets, tie-down devices, or box structures during a crash, endangering personnel safety. This program verifies the structural integrity of the equipment's mounting brackets, tie-down devices, or box structures under simulated crash conditions. This program also verifies the integrity of the overall structure of the equipment, such as preventing components from popping out under impact. This program is not applicable to equipment transported as cargo, which should be tested according to GJB150.15A-2009 or GJB150.16A-2009.

⑥ Program VI - Workbench Operation. Used for equipment that needs to be operated, maintained, or packaged on a workbench. This program is used to determine whether the equipment can withstand the impacts generated during typical workbench operation, maintenance, or packaging. Such impacts may be encountered during equipment repair. This program can also be applied to test equipment with protruding parts, as even if the entire equipment is not impacted, it is extremely vulnerable due to the protruding parts. This test should pay special attention to the damage to the structure of the protruding parts of the equipment during workbench operation, maintenance, or packaging. This program is applicable to equipment removed from transport boxes with the longest side greater than 23 cm, while for equipment smaller than this dimension, it is generally tested according to Program IV (Transportation Drop) at a higher level.

⑦ Program VII - Rail Impact. Used for equipment transported by rail. This program is used to verify the structural integrity of the equipment during conventional rail vehicle impacts in rail transportation, and to evaluate the applicability of tie-down systems and tie-down procedures. If there are no specific requirements for equipment transportation, all equipment should be tested at maximum rated gross weight (full load). This program is not applicable to small, individually packaged equipment that is usually transported (or tested) mounted on racks or as part of large equipment.

⑧ Program VIII - Ejection Takeoff and Arresting Landing. Used for equipment installed inside or on fixed-wing aircraft that undergoes ejection takeoff and arresting landing. For ejection takeoff, the equipment first experiences an initial impact, followed by a low-level transient vibration with a certain duration, the frequency of which is close to the lowest frequency component of the mounting platform, and finally experiences another impact according to the ejection procedure. For arresting landing, the equipment will experience an initial impact, followed by a low-level transient vibration with a certain duration, the frequency of which is close to the lowest frequency component of the mounting platform.
(3) Determine Test Conditions

1) Overview. After selecting this test and the corresponding program, the test conditions and test techniques for that program should also be selected according to the requirements of relevant documents and the information provided for that program. When determining test parameters, the content of 2.(3)2) to 2.(3)4) should be considered.

2) General Considerations. The description of impact environment and impact response can be found in Appendix A of GJB150.18A-2009. The time-domain characteristics of impact response can be described by amplitude and duration. There are two definitions of effective impact duration, and the effective duration Te is recommended; the frequency-domain characteristics of impact response can be described by shock response spectrum, energy spectrum, and Fourier spectrum. There are several definitions of shock response spectrum, and it is recommended to use the maximum absolute acceleration shock response spectrum as the method to describe impact response, with the maximum

sections.text: The shock response spectrum of the pseudo-velocity is used as an alternative method. Shock tests typically measure the input acceleration shock environment and the equipment's acceleration response, and may also measure other responses of the equipment, such as velocity, displacement, strain, force, or pressure.

Usually, if the requirements for system integrity are comparable, no further shock test procedures are needed along the axes that have undergone a sufficiently severe random vibration test. If the relevant standards stipulate that the equipment must undergo both random vibration and shock tests, the Gaussian 3σ acceleration response spectrum obtained from the specified random vibration excitation spectrum, at every point within the specified natural frequency range, exceeds the maximum acceleration shock response spectrum obtained from the specified shock excitation, then the random vibration test is considered sufficiently severe and can be replaced by a relatively high-level random vibration test instead of a relatively low-level shock test. The Q value used for response spectrum analysis is generally taken as 10, corresponding to 5% critical viscous damping. The 3σ shock response spectrum of the random vibration test is a function of the natural frequency of the single-degree-of-freedom system, and can be given by equation (5-2):
Where A(f) is the amplitude of the acceleration shock response spectrum at frequency f; G(f) is the value of the acceleration spectral density at frequency f.
The relationship between the level of acceleration spectral density and the corresponding level of shock response spectrum is discussed in Appendix D of GJB 150.18A-2009.
3) Determination of the shock response spectrum and effective duration in the test

① Overview. The shock response spectrum SRS and effective duration Te (see Appendix C of GJB 150.18A-2009) can be determined by statistical processing of the measured time history data of the equipment's operating environment, extrapolated data of similar dynamic environment measurement data, predicted data, or a combination of these three types of data. To facilitate trimming, it is advisable to use measurement data under environmental conditions similar to those within the equipment's lifetime (cycle) profile. After deriving the shock response spectrum SRS and effective duration Te, the test method should be selected based on the data acquisition situation:
a) If measurement data is available, use the waveform control method to reproduce the measured shock waveform on the vibration table.

b) If measurement data is available, synthesize the shock waveform through a complex transient process, where the effective duration Te of the shock is approximately equal to the effective duration Te of the measured shock, with similar waveforms, peak values, and zero-crossing points.

c) If no measurement data is available, but previous shock response spectrum estimates are available, the shock waveform can be synthesized through a complex transient process, and the determination of the effective duration Te should appropriately consider the natural frequency response characteristics of the equipment.

d) If no measurement data is available, but the shock can be reproduced using classic pulses, the shock waveform can be reproduced using classic pulses. Classic pulses can only be used if their use is justified in the analysis.

② If measurement data is available. The effective duration Te of the test is determined by analyzing typical shock time histories. Te starts from the first point of response on the shock time history and extends to the shorter value between the effective duration obtained from the analysis and the background noise of the instrument system. The required shock response spectrum for the test is determined through analytical calculation. If the effective duration Te < 1/(2fmin) (where fmin is the lowest frequency of the shock response spectrum), the effective duration Te of the test can be extended to 1/(2fmin); at least within 5-2000 Hz, take Q=10, and perform shock response spectrum analysis on the AC-coupled time history with a frequency interval of 1/12 octave or smaller. Process according to the following requirements:

a) When there are sufficient representative shock response spectra, use appropriate statistical envelope techniques to determine the required test spectrum (see Appendix B of GJB 150.18A-2009), and the effective duration Te of the test should take the larger value between the Te obtained from the analysis and 1/(2fmin).

b) When there is not enough data available for statistical analysis, considering the randomness of the shock environment and the uncertainty of the prediction method used, determine the required test spectrum by adding a certain margin to the maximum spectrum value obtained based on theoretically justified engineering judgment. Based on the degree of conservatism expected for the test level (see Appendix B.4.2 of GJB 150.18A-2009), typically add a margin of 3 dB or 6 dB to the envelope of the estimated shock response spectrum. The effective duration Te of the test should take the larger value between the Te obtained from the analysis and 1/(2fmin).

③ If no measurement data is available. If no measurement data is available, for procedures I (functional shock) and V (crash safety), a suitable spectrum from Figure 1 of GJB 150.18A-2009 can be used as the test spectrum for each axis, and the duration Te of the shock time history should be between the values given in Table 5-35. The spectrum given in Figure 1 of GJB 150.18A-2009 is similar to the shock response spectrum of the post-peak sawtooth pulse. There are two recommended methods for synthesizing the shock waveform: one is the superposition of decaying sine waves at a finite number of specified frequencies; the other is the superposition of amplitude-modulated sine waves (wavelets) at a finite number of specified frequencies. The shock response spectrum of this waveform is similar to the shock response spectrum in Figure 1 of GJB 150.18A-2009, and the duration of the shock waveform is the maximum value of Te provided in Table 5-35. As long as the response spectrum of the transient pulse is equal to or exceeds the spectrum given in Figure 1 of GJB 150.18A-2009 within the frequency range of 5-2000 Hz, and the duration meets the requirements, it can be used as the shock waveform. The use of classic post-peak sawtooth pulses and trapezoidal pulses is the lowest acceptable choice when no measurement data is available.
If the equipment is required to undergo both shock and random vibration tests in addition to shock vibration tests, it is possible to replace the shock test with a random test during test trimming.
