sections.text: ④ Classical Shock Pulse. If the procedure requires the use of a classical shock pulse, and the measured data is within the tolerance of the classical pulse, then the classical shock pulse may be used; otherwise, it shall not be used.
4) Test Axis Orientation and Number of Shocks.

① General Requirements. The test item should withstand a sufficient number of shocks. To meet the specified test conditions, at least three shocks should be applied in each of the two directions of each of the three orthogonal axes. For each classical shock pulse or complex transient shock pulse applied to each direction of each test axis, the shock response spectrum within the specified frequency range should be within the tolerance of the required test spectrum. And its effective duration should be within 20% tolerance. When calculating the maximum absolute acceleration spectrum (or equivalent static acceleration spectrum), Q is generally taken as 10, and the frequency interval should be less than or equal to 1/12 octave. If the required test spectrum is satisfied in both directions of an axis simultaneously, then repeating three shocks can meet the requirements of that axis. If only one direction can meet the test requirements, three more shocks can be applied to the equipment after changing the polarity of the shock time history or changing the direction of the equipment, to meet the test requirements of the other direction (for complex transient pulses, changing the polarity of the test shock time history usually does not significantly affect the test level). The following considerations apply to both classical shock pulses and complex transient pulses:

items: a) For equipment that may rarely be subjected to shocks, one shock can be applied under each environmental condition; at least one shock should be applied to each axis; if polarity is considered, two shocks can be applied to each axis. For shocks with large velocity changes, only one shock is applied under each shock environment.

b) For equipment that may frequently be subjected to a certain shock, but the number of such shocks cannot be determined, three or more shocks should be applied under each shock environment according to the expected use of the equipment; at least three shocks should be applied to each axis; if polarity is considered, at least six shocks should be applied to each axis.

c) If the test item has no obvious low-frequency modal response, the low-frequency part of the shock response spectrum may exceed the tolerance limit to meet the requirements of the high-frequency part of the response spectrum. The high-frequency part should start at least from one octave below the first-order natural frequency of the equipment. The duration should be kept within the tolerance.

d) If the test item has an obvious low-frequency modal response, to meet the requirements of the shock response spectrum for the low-frequency part, if the duration of the complex transient pulse does not exceed Te+1/2fmin, the duration of the complex transient pulse may exceed the tolerance range. If the duration must exceed Te+1/2fmin, other shock procedures should be adopted.

sections.text: ② Special Handling for Complex Transient Pulses. The synthesized complex transient shock waveform that satisfies the given pulse response spectrum is not unique. If the complex transient shock pulse synthesized from the shock response spectrum exceeds the capability of the shock application system (usually in displacement or velocity), or if the duration is more than 20% longer than the given Te, a compromise should be considered for the tolerance of the spectrum shape and duration. The handling methods are as follows:

items: a) If the test item has no obvious low-frequency modal response, to meet the requirements of the shock response spectrum for the high-frequency part, the low-frequency part of the shock response spectrum may exceed the tolerance limit, and the high-frequency part is specified to start at least from one octave below the first-order natural frequency of the equipment. The duration should be kept within the tolerance.

b) If the test item has an obvious low-frequency modal response, to meet the requirements of the shock response spectrum for the low-frequency part, if the duration of the complex transient pulse does not exceed Te+1/2fmin, the duration of the complex transient pulse may exceed the tolerance. If the duration exceeds Te+1/2fmin in order to keep the low-frequency part of the SRS within the tolerance, other shock procedures should be adopted.

sections.text: The method of decomposing a shock response spectrum into low-frequency (large velocity and displacement) and high-frequency parts cannot be used to meet the shock requirements. To achieve the best solution to meet the test requirements, the input parameters of the complex transient pulse synthesis algorithm can be reasonably set.
(4) Technical Status of Test Items

The technical status of the test items will seriously affect the test results. The technical status expected in the life (phase) cycle profile of the equipment should be used, and at least the following technical statuses should be considered:

items: a) In the container/storage container or transport box.
b) In the working environment.

sections.text: 3. Information Requirements
(1) Information Required Before the Test
General information is shown in 3.8 of GJB150.1A-2009, and special information is as follows:

items: 1) Information related to modal measurement of test fixtures.
2) Information related to modal measurement of test items/fixtures.
3) One of the following shock environments:

a) Estimated shock response spectrum or synthesized wave of complex shock pulse (superposition of attenuated sine, amplitude-modulated sine, or other waveforms, etc.), with specified spectrum shape, peak value, breakpoints, and pulse duration.

b) Selected measured data along with shock response spectrum synthesis technology (if shock response spectrum synthesis technology is used, ensure that the spectrum shape and shock duration are the same as the specified values).

sections.text:
c) Waveform input that has been compensated under direct waveform control into the vibration/impact system for measured data.
4) Technology for processing input and output response data.

(2) Information needed during the test
1) General information. See 3.1.11 in GJB 150.1A—2009.
2) Special information. Including information related to failure criteria of equipment under acceleration action. Pay special attention to the measuring instrument receiving signals from sensors. For high-speed impact tests, avoid noise brought to the measuring instrument by cable swinging.

(3) Information needed after the test
General information see 3.1.4 in GJB 150.1A—2009. Special information is as follows:
a) Duration and number of impacts for each impact.
b) Status of the specimen after each appearance inspection.
c) Response time history and information processed from the response time history. Generally, the shock response spectrum of maximum absolute acceleration and pseudo velocity shock response spectrum should be provided as a function of undamped natural frequency of single degree of freedom system. Sometimes, energy spectrum density and Fourier spectrum need to be provided.
d) Modal analysis data of specimen/fixture.
4. Test Requirements
(1) Test Equipment

The impact test equipment used should be able to produce the test conditions specified in the relevant documents of this test. Impact test equipment can be free fall, elastic rebound, inelastic rebound, hydraulic, compressed gas, electric vibrator, electrohydraulic vibrator, rail vehicle and other excitation devices. When selecting test equipment, consider whether the test equipment can produce the impact duration, amplitude and frequency range required by the specimen. For example, the frequency range that can be produced by electric vibrator is 5~3000Hz, while the controllable frequency range of electrohydraulic vibrator is DC~500Hz. Programs II and III require impact test equipment with relatively large displacement. Program VII uses a special test device for railway carriages, which can provide both very low frequency and medium-high frequency responses at the same time. Program VIII meets the catapult take-off requirements by using two impact pulses and a transient vibration located between these two impact pulses.

Author's note: The above statement "The controllable frequency range of electrohydraulic vibrator is DC~500Hz" in GJB 150.1A—2009 is unknown where it comes from. There is no "electrohydraulic vibrator" standard yet, and in GB/T 21116—2007 "Hydraulic Vibrator" the (maximum) rated frequency range is specified as: "0.1 (1)~1000Hz."
(2) Test Control

1) Calibration. Calibrate the performance of the test device according to the test requirements specified in the selected test program. The equipment for measuring the response of the device should be calibrated. Generally, a "simulated load" is used to meet the requirements of the test specification. The mass and stiffness of the "simulated load" should be similar to the equipment, that is, the "simulated load" should reproduce the modal characteristics of the equipment as much as possible, especially those characteristics that are coupled with the fixture/test equipment. During calibration, perform two consecutive impacts on the "simulated load" to meet the test conditions described in Program I, Program II, Program III, Program V or Program VI (Program IV does not require calibration, Program VII has a special calibration procedure). If the response data on the "simulated load" meets the test tolerance requirements, remove the "simulated load" and install the equipment for the impact test. It is recommended to use the "simulated load" for calibration in all tests.
2) Tolerance

① Overview. In order to ensure the validity of the test, the tolerances specified by each program and the requirements of the following guidelines should be met. If this tolerance cannot be met, the requirements for the tolerance need to be relaxed after being agreed by the relevant departments before the test. The tolerance independently formulated according to the following guidelines should be within the limitations of the specified measurement calibration, instrument, signal conditioning and data analysis methods.

② Time domain tolerance of impact pulse. The time domain tolerance is useful for reproducing impact measurement data and using electric vibrators and electrohydraulic vibrators for damage tests. The peak and duration tolerances of classical post-peak sawtooth wave and trapezoidal wave pulses are shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4 of GJB 150.1A—2009 respectively. The formulation of tolerance requirements for complex transient pulse is based on the following assumptions: the peak-valley sequence of the required measurement data is arranged according to the peak-valley sequence of the specified time history. The main peaks and valleys of complex transient impact pulse are defined as the peaks (valleys) exceeding 75% of the maximum peak (valley) value, and the tolerances of 90% of the main peaks and valleys should be within ±10% of the required peak (valley) value respectively. This tolerance limit assumes that the impact test equipment can accurately reproduce the required impact waveform using the waveform control program.

③ Tolerance of response spectrum. For the transient impact pulse obtained from the maximum impact response spectrum specified in Figure 1 of GJB 150.1A—2009 and the complex transient impact pulse obtained from other measurement data, the tolerance is generally given based on the tolerances of amplitude and duration in the given frequency band. If the previous measured data is applicable or a series of impact measurements are made, the tolerance of the maximum acceleration response spectrum calculated with a frequency resolution of 1/12 octave in at least 90% of the frequency bands within the frequency band of 10~2000Hz should be within the range of -1.5~3dB, and for the remaining 10% of the frequency bands, the tolerance should be within -3~6dB. The tolerance of the duration of the complex transient pulse should be within ±20% of the effective duration Te of the measured pulse.

The tolerance specified by the pseudo velocity impact response spectrum should be derived from the tolerance of the maximum acceleration response spectrum, and be consistent with the tolerance of the maximum acceleration response spectrum and the effective duration tolerance; for a set of measurement data defined by "region", the amplitude tolerance is specified according to the average value of the measurement data in the "region". But it should be noted that this actually relaxes the tolerance of individual measurement data, that is, individual measurement values may actually exceed the tolerance, but the average value is within the tolerance.

When the mean value of the measured data is specified with permissible tolerances, the tolerance band should not exceed the upper limit of the unilateral normal tolerance of 95/50 obtained from its logarithmic transformation of the shock response spectrum estimation, or should not be lower than 1.5 dB below the mean value. When any "regional" tolerances and averaging techniques are used, relevant technical documents should be provided to support them. The tolerance for the pulse duration also applies to the pulse duration of the set of measured data.
(3) Test Interruption

items: General requirements: see GJB 150.1A—2009 section 3.1.2.
Special requirements: In general, the interruption of the shock test procedure will not cause any harmful effects, and the test can be continued from the interruption point.

sections.text: (4) Test Instruments

Overview: Accelerometers are usually used for quantitative measurement, and sometimes other types of sensors can be used, such as linear displacement/voltage sensors, force sensors, laser velocimeters, rate gyros, etc. The performance of these devices should meet the technical requirements for calibration, measurement and analysis. All measuring instruments should be qualified by metrological verification and within the validity period. In addition, the instruments for the function verification of the measuring equipment should also be verified.
(2) Accelerometers

items: a) The transverse sensitivity is less than or equal to 5%.
b) Within 5% to 100% of the peak acceleration required by the test, the amplitude linearity is within 10%.
c) For procedures I, II, III, IV, V, VI and VIII, the flatness of the frequency response is within ±10% in the frequency range of 2 to 2000 Hz.
d) When the response is lower than 2 Hz, a piezoresistive accelerometer should be used, and the flatness of the frequency response should be within ±10% in the specified measurement frequency band.
e) The measurement sensor and installation should be consistent with the relevant technical requirements.

sections.text: 3) Other measuring instruments: All other measuring instruments used for data acquisition should meet the test requirements, especially the calibration and tolerance requirements specified in 4.(2).

4) Signal conditioners: The signal conditioners used should meet the technical requirements of the relevant test procedures for the instruments, especially the filtering of analog voltage signals should meet the requirements of the time response process (usually it should have a linear phase characteristic within the response frequency band), and the configuration of the filter will not mistakenly treat the abnormal acceleration data caused by clipping as response data. Special care should be taken when filtering the acceleration signal at the input end of the amplifier. In order to prevent the inability to detect distorted data due to filtering out distorted data, do not filter the signal entering the amplifier. The signal after signal conditioning should be anti-aliasing filtered before digitization.
(5) Data Analysis
The following issues should be considered:

items: 1) The performance of the analog anti-aliasing filter in the analysis frequency band should meet: a) The aliasing measurement error does not exceed 5%. b) It has a linear phase shift characteristic. c) The amplitude flatness should be within ±1 dB.

2) In the subsequent data processing, the performance of the digital filter used should be comparable to that of the analog anti-aliasing filter, especially the digital filter used for time history processing should have a linear phase characteristic.

3) The analysis process should be carried out according to the relevant technical requirements, especially to verify the amplitude time history of the shock acceleration. Before processing the response time history, integrate each amplitude time history to check the abnormal phenomena of the measurement system, such as broken wires, amplifier slew rate exceeding the limit, data clipping, unexplainable accelerometer zero drift, etc. If abnormal phenomena are found, the invalid response time history measurement data should be eliminated.

sections.text: 5. Test Procedures
(1) Test Preparation

items: 1) Preparation before the test: Before the test starts, determine the test procedure, simulated load, technical status of the test piece, technical status of the measuring instrument, shock level, duration, number of shocks, etc. according to the relevant documents.

2) Initial inspection: Before the test, all test pieces need to be inspected under standard atmospheric conditions to obtain benchmark data. The inspection is carried out in the following steps: a) Carry out a comprehensive appearance inspection of the test piece, pay special attention to key parts or damaged areas, and record the results. b) If the test piece is qualified, install the test piece on the fixture. c) Carry out the operation inspection of the test piece according to the provisions of the technical document, and record the inspection results. d) If the test piece works normally, continue with the subsequent test procedure; if the test piece does not work normally, try to solve the problem, and then start from step a).

sections.text: (3) Overview of Test Procedures

For the requirements of collecting information related to shock tests, see 5.(2). In addition to the general guidelines provided by GJB 150.1A—2009 3.1.7, each test procedure also contains information useful for evaluating test results, which is used for fault analysis. Analyze all cases where the test piece fails to meet the system specification requirements.
(2) Test Procedures

items: 1) Procedure I—Functional shock. ① Overview: The purpose of this test procedure is to find out the equipment faults that may be caused by shocks during use in the field. Although the equipment has successfully withstood relatively severe shocks in the packaging/transportation shock test, due to the differences in support and fixing methods, as well as the differences in functional inspection requirements, it is also necessary to carry out this test. When there are available data, measurable data or usable dynamic analog techniques to estimate according to the relevant data, it is required to tailor the test. When there is no field measurement data available for tailoring, the input shock response spectrum of the shock test is determined by the information in Figure 1 and Table 5-35 of GJB150.18A-2009. When the shock test is carried out with an electric vibration table or an electro-hydraulic vibration table, the calibration procedure should apply the above shock response spectrum after compensation to the complex waveform acting on the simulated load. In the tailoring, if it cannot be proved that the field shock environment

sections.text: The approximate classical impact pulse (such as half-sine, post-peak sawtooth, etc.) generally cannot be used with the classical impact pulse; but if no other method is available, the post-peak sawtooth wave in Figure 3 of GJB150.18A-2009 can be used for testing. To ensure that both positive and negative directions meet the spectrum requirements in Figure 1 of GJB150.18A-2009, the test should be conducted in both positive and negative directions. Figure 2 of GJB150.18A-2009 gives the acceleration spectral density of random vibration equivalent to the impact test response spectrum in Figure 1 of GJB150.18A-2009. If the test piece has undergone random vibration before the impact test, and the acceleration spectral density of the random vibration reaches or exceeds the level of the acceleration spectral density in Figure 2 of GJB150.18A-2009, and the functional test requirements in the random vibration test are the same as those in the impact test, then the functional impact test may not be conducted after permission.

② Control. When there is no measurement data and the test piece is an aircraft equipment or ground equipment, Figure 1 of GJB150.18A-2009 gives the predicted input impact response spectrum of the functional impact test, and the duration Te is given in Table 5-35. Figure 2 of GJB150.18A-2009 provides the acceleration spectral density of random vibration equivalent to the impact test response spectrum in Figure 1 of GJB150.18A-2009. If the test piece has undergone random vibration before the impact test, and the acceleration spectral density of the previous random vibration reaches or exceeds the level of the acceleration spectral density in Figure 2 of GJB150.18A-2009, and the functional test requirements in the random vibration test are the same as those in the impact test, then the functional impact test may not be conducted after approval.
Author's note: The content of "Control" and "Overview" in GJB150.18A-2009 is repetitive.

③ Test tolerance. For measurement data with complex transient waveforms, the test tolerance should meet the requirements of 4.(2)2). When using the acceleration spectral density of random test for equivalent impact response spectrum test, the lower limit of the acceleration spectral density tolerance in Figure 2 of GJB150.18A-2009 is -1dB in the entire frequency band, and the upper limit of the tolerance band is not specified (in general, equivalent test is used because the vibration environment is usually more severe than the acceleration spectral density specified in Figure 2 of GJB150.18A-2009). Appendix D of GJB150.18A-2009 gives the empirical distribution information of the maximum impact response spectrum corresponding to the random acceleration spectral density in Figure 2 of GJB150.18A-2009 when Q=5.
For the classical post-peak sawtooth pulse test, the test parameter tolerance requirements specified in Table 5-36 are shown in Figure 3 of GJB150.18A-2009.

② For equipment installed on trucks and trailers, use a peak value of 20g.
④ Test steps. The steps of Procedure I are as follows:

items: a) Select test conditions and calibrate the impact test equipment as follows:
- Select accelerometers and analysis techniques that meet or exceed the relevant technical requirements.

- Install a simulated load in a state similar to the technical state of the test piece on the impact test equipment. If the equipment is installed on a vibration/shock isolator, ensure that the isolator is functioning during the test. If the input waveform of the impact test equipment is obtained through input/output pulse response function compensation in waveform control, special attention should be paid to the calibration state and subsequent data processing details.

- Conduct impact calibration until the waveform generated by the continuous secondary impact on the simulated load reaches or exceeds the specified test conditions in at least one axis and meets the test tolerance requirements specified in 5.(2)1)③.
- Remove the simulated load and install the test piece on the impact equipment.
b) Perform a functional check on the test piece before impact.
c) Apply impact excitation to the test piece in working condition.

d) Record necessary data to check whether the test meets or exceeds the required test conditions and meets the tolerance requirements specified in 5.(2)1)③. This data includes photos of the test device, test records, photos of actual impact waveforms obtained from the data acquisition system, etc. For test pieces with internal vibration isolation components, measure/check the vibration isolation components to ensure that they do not collide with adjacent components. If necessary, the recorded data can show that the equipment's functionality meets the requirements during impact.
e) Perform a functional check on the test piece after impact and record performance data.

sections.text: f) If the impact response spectrum specified in the standard is used, repeat steps b) to e) three times on each orthogonal axis. If a classical impact pulse is used, the test piece should withstand input pulses in both positive and negative directions. If the waveform of the impact response spectrum meets the pulse time history tolerance and the impact response spectrum tolerance, considering the influence of polarity, two impact tests should be conducted on each orthogonal axis, for a total of six impact tests. If the time history of the test pulse and the impact response spectrum are both out of tolerance or both are out of tolerance, the waveform needs to be adjusted continuously until both tests meet the tolerance. If the two tolerances cannot be met simultaneously, priority should be given to meeting the impact response spectrum test tolerance.
⑤ Result analysis. Conduct test result evaluation according to 3.1.7 of GJB150.1A-2009. Pay attention to any equipment functionality during or after impact.
The interruption capability is closely related to the requirements of equipment functional testing. This information also helps in evaluating the test results.
2) Procedure II — Packaged Equipment
① Overview. The purpose of this test is to ensure that the packaged equipment can function normally after being accidentally dropped before, during, or after packaging.
② Other. For other contents in the overview as well as control, test tolerances, test steps, and result analysis, refer to GJB150.18A-2009.
3) Procedure III — Fragility

① Overview. The purpose of this test is to determine the maximum impact level that the equipment can withstand (at this level, the equipment can still continue to operate as required without structural damage) or the minimum input impact level that damages the equipment (if subjected to a slightly higher level of impact input, the equipment is likely to experience functional failure or structural damage). The level of fragility should be determined by testing the specimen starting from a lower impact level and then gradually increasing the impact level until one of the following conditions occurs:
a) The specimen fails.
b) The predetermined test purpose is achieved without the specimen failing.
c) The critical impact level is reached, indicating that failure will definitely occur under an impact level slightly higher than this.

The last point c) implies that the equipment has been analyzed before the test; the key components and their "stress thresholds" have been determined; and a failure model related to the impact input level has been established. Additionally, during the test, the "stress thresholds" of these key components can be monitored and input into the failure model to predict the failure situation at a given impact level. Usually, this input will cause a large velocity/velocity change in the equipment. If the large velocity/velocity change exceeds the capability of the electric shaker or electro-hydraulic shaker, the classic trapezoidal wave can be implemented on a calibrated drop shock machine (for testing). However, if the electric shaker or electro-hydraulic shaker can meet the requirements of large velocity/velocity change, it is advisable to consider using complex transient waveforms for cutting the test. If there is no available impact input data that can be cut into complex transient waveforms, using the classic trapezoidal pulse on the electric shaker or electro-hydraulic shaker can be considered. During the test, attention should be paid to: under the condition of keeping the maximum velocity change of the impact test approximately constant, only a single parameter (impact input peak) is used to define the fragility level. In the impact response spectrum synthesis waveform test, the maximum velocity change is not as clearly defined as in the classic trapezoidal pulse, nor is it important or easy to control. When data is available, measurable, or can be estimated from relevant data using dynamic analogy techniques, the test should be cut. An important assumption of the fragility test is that the damage potential energy increases linearly with the impact level; otherwise, other test procedures need to be used to determine the fragility level of the equipment.
② Other. For control, test tolerances, test steps, and result analysis, refer to GJB150.18A-2009.
4) Procedure IV — Transportation Drop
① Overview. The purpose of the test is to determine the structural and functional integrity of the equipment installed in a transportation box or assembly box under transportation drop conditions.
② Other. For other contents in the overview as well as control, test tolerances, test steps, and result analysis, refer to GJB150.18A-2009.
5) Procedure V — Crash Safety
① Overview. The purpose of this test (procedure) is to expose structural faults in equipment or equipment brackets on airborne or ground transportation vehicles.
② Other. For other contents in the overview as well as control, test tolerances, test steps, and result analysis, refer to GJB150.18A-2009.
6) Procedure VI — Workbench Operation

① Overview. The purpose of this test is to determine the equipment's ability to withstand impact during maintenance and repair on a typical workbench. All equipment that may undergo maintenance on a workbench or similar workbench should undergo this test. It mainly assesses the structural and functional integrity of the equipment.

② Control. Ensure that the specimen has exactly the same function as the actual equipment. Raise one side of the specimen to 100 mm above the solid wooden workbench surface, or form a 45° angle between the chassis and the workbench surface, or reach the balance point, whichever is the lowest (the workbench surface thickness should be at least 42.5 mm), and conduct a series of drop tests as required by the specifications. The height used in the test is determined by some typical actual drop data, which are usually caused by workbench technicians and assembly personnel.
③ Test Tolerances. Ensure that the test drop height tolerance is within 2.5% of the drop height specified in 6)②.
④ Test Steps. The steps of Procedure VI are as follows:

a) After functional and structural inspection, assemble the specimen according to the actual use state, such as removing the chassis bottom and front panel assembly, and place the specimen in the actual use state. The specimen generally does not operate during the test.

items: Use one side as the axis of rotation, lift the other side of the chassis, and lift it until one of the following conditions occurs (depending on which occurs first): • The lifted side of the chassis has been raised 100 mm above the horizontal workbench surface. • The chassis forms a 45° angle with the horizontal workbench surface. • The lifted side of the chassis is just below the complete balance point.

Allow the chassis to freely fall onto the horizontal workbench surface, and repeat the above process using the other available sides of the same horizontal plane as the axis of rotation, for a total of four drops.
Repeat steps b) and c) for the remaining surfaces of the specimen, so that each surface that the specimen may be placed on in actual use undergoes a total of four drop tests.
Perform an external inspection of the specimen.
Record the test results.
Operate the specimen according to the specifications in the technical documentation.

⑤ Result analysis. Evaluate the test results according to 3.1.7 of GJB150.1A-2009. Generally, all differences between the specimen and those in 5.(2)6)④ a) should be recorded and analyzed.
7) Procedure VII - Railway Impact.

① Overview. The purpose of this test is to determine the effect of impacts from ordinary railway vehicles during transportation on the equipment, to verify the structural integrity of the equipment, and to evaluate the adaptability of the securing system and securing procedures.
② Others. See GJB150.18A-2009 for control, test tolerances, test procedures, result analysis, etc.
8) Procedure VIII - Catapult Takeoff and Arresting Landing.

① Overview. The purpose of this test (is) to verify the functional and structural integrity of equipment installed on or within a fixed-wing aircraft when subjected to catapult takeoff and arresting landing.
② Others. See GJB150.18A-2009 for control, test tolerances, test procedures, result analysis, etc.
5.6.9 Incline and Sway Test

Although GJB150.23A-2009 "Environmental Test Methods for Military Equipment - Part 23: Incline and Sway Test" stipulates that this standard is applicable to incline and sway tests for military equipment, it has reference value for incline and sway tests of hydraulic cylinders applied in other fields.

GJB150.23-1986 "Environmental Test Methods for Military Equipment - Incline and Sway Test" is a normative referenced document for CB1374-2004 "Specification for Reciprocating Hydraulic Cylinders for Ships".
1. Purpose and Application
(1) Purpose
The purpose of this test is to determine whether the equipment can:

items: a) Maintain structural integrity in incline and sway environments.
b) Operate in incline and sway environments.

sections.text: (2) Application
This test is applicable for evaluating:

items: a) Equipment used, transported, or stored on surface ships.
b) Equipment used, transported, or stored in submarines.

sections.text: (3) Limitations
This test is not applicable to aircraft.
2. Tailoring Guide
(1) Selection of Test Method

1) Overview. Analyze the requirements of relevant technical documents, apply the results obtained from implementing GJB4239-2001 "General Requirements for Environmental Engineering of Equipment" during the equipment (product) ordering process, determine the stages in the equipment life (service) cycle when incline and sway environments occur, and determine whether this test is needed based on the following environmental effects. When it is determined that this test is needed and this test is to be conducted using the same specimen as other environmental tests, it is also necessary to determine the sequence of this test relative to other tests.
2) Environmental Effects. Incline and sway may cause the following effects on equipment (product):

items: a) Changes or destruction of the original force balance within the equipment system.
b) Deterioration of lubrication conditions.
c) Changes in liquid level position leading to operational failure or external leakage.

sections.text: 3) Selection of Test Sequence.
① General Requirements. See 3.6 in GJB150.1A-2009 "Environmental Test Methods for Military Equipment - Part 1: General Requirements".
② Special Requirements. If multiple environmental tests are conducted using the same specimen, this test should generally be conducted after high and low temperature tests.
(2) Selection of Test Procedure

1) Overview. This test includes three test procedures: Procedure I - Incline, Procedure II - Sway, and Procedure III - Combined Incline and Sway Test. Unless otherwise specified, Procedure I (Incline) can generally be conducted first, followed by Procedure II (Sway). The combined incline and sway test can also be conducted simultaneously.

2) Factors Considered in Selecting the Procedure. When selecting the procedure, consider the most severe exposure procedure foreseeable during the equipment's life (service) cycle under logistics support and operational conditions, while also considering:

items: a) Technical status of the equipment.
b) Logistics support and operational requirements (purpose) of the equipment.
c) Equipment usage.
d) Procedure sequence.

sections.text: 3) Differences Among Procedures:

items: a) Procedure I - Incline. Applicable to equipment that needs to operate normally when the ship is inclined.
b) Procedure II - Sway. Applicable to equipment that needs to operate normally when the ship is swaying in wind and waves.
c) Procedure III - Combined Incline and Sway Test. Applicable to equipment that needs to operate normally when the ship is both inclined and swaying.

sections.text: (3) Determination of Test Conditions

1) Overview. After selecting this test and the corresponding procedure, the test conditions and test techniques for that procedure should also be selected based on the provisions of relevant documents and the information provided for that procedure. Additionally, determine the functions that the equipment can perform in incline and sway environments. Equipment whose performance is affected by incline and sway states or whose structure has rotational motion, liquid medium, and gravity imbalance motion systems should undergo incline and sway testing. Test parameters such as pitch and roll angles, pitch and roll angles, sway period, test duration, and technical status of the specimen should be determined, considering the content of 2.(3)2) to 2.(3)5).
2) Test Incline and Sway Angles. Determine the test incline and sway angles based on the equipment's purpose, product specifications, or actual measurement data.
Unless otherwise specified, the inclination and swing angles for testing can be determined according to Tables 5-37 and 5-38.
The inclination and swing angles are given in GB/T 24946-2010 (Marine Digital Hydraulic Cylinder), but the referenced standard is CB1146.8.

3) Test swing period. The swing period should be determined based on the ship's displacement and sea conditions. The pitch and roll of the same ship are also different. When the technical documentation of the equipment can provide its actual swing period, the test period should be determined according to the actual usage conditions. Unless otherwise specified, the swing test period can be determined according to Tables 5-37 and 5-38.

4) Test duration. The test times for Procedures I, II, and III should represent the use of specimens under expected inclination and swing environments, but for most equipment, if this time is too long, the test duration should be at least 30 min.

5) Technical state of specimens. Based on the actual state of equipment transportation, storage, or operation, determine the technical state of specimens. The test should at least consider the following technical states:

items: a) Inside the transportation and storage container or transport box.
b) In its normal working technical state.

sections.text: 3. Information Requirements
(1) Information needed before testing. General information is in 3.8 of GJB 150.1A-2009, and special information is as follows:

items: a) Inclination and swing angles.
b) Swing period.

sections.text: c) Technical state of specimens.
d) Test duration.
(2) Information needed during testing. See 3.11 of GJB 150.1A-2009.
(3) Information needed after testing. General information is in 3.14 of GJB 150.1A-2009, and special information is as follows:

items: a) Tests that specimens have undergone.
b) Effects of inclination and swing angles on specimen performance.
c) Effects of swing period on specimen performance.

sections.text: 4. Test Requirements
(1) Test equipment
1) Test platform. The test platform is used for inclination testing; the test platform should be firmly leveled.
2) Swing test stand.

① The swing test stand is used for swing or combined inclination and swing testing. When conducting inclination testing on the swing test stand, specimens should be able to stably maintain the specified position under maximum test load without obvious shaking or drifting.

② The swing test stand should at least be able to simulate one form of ship swing, usually roll (or) pitch, with the swing angle and period being arbitrarily adjustable, and should meet the tolerance requirements of 4.(2) for testing, with waveform distortion less than 15%.

3) Measurement system. When conducting swing testing, the swing angle and period of the swing test chamber should be monitored, and the accuracy of the measurement system should comply with the relevant provisions of GJB 150.1A-2009.

(2) Test control. The additional mass and constraints formed by testing, monitoring, and external connections to ensure specimen operation or energization should be kept to a minimum or as similar as possible to actual installation, and the tolerances for swing angle, swing period, and inclination angle should not exceed ±5% of the specified values.
(3) Test interruption

items: 1) General requirements. See 3.12 of GJB 150.1A-2009.
2) Special requirements. If testing is interrupted, it should be retested.

sections.text: (4) Installation and debugging of specimens. See 3.9 of GJB 150.1A-2009.
5. Test Process

(1) Overview. The following steps are performed individually or in combination to provide a basis for collecting necessary information about specimens in inclination and swing environments. Unless otherwise specified, the laboratory temperature should be maintained at the standard ambient temperature.
(2) Test preparation

1) Preparation before testing. Before testing begins, determine the test procedure, specimen technical state, test angles, swing period, test duration, storage or operational parameter values, etc., according to relevant documents.
2) Initial Testing. All specimens must be tested under standard atmospheric conditions before the test to obtain baseline data. Testing shall be performed according to the following steps:

items: a) Install test sensors on the specimen as specified in the technical documentation (if necessary).
b) Mount the specimen on the test stand under standard atmospheric conditions.
c) Visually inspect the appearance of the specimen and record the results.
d) Perform operational performance testing according to the technical documentation and record the test results.
e) If the specimen operates normally, continue with the corresponding test procedure; if the specimen does not operate normally, resolve the problem and repeat step d).

sections.text: (3) Test procedure
1) Procedure I—Tilt. The steps for Procedure I are as follows:

items: a) Install the specimen on the test stand in its actual working state.

b) Unless otherwise specified in the technical documentation, the specimen should be in its working state and stabilized at the required temperature (if applicable), with test parameters monitored using monitoring instruments.
c) Adjust the test stand to the specified tilt angle according to the technical documentation.
d) Perform operational performance testing on the specimen according to the technical documentation and record the test results (excluding storage or transportation).
e) Unless otherwise specified in the technical documentation, maintain this condition for at least 30 minutes.
f) Restore the test stand to its pre-test angle at the rate specified in the technical documentation.
g) Perform as comprehensive a visual inspection and operational performance testing as possible on the specimen and record the test results.

sections.text: 2) Procedure II—Oscillation. The steps for Procedure II are as follows:

items: a) Install the specimen on the test stand in its actual working state.

b) Unless otherwise specified in the technical documentation, the specimen should be in its working state and stabilized at the required temperature (if applicable), with test parameters monitored using monitoring instruments.
c) Perform the test according to the specified test oscillation angle and oscillation period determined by the technical documentation.
d) Perform operational performance testing on the specimen according to the technical documentation and record the test results (excluding storage or transportation).
e) Unless otherwise specified in the technical documentation, maintain this condition for at least 30 minutes.
f) Restore the test stand to its pre-test state.
g) Perform as comprehensive a visual inspection and operational performance testing as possible on the specimen and record the test results.

sections.text: 3) Procedure III—Combined Tilt and Oscillation. The steps for Procedure III are as follows:

items: a) Install the specimen on the test stand in its actual working state;

b) Unless otherwise specified in the technical documentation, the specimen should be in its working state and stabilized at the required temperature (if applicable), with test parameters monitored using monitoring instruments;
c) Perform the test according to the specified tilt angle, oscillation angle, and oscillation period determined by the technical documentation;
d) Perform operational performance testing on the specimen according to the technical documentation and record the test results (excluding storage or transportation);
e) Unless otherwise specified in the technical documentation, maintain this condition for at least 30 minutes;
f) Restore the test stand to its pre-test state;
g) Perform as comprehensive a visual inspection and operational performance testing as possible on the specimen and record the test results.

sections.text: 6. Result Analysis
In addition to the guidelines provided in 3.1.7 of GJB150.1A-2009, the following information also helps in evaluating test results:

items: a) Test results of performance parameters exceed the allowable limits specified in relevant standards or technical documentation.
b) Structural seizure or damage.
c) Abnormal lubrication or leakage.
d) Bearing temperature rise exceeds allowable value.
e) Erroneous operation, false contact, or sluggishness.
f) Indicator failure or error.

sections.text: 5.7 Reliability Assessment Methods for Hydraulic Components

GB/T 35023-2018 'Reliability Assessment Methods for Hydraulic Components' was issued on May 14, 2018, and implemented on December 1, 2018. This standard specifies reliability assessment methods applicable to hydraulic components (referring to cylinders, pumps, motors, valves, filters, and other hydraulic components) defined in GB/T 17446:

items: a) Failure or suspension of laboratory testing analysis.
b) Field data analysis.
c) Empirical test analysis.
Applicable to the first failure of hydraulic components under non-repairable conditions.

sections.text: 1. General Requirements for Reliability

items: Reliability can be obtained through the three methods given in 'Methods for Assessing Reliability' below.
Mean Time To Failure (MTTF) and B₁₀ life should be used for representation.
Reliability results should be associated with confidence intervals.
Intervals indicating possible failure distributions should be provided.
Before determining reliability, 'failure' should be defined and component failure modes specified.

Analysis methods and test parameters should determine threshold levels, typically including: a) Dynamic leakage (including dynamic internal and external leakage). b) Static leakage (including static internal and external leakage). c) Changes in performance characteristics (such as instability, increased minimum operating pressure, reduced flow, increased response time, changes in electrical characteristics, contamination).

sections.text: and random failure events, etc.).
Note: In addition to the above-mentioned factors, failures can also result from accidental events. For example, cracks or manufacturing defects cannot be avoided.
2. Method for Estimating Reliability

The reliability of hydraulic components is assessed by analyzing laboratory tests that result in failure or termination, field data analysis, and empirical test analysis. Regardless of the method used, environmental conditions will affect the assessment results. Therefore, the assessment should follow the provisions for environmental conditions specified in each method.
3. Laboratory Test Analysis for Failure or Termination
(1) Overview

items: Conduct accelerated tests under environmental conditions and parameters higher than specified values, and clearly define the purpose and objectives of the accelerated test method.

The failure modes or mechanisms of the components should not conflict with or differ from the expected results of non-accelerated tests. The test cycle period should be consistent with the accelerated test.

The test stand should be able to operate reliably under the planned environmental conditions, and its layout should not affect the test results of the tested component. During the reliability test, the measurement error of the parameters should be within the specified range.
Appropriate test planning should be conducted to ensure that the obtained results can accurately predict the reliability of the component under specified conditions.

sections.text: (2) Test Basic Requirements
The test should be conducted according to the relevant clauses of the standard applicable to the evaluated component, and should include:

items: a) The statistical analysis methods used.
b) The parameters to be tested during the reliability test and the threshold levels of each parameter, with some parameters applicable to all components and threshold levels also classified by group.
c) The measurement error requirements as specified in JB/T 7033.

d) The number of samples for the test, which can be determined based on practical methods (such as experience or cost) or statistical methods (such as analysis), with the samples being representative and randomly selected.
e) All preliminary measurements or bench test conditions required for baseline measurements.
f) The conditions for the reliability test (such as supply pressure, cycle rate, load, duty cycle, oil contamination level, environmental conditions, component installation and positioning, etc.).
g) The frequency of parameter measurements during the test (such as specific time intervals or continuous monitoring).
h) The measures to be taken when a sample fails and the measured parameter is not related.
i) The minimum sample proportion required to reach the termination cycle count (such as 50%).

j) The maximum number of sample terminations allowed before the test is stopped, with a clear indication of whether it is necessary to specify a minimum number of cycles (only when a minimum number of cycles is specified can a sample be classified as a terminated sample or an uncounted sample).

sections.text: k) After the test, a final inspection of the samples and test instruments should be conducted, with a clear indication of the impact of these inspections on the test data, a conclusion on whether the test passed or failed, and ensuring the validity of the test data (such as an electromagnet that may not be observed during a cyclic test but can only be discovered during a separate inspection; or a crack that may not be observed unless a separate inspection is conducted).
(3) Data Analysis Method

items: 1) The test results should be evaluated. Weibull analysis can be used for statistical analysis.
2) The analysis of the test data should be conducted according to the following steps:

a) Record the cycle count at which any parameter of a sample first reaches the threshold as the termination cycle count for that sample. If other parameters are needed, the sample can continue the test, but this data should not be used for subsequent reliability analysis.

b) Draw a statistical distribution graph based on the test data. If Weibull analysis is used, the median rank should be used. If the test includes censored data, the modified Johnson formula and Bernard formula can be used to determine the position of the graph. See Annex A of GB/T 3502.3-2018 for examples of data analysis.

c) Perform curve fitting on the test data to determine the characteristic values of the probability distribution. If Weibull analysis is used, these include the minimum life t₀, slope β, and characteristic life η. Additionally, the confidence interval for the B₁₀ life should be determined using the Type I Fisher matrix.

sections.text: Note: Commercial software can be used for curve fitting.
4. Field Data Analysis
(1) Overview

items: 1) Reliability assessment is based on collecting field data from products in operation, with failure data serving as the basis for reliability assessment. The causes of failures include design defects, manufacturing deviations, product overuse, cumulative wear and degradation, and random events. Factors such as product misuse, operating environment, improper operation, installation, and maintenance directly affect the product's life. Field data should be collected to assess the impact of these factors, recording detailed product information such as batch code, date, code, and specific operating environment.

2) Data collection should adopt a formal structured process and format to facilitate the allocation of responsibilities, identification of required data, formulation of processes, and analysis and reporting. Reliability data can be collected based on the time interval of events or inspections (monitoring).
3) The design of the data collection system should minimize human bias.
4) When developing the aforementioned data collection system, consideration should be given to the individual's position, experience, and objectivity.
5) The data to be collected should be selected based on the type of performance indicators used for evaluation or estimation. The data collection system should at least provide:
a) Basic product identification information, including the total number of working units.
b) Equipment environmental level.
c) Environmental conditions.
d) Operating conditions
e) Performance measurements
f) Maintenance conditions
g) Failure description
h) Changes after system failure
i) Corrective actions and specific details for replacement or repair
j) Date, time, and/or cycle for each failure

sections.text: 6) Before recording data, the validity of the data should be checked. Before entering data into the database, the data should be verified and subjected to consistency checks.
7) To ensure confidentiality of data sources, the data used for retrieval should be structured.
8) The specific distribution type of data can be identified through the following three principled methods:

items: a) Engineering judgment, based on analysis of the physical processes generating the data
b) Plotting method using special charts, forming a data graphical table (see GB/T 4091-2001 'Conventional Control Charts')

c) Measuring the deviation between statistical tests on the given sample and the assumed distribution; GB/T 5080.6-1996 'Equipment Reliability Test Validity Test of Constant Failure Rate Hypothesis' provides a test of this type for exponentially distributed data

sections.text: 9) Methods for analyzing field reliability data include:

items: a) Pareto chart
b) Pie chart
c) Bar chart
d) Time series chart
e) Custom charts
f) Non-parametric statistical method
g) Cumulative probability chart
h) Statistical method and probability distribution function
i) Weibull analysis method
j) Extreme value probability method

sections.text: Note: Many commercial software packages support the analysis of field reliability data.
(2) Reliability Estimation Methods for Field Survey Data

The method for calculating the mean time to failure (MTTF) or mean cycles to failure (MCTF) from field data should be the same as that for processing laboratory data. The method given in 3.(3) is used, with examples provided in Appendix A of GB/T 3502-2018, and supplementary information in Appendix B of GB/T 3502-2018.
5. Empirical Test Analysis
(1) Overview

1) Empirical tests should use the Weibull method, which is an empirical test method based on statistical methods, divided into zero-failure and zero/single-failure test schemes. By using valid historical data to define the failure distribution, it is an efficient method for verifying the reliability of small samples.

2) The empirical test method can verify the minimum reliability level of new samples similar to existing samples, but cannot provide an exact value for reliability. If the new sample passes the empirical test, it proves that the sample's reliability is greater than or equal to the test target.

3) During the test process, first select the Weibull slope β; then calculate the test time required to support the empirical test (historical data has shown that for a specific failure mode, β tends to be consistent); finally, conduct small sample tests on the new samples. If the test is successful, it confirms the lower limit of reliability.
Note: Reference [2] of GB/T 3502-2018 introduces the slope value β provided by the Korea Institute of Machinery and Materials for hydraulic components.
4) During the zero-failure test process, if no failure occurs during the test period, a specific Bi life can be obtained.
Note: i is the subscript variable representing the cumulative failure percentage, such as for B10 life, i=10.

5) In addition to allowing one failure during the test, the zero/single-failure test scheme is similar to the zero-failure test scheme. The cost of the zero/single-failure test is higher (due to more tests), but it can reduce the risk of design rejection. One advantage of the zero/single-failure test scheme is that when samples are grouped for testing (such as due to test capacity limitations), if no sample fails, the last sample does not need to be tested. This assumption holds that when one sample fails, the design still meets the reliability requirements.
(2) Zero-Failure Method
1) Based on known historical data, select a Weibull slope value for the component to be tested.
2) Determine the test time according to formula (5-3) or the sample number according to formula (5-4) (derivation process see Appendix C of GB/T 3502-2018)
n = A(ti/t)^β
where t—test duration, expressed in time, cycles, or time intervals;
ti—reliability test index, expressed in time, cycles, or time intervals;
β—Weibull slope, obtained from historical data;
Ri—reliability (100-i)/100;
i—subscript variable representing the cumulative failure percentage (e.g., for B10 life, i=10).
Life, j = 10); n—sample size; C—test confidence; A—see Table 5-39 or formula (5-3) calculation.

sections.caption: Table 5-39  A Value

sections.text: The minimum life can reach at least tⱼ (in cycles, hours, or kilometers).
(3) Zero/Single Failure Method
1) Determine the Weibull slope value β of the component under test based on known historical data.
2) Determine the test duration using Equation (5-5) (see Appendix C of GB/T 35023—2018).
t₁ = tⱼ(lnR₀/lnRⱼ)^(1/β)  (5-5)

Where: t₁—test duration, expressed in time, cycles, or time intervals; tⱼ—reliability test index, expressed in time, cycles, or time intervals; β—Weibull slope, obtained from historical data; Rⱼ—reliability (100-j)/100; R₀—zero (single) failure reliability root value (see Table 5-40); j—subscript variable for cumulative failure rate percentage (e.g., for B₁₀ life, j = 10).

The test report should include the following data:

7. Marking Instructions

When following the GB/T 35023—2018 standard, make the following statement in the test report, product samples, and sales documents: "Hydraulic component reliability testing and trials comply with the provisions of GB/T 35023 'Hydraulic Component Reliability Assessment Methods'."
8. Explanation

1) The standard GB/T 35023—2018 'Hydraulic Component Reliability Assessment Methods' was released on May 14, 2018, and implemented on December 1, 2018. Among them, the normative referenced document GB/T 2900.13—2008 'Electrical Engineering Terminology - Reliability and Service Quality' was abolished on July 1, 2017 (announced on December 13, 2016).

2) In the terminology and definitions of this standard, the term 'component' is defined. However, after comparing it with the definition of 'component' in GB/T 17446—2012, it should belong to rewriting (rearranging words), but the rewriting is not entirely reasonable.

See GB/T 2900.99—2016 Section 1.3.1 for details.
3) The reliability assessment methods within the scope of Chapter 1 of this standard repeat the content of the methods for assessing reliability in Chapter 6.

4) After the withdrawal of JB/T 5924—1991 "Verification Methods for Rated Fatigue Pressure and Rated Static Pressure of Hydraulic Component Pressure Chambers" on May 12, 2017, it is debatable how to determine the failure modes of hydraulic cylinders.

6) The sentence "The failure mode or failure mechanism of the component should not conflict with or differ from the expected results under non-accelerated testing conditions" is difficult to understand or may be incorrect.

This may lead to problems not only in the selection of sample sizes but also in determining whether the test should be proposed by the component manufacturer or the user. Chapter 6 Hydraulic Cylinder Remanufacturing
6.1 Overview of Hydraulic Cylinder Remanufacturing

According to current standards, remanufacturing is the process of specialized repair or upgrading of remanufacturing blanks to make the quality characteristics and safety performance of remanufactured products not lower than those of prototype new products.

The remanufacturing process generally includes recycling, inspection, disassembly, cleaning, classification, evaluation, repair processing, reassembly, testing (verification), identification, and packaging of remanufacturing blanks.

Remanufacturing is the advanced form of "reutilization" in the circular economy advocated by China. It is both an innovation in manufacturing and an innovation in economic model, and has become an important part of modern manufacturing services.

According to the scope of remanufacturing processing, remanufacturing can be divided into restorative remanufacturing and upgrade remanufacturing. 1) Restorative remanufacturing is a remanufacturing model that restores the quality characteristics and safety performance of remanufacturing blanks. 2) Upgrade remanufacturing is a remanufacturing model that involves technical transformation, partial updating, improvement, or enhancement of the quality characteristics and safety performance of remanufacturing blanks.

According to relevant literature and information, remanufacturing technology originated from manufacturing and maintenance technology, and is an extension and expansion of the manufacturing and maintenance process. Remanufacturing has the following characteristics: (1) Advanced nature: During the remanufacturing process, more advanced high-tech and modern production management are adopted than in the original product manufacturing, including modern surface engineering technology, advanced inspection technology, advanced processing technology, etc. (2) Innovation: The object of remanufacturing is retired products. Different types of waste products, different usage environments, and different failure modes require remanufacturing to innovate on the basis of traditional manufacturing, continuously adopting new methods and new equipment, presenting dynamic characteristics, to solve the problem of products facing elimination due to performance lag. (3) Reliability: The basic requirement of remanufacturing is to comprehensively restore the performance of no longer used waste products. It is also a batch production method with industrialized scale, and has a sound quality assurance system. According to Chinese regulations, enterprises engaged in remanufacturing must obtain certification, and remanufactured products sold must have clear identification. China (will also) promulgate and implement various remanufacturing standards to enable remanufactured products to be designed and manufactured according to relevant standards. These measures have played a promoting and supervisory role in ensuring the quality of remanufactured products.

(4) Economy: Remanufacturing involves the reuse of several parts of waste (or scrapped) products, reducing the amount of waste, largely preserving the residual value in waste parts, reducing various pollutions in the process of raw material and new product production, and protecting the environment, thereby reducing processing costs. This not only extends the service life of products but also indirectly saves resources, and has certain economic benefits for both producers and consumers.

For hydraulic cylinders, from the perspective of product quality characteristics (generally including product function, technical performance, greenness, economy, etc), remanufacturing of waste hydraulic cylinders such as those for construction machinery, hydraulic support columns, jacks, and proportional/servo control hydraulic cylinders should have a relatively broad prospect.

For the key areas of remanufacturing industry development, further reference can be made to the "Opinions on Promoting the Development of Remanufacturing Industry" (Development and Reform Commission and Environmental Resources Department [2010] No. 991).
6.2 General Technical Requirements for Hydraulic Cylinder and Parts Remanufacturing
1. General Provisions

items: The remanufacturing of waste hydraulic cylinders should comply with relevant regulations on resource utilization, environmental protection, and related standards of China.
After remanufacturing, the quality characteristics and safety performance of waste hydraulic cylinders should not be lower than those of prototype new products.
The basic process flow of waste hydraulic cylinder remanufacturing is shown in Figure 6-1.
Waste hydraulic cylinders and their parts after and/or before disassembly should be cleaned.
Waste hydraulic cylinders and their parts after disassembly and cleaning should be evaluated for remanufacturability and classified.
Remanufacturable waste hydraulic cylinders should be designed for remanufacturing, including formulating remanufacturing technical solutions and implementation technical basis.
Remanufactured hydraulic cylinders should pass product performance testing before leaving the factory.
Remanufactured hydraulic cylinders must clearly indicate remanufacturing identification, which should comply with the provisions of GB/T 27611.
The packaging and random technical documents of remanufactured hydraulic cylinders should be implemented according to the requirements of prototype new products.

sections.text: In GB/T 27611-2011, the general requirements for remanufactured products are: Based on the corresponding new product testing methods, the quality, safety, performance, environmental protection, and other indicators of remanufactured products should not be lower than the relevant standard requirements of prototype products.

2. General Technical Requirements
(1) Preliminary Inspection of Used Hydraulic Cylinders

items: Used hydraulic cylinders should be preliminarily inspected before remanufacturing to determine whether they meet the requirements for remanufacturing.
For used hydraulic cylinders preliminarily judged to have remanufacturing value, further remanufacturing evaluation should be conducted after disassembly or cleaning.

sections.text: (2) Disassembly of Used Hydraulic Cylinders

items: The structure and condition of used hydraulic cylinders should be confirmed before disassembly, and different disassembly schemes should be selected accordingly.

Used hydraulic cylinders should generally be disassembled to the smallest indivisible unit. During the disassembly process, damage to parts should be minimized as much as possible, but seals should all be scrapped.

sections.text: (3) Cleaning of Cylinder Parts

items: Disassembled cylinder parts should be classified and treated, and appropriate cleaning methods should be selected for cylinder parts with different physical shapes and chemical properties.
After cleaning, cylinder parts should be free of dirt and residual cleaning solution to prevent rust.
Different dirt should be treated using appropriate methods to avoid secondary damage and meet China's environmental protection requirements.
The treatment of waste generated during the cleaning process should meet China's environmental protection requirements.

sections.text: (4) Inspection and Classification of Parts

items: Cleaned cylinder parts should be inspected and classified, generally divided into three categories: parts for direct use, parts for remanufacturing, and parts to be scrapped.
Corresponding inspection records should be made for inspected cylinder parts and they should be classified and stored.
Necessary protective measures should be taken during storage, and the storage and disposal of scrapped parts should comply with relevant laws, regulations, and standards of China.

sections.text: (5) Evaluation of Remanufacturability

items: Based on performance testing and condition index analysis of used hydraulic cylinders and their parts, remanufacturability should be evaluated by comprehensively considering factors such as technology, economy, environment, and resources.

sections.text: 2) The evaluation generally includes failure analysis of used hydraulic cylinders and their parts, remaining life evaluation, environmental impact analysis, resource utilization and cost analysis, energy efficiency analysis, etc.
(6) Remanufacturing Design

items: Combined with the results of remanufacturability evaluation and the requirements for remanufacturing hydraulic cylinders, technical schemes and process schemes for remanufacturing hydraulic cylinders should be designed.
Design documents should meet the needs of production, inspection, and management of remanufactured hydraulic cylinders.

sections.text: (7) Remanufacturing Processing

items: The processing process should strictly follow the drawings and technical documents for remanufacturing design.
Appropriate repair technology should be selected according to the characteristics and damage degree of remanufacturable parts.
Repaired and processed remanufacturable parts should meet or exceed the quality and performance requirements of prototype new products.
Remanufacturable parts should be inspected and accepted by process. Only after passing the inspection of the previous process can they be transferred to the next process for production.
For cylinder parts processed by size repair method, the main matching dimensions after processing should comply with the drawings and technical requirements.
For cylinder parts processed by group matching, matching marks should be provided.

sections.text: (8) Remanufacturing Assembly

items: Remanufacturing assembly should refer to the assembly requirements of prototype new products and relevant regulations.
The assembly environment, such as temperature, humidity, dust level, lighting, vibration prevention, etc., must comply with relevant regulations.
Cylinder parts (including new parts) must pass inspection before assembly.
The remanufacturing assembly process should be inspected according to process requirements and assembly records should be kept.

sections.text: (9) Identification

items: The identification of remanufactured hydraulic cylinders should comply with relevant laws and regulations of China.

sections.text: In addition to the provisions of the standard, a remanufacturing mark should also be clearly marked on the product, product manual, or product packaging (if applicable). The mark on the remanufactured hydraulic cylinder should be permanently maintained.
2) The identification of the remanufactured hydraulic cylinder should contain at least the following contents:

items: a) Name of the remanufactured hydraulic cylinder.
b) Name of the remanufacturer.
c) Model of the remanufactured hydraulic cylinder.
d) Date of remanufacturing.

sections.text: (10) Quality Assurance and Packaging
1) The quality management of the remanufactured hydraulic cylinder should comply with the provisions of GB/T 3207.
2) The quality inspection of the remanufactured hydraulic cylinder should meet the requirements of the prototype new product or the remanufactured hydraulic cylinder.
3) The quality assurance requirements for the remanufactured hydraulic cylinder should be the same as those for the prototype new product.
4) The factory documents for the remanufactured hydraulic cylinder should include the following contents:

items: a) Certificate of conformity for the remanufactured hydraulic cylinder.
b) User manual for use and maintenance.
c) Warranty card.

sections.text: 5) Necessary measures should be taken for the remanufactured hydraulic cylinder to prevent dust, corrosion, and physical damage.
6) The packaging of the remanufactured hydraulic cylinder should comply with the provisions of standards such as GB/T 191 and GB 6388.
6.3 Guidelines for Engineering Design of Hydraulic Cylinder Remanufacturing

The engineering design of hydraulic cylinder remanufacturing is a process of comprehensive planning of all links, technical units, and resource utilization in the remanufacturing of hydraulic cylinders, including the recycling of waste hydraulic cylinders, remanufacturing production, and remanufacturing market marketing, through the application of scientific decision-making methods and advanced technology, based on the requirements of hydraulic cylinder remanufacturing production, to form the most optimized hydraulic cylinder remanufacturing scheme.

Establishing guidelines for engineering design of hydraulic cylinder remanufacturing can standardize the construction of the hydraulic cylinder remanufacturing production system and the evaluation of production process management, so that hydraulic cylinder remanufacturing production enterprises can optimize the overall design, macro management, and engineering application of hydraulic cylinder remanufacturing production according to standard specifications, promote the best matching and coordination between various systems of hydraulic cylinder remanufacturing production, and realize timely, efficient, economic, and environmentally friendly hydraulic cylinder remanufacturing production. This can achieve the maximization of resource recovery, minimization of environmental load, and optimization of product performance in the entire process of hydraulic cylinder remanufacturing, and provide the optimal hydraulic cylinder remanufacturing production implementation scheme based on current conditions, and propose the most optimized hydraulic cylinder remanufacturing scheme for improvement.
1. Basic Principles
(1) Principle of Whole Process

Design should be oriented towards the entire process of hydraulic cylinder remanufacturing, mainly including the waste hydraulic cylinder recycling stage, remanufacturing production stage, and remanufacturing product marketing service stage, as shown in Figure 6-2.
